title: Late Fees in Wisconsin
bodyText: Wisconsin sets no cap or grace period for late fees, but you may charge one only if the lease specifically provides for it. Before charging a late fee you must apply any rent the tenant prepaid to the rent owed, and you may never charge a fee for not paying a late fee. Keep the fee in line with your real cost of late payment. To be safe, list unpaid late fees in a NONSTANDARD RENTAL PROVISIONS document if you want to deduct them from the security deposit.

title: Late Fees in a Nonpayment Notice
bodyText: For a Wisconsin pay-or-vacate notice, rent expressly includes past-due rent and late fees owed on that past-due rent; the statute does not say other charges count, so treat unpaid non-rent charges as a breach under the notice-to-cure rules rather than adding them to a pay-rent notice. State the amount due carefully: a notice with a wrong amount is still valid unless the error was intentional or the tenant paid or offered what the tenant believed was due. Accepting past-due rent after the notice or after filing does not by itself end an eviction case.

title: Application and Screening Charges
bodyText: The only application charge Wisconsin expressly allows is the actual cost of a consumer credit report, up to $25, and for a nonresident applicant the actual cost of a background check, up to $25. Tell the applicant about the charge before ordering the report and give them a copy. You may not charge for a credit report if the applicant gives you a nationwide report less than 30 days old. Any other money taken to have an application considered is an earnest money deposit that must be refunded or credited under DATCP's rules.

title: Earnest Money (Holding) Deposits
bodyText: Before taking earnest money or a deposit from an applicant, identify the unit or units they are being considered for. Return the full earnest money by the end of the next business day if you reject the applicant, the applicant withdraws before you accept, or you have not approved the application within 3 business days (or a later date the applicant agrees to in writing, no more than 21 days out). If you sign a lease, apply it to rent or the security deposit, or return it. If an approved applicant backs out (and you have not significantly altered the rental terms you disclosed), you may keep only your actual costs and damages, and lost rent only after reasonable efforts to rerent.

title: No Local Rent Control in Wisconsin
bodyText: Wisconsin bars cities, villages, towns and counties from regulating the amount of rent or fees for residential rental units, and from inclusionary zoning. There is no statewide rent cap (whether the emergency price-gouging law reaches rent is unresolved). Limits can still come from your own agreements, such as a subsidy contract or a deal with a housing authority, and you may not raise rent in retaliation.

title: Raising Rent in Wisconsin
bodyText: Wisconsin has no statute setting a notice period for a rent increase. During a fixed-term lease you can raise rent only as the lease itself provides. For a month-to-month tenancy, the safe course is to give written notice of the new rent at least 28 days before the end of a rental period, the same notice that ends a periodic tenancy. You may not raise rent in retaliation for a tenant's good-faith complaint or for exercising a legal right, and a lease that lets you raise rent because a tenant contacted police, health or safety services is void. (Manufactured home community operators follow separate DATCP rules: no increases during the term (with limited exceptions) and 28 days' written notice of changes at renewal.)

title: Algorithmic Rent-Setting
bodyText: Wisconsin has no statute specific to setting rents with pricing software or shared algorithms, but Wisconsin's antitrust law and federal antitrust law both prohibit agreements that restrain trade, so do not share competitors' nonpublic rent data or agree on prices through a common tool.

title: Disclosing Non-Rent Charges
bodyText: When you quote rent to a prospective tenant, you must disclose any non-rent charges that will increase the total the tenant pays during the tenancy, and you may not misstate rent or non-rent charges. Wisconsin has no rule that every fee appear in a single all-in figure, but listing every fee in the lease and in your advertising is the safest way to comply.

title: Receipts for Deposits and Cash Rent
bodyText: Give a written receipt immediately when you accept earnest money or a security deposit, stating what it is and how much. No receipt is needed for a check whose memo describes the payment, unless the tenant asks. If a tenant pays rent in cash, give a written receipt stating the nature and amount of the payment; receipts are not required for rent paid by check.

title: Sales Tax and Rent
bodyText: Wisconsin sales tax applies to furnishing rooms or lodging to transients, meaning people staying for a continuous period of less than one month in a hotel, motel or other furnished accommodations available to the public. Ordinary residential rentals of a month or longer are not taxed. If you rent furnished units for shorter stays, check state and local room-tax rules.

title: Nonresident Landlords Must Name a Wisconsin Agent
bodyText:
If you are not a Wisconsin resident and rent out a home in Wisconsin, you must designate an agent in Wisconsin to accept service of process for actions about the tenancy. The agent must be a Wisconsin resident or a corporation authorized to do business here, and the designation must be in writing and filed with the Department of Financial Institutions.

A corporate landlord's agent is its registered agent. Separately, DATCP requires you to give tenants a Wisconsin address for service, except in an owner-occupied building of 4 or fewer units.

If you own through an out-of-state LLC or corporation, it may not do business in Wisconsin until it registers with the Department of Financial Institutions: an LLC files a foreign registration statement naming a Wisconsin registered agent, and a corporation obtains a certificate of authority. While it does business here unregistered, it may not maintain an eviction or any other action or proceeding in Wisconsin. Its leases and its title to the property stay valid, but for each year it owes the fees it should have paid plus half that amount or $5,000, whichever is less (Wis. Stat. §§ 183.0902, 183.0903, 180.1501, 180.1502).

Owning property, without more, is not doing business, so whether renting it out is depends on the facts; get advice before filing an eviction (Wis. Stat. §§ 183.0905(1)(j), 180.1501(2)(i)).

And whoever you are, a Wisconsin court can hear a claim against you that arises out of a promise to rent, use, own or possess Wisconsin real property, such as a lease (Wis. Stat. § 801.05(6)(a)).

title: Accepting Rent After a Notice
bodyText: In Wisconsin, accepting past-due rent after serving a notice or filing an eviction does not by itself require dismissal, and a past waiver or a custom of accepting late rent is not a defense to eviction or damages. But accepting rent for a period after a lease expires can turn the tenant into a month-to-month (or week-to-week, if rent is weekly) tenant unless you have already started proceedings or the lease provides otherwise. Be clear in writing about what a payment covers.

title: Interest on Unpaid Amounts
bodyText: Wisconsin's legal rate of interest is 5% a year. A higher contractual rate is possible only within the limits of other statutes and only if clearly stated in writing. The clause library does not offer a lease clause charging interest on unpaid rent; a court judgment carries its own interest.

title: Government Shutdowns and Rent
bodyText: Wisconsin has no law delaying rent or evictions for federal employees during a government shutdown. Ordinary notice and eviction rules apply, though a payment plan agreed in writing can avoid a costly eviction.

title: No Security Deposit Cap
bodyText: Wisconsin sets no maximum security deposit for an ordinary rental (manufactured home community site rentals are different: DATCP limits that deposit to 2 months' rent or $750, whichever is less), and cities and counties may not add deposit requirements beyond DATCP's rules. Every payment held as security counts as part of the security deposit, including a pet deposit and any prepaid rent beyond one month.

title: No Interest on Security Deposits
bodyText: Wisconsin does not require landlords to pay interest on security deposits for ordinary residential rentals.

title: Where You Keep the Deposit
bodyText: Wisconsin does not require a separate or escrow account for security deposits. The exception is a landlord who is a Wisconsin real estate licensee: a licensee with an ownership interest must either keep the deposits in a real estate trust account or say in the lease that they are held in an account in the owner's name.

title: Deposits When the Property Is Sold
bodyText: Wisconsin has no statute on transferring security deposits when a rental is sold. The lease and its obligations generally bind the buyer, so transfer the deposits to the buyer at closing and tell tenants in writing within 10 business days who now manages the property and where to send notices (unless the building is owner-occupied with 4 or fewer units).

title: Deposits You Cannot Return
bodyText: Wisconsin has no rule specific to unclaimed security deposits. Deliver or mail the deposit and any withholding statement within 21 days (mailing to the tenant's last-known address is the practical course); you are not in violation solely because the postal service could not deliver it. Money that stays unclaimed may become reportable under Wisconsin's unclaimed property law.

title: Penalties for Deposit Violations
bodyText: A security deposit violation is enforced through Wisconsin's consumer-protection law: a tenant can sue for twice the amount of the loss, plus costs and reasonable attorney fees, and DATCP or a district attorney can seek forfeitures of $100 to $10,000 per violation. Missing the 21-day deadline or withholding for items not allowed can therefore cost far more than the deposit.

title: The NONSTANDARD RENTAL PROVISIONS Document
bodyText: Wisconsin limits what you can deduct from a deposit to tenant damage, unpaid rent, certain unpaid utility charges and municipal permit fees, unless you add other reasons in a separate document titled "NONSTANDARD RENTAL PROVISIONS." Go over each provision with the tenant before signing and have the tenant sign or initial next to each one. You can never deduct for normal wear and tear, and DATCP says routine painting or carpet cleaning without unusual damage is not deductible, and that routine carpet cleaning is not deductible even if the lease requires the tenant to pay for it.

title: Paying the Deposit in Installments
bodyText: Wisconsin neither requires nor forbids letting a tenant pay the security deposit in installments. If you agree to installments, put the schedule in writing and give a receipt for each payment.

title: Deposit Alternatives and Fees in Lieu
bodyText: Wisconsin has no statute on deposit-alternative products or monthly fees in lieu of a deposit. Any payment held as security is a security deposit under DATCP's rules, so a product that is really security must follow the deposit rules.

title: Nonrefundable Deposits and Fees
bodyText: Wisconsin has no category of nonrefundable deposit: anything given as security is a refundable security deposit subject to the 21-day return rules. Money paid to have an application considered is earnest money that must be refunded in the situations DATCP lists. Tell an applicant about a credit-report charge before ordering the report, and disclose any non-rent charge that will increase what the tenant pays during the tenancy whenever you quote rent. Money collected up front to cover a future cost, such as move-out carpet cleaning, is treated by DATCP as part of the security deposit and must be accounted for and refunded.

title: Prepaid Last Month's Rent
bodyText: In Wisconsin, any rent a tenant prepays beyond one month counts as part of the security deposit. You may collect it, but if you still hold more than one month's prepaid rent when the tenant leaves, you must account for it and return it like a security deposit.

title: Check-in Notice and Previous Damage List
bodyText: Before accepting a security deposit, give the tenant written notice that they may inspect the unit and report preexisting damage, and may ask for the list of damages charged to the previous tenant, by a deadline at least 7 days after the tenancy starts. At move-in you must also give a check-in sheet the tenant can return within 7 days. If asked, provide the prior damage list within 30 days or 7 days after you notify the previous tenant of deductions, whichever is later.

title: Returning the Deposit Within 21 Days
bodyText: Deliver or mail the deposit, less lawful deductions, within 21 days. The clock starts on the lease end date if the tenant leaves on time; on the lease end date, or the new tenant's start date if you rerent sooner, if the tenant leaves early; and on the day you learn the tenant has gone if the tenant leaves after the lease ends. If you withhold anything, send an itemized written statement in the same period describing each item and the amount withheld.

title: Tenant Duties Under Wisconsin Law
bodyText: Wisconsin tenants may not make physical changes, including decorating, without your consent, may not use the unit for an unlawful purpose or unreasonably interfere with other occupants, and must comply with any local housing code. If the tenant damages the unit, including through a pest infestation the tenant caused, you may let the tenant repair it or do the work yourself and bill the tenant; your cost is presumed reasonable and may include your own time at a reasonable hourly rate. Where no local housing code applies, the tenant also makes minor repairs to furnished equipment when the cost is small relative to rent.

title: Occupancy Limits and Children
bodyText: Wisconsin sets no statewide persons-per-bedroom limit for rentals. Your occupancy limit may not discriminate based on family status, so do not use it to exclude households with children; following reasonable government occupancy limits is not family-status discrimination. Check local housing codes for floor-area or occupancy rules.

title: Smoking in Rental Housing
bodyText: Wisconsin's smoking ban covers enclosed common areas of multiple-unit residential properties (and reaches tobacco, not cannabis or vaping), and as the person in charge you must make reasonable efforts to stop smoking there. The ban does not reach the inside of a private residence, so smoking inside units is governed by your lease. Wisconsin has no statute on smoke drifting between units.

title: Marijuana in Wisconsin Rentals
bodyText: Possessing THC remains a crime in Wisconsin, and Wisconsin has no law protecting tenants who use marijuana or requiring landlords to allow it. You may prohibit it in the lease. Manufacturing or distributing a controlled substance on or near the premises is drug-related criminal activity for which you may end a tenancy on 5 days' notice without an opportunity to cure; simple use or possession is usually handled as a lease breach (a 5-day notice to remedy, or a 14-day notice for a month-to-month tenant), unless it is criminal activity that threatens other tenants' health, safety or peaceful enjoyment, which also allows a 5-day no-cure notice.

title: Unpaid Municipal Utility Bills
bodyText:
A tenant's unpaid bill to a city, village or town utility (water and sewer, and electric where the statute allows) can become a lien on your property: each October the utility gives notice to the owner or occupant, a 10% penalty is added if not paid by November 1, and unpaid amounts after November 15 go on the tax roll as a special charge.

For water or electric service, you can shift collection toward the tenant by notifying the utility in writing of your name and address and the responsible tenant's name and address (and giving it the lease if asked); when the tenant moves out, give the utility the tenant's forwarding address within 21 days.

Even then, the utility can still put the arrears on your tax bill if it notifies you within 14 days after the tenant's charges become past due; you may, at least 14 days after that notice, ask it to shut off electric service.

You may also ask the utility whether a prospective tenant owes it past-due charges at another address.

title: Utility Accounts and Shutoffs
bodyText:
If gas, electric or water service is measured jointly for 2 or more rental units, the account must be in your name or your managing agent's name.

When a tenant ends service, the utility may hold you responsible unless you name the responsible party, or ask for shutoff within 15 days of its notice and confirm that shutoff will not endanger health or property.

A utility may not require proof of eviction to start service in your name, and a gas or electric utility may not knowingly help a landlord remove a tenant. Cutting off heat, water or electricity to force a tenant out is an unlawful constructive eviction.

title: Separate Electric Meters
bodyText: Each unit in a multi-unit residential building built after March 1, 1980 must have its own electric meter, with limited exceptions in the Public Service Commission's rules. If units or common areas share a meter and the charges are not in the rent, you must tell prospective tenants before signing how the charges will be split.

title: Waterbeds
bodyText: Wisconsin has no statute on waterbeds in rentals. You may restrict them in the lease or require insurance for them.

title: Repair Duties Cannot Be Waived
bodyText: Wisconsin requires you to keep the parts of the property you control in reasonable repair, maintain equipment for services you agreed to provide, make structural repairs, repair furnished plumbing, wiring and equipment (where no local housing code applies), and comply with any local housing code. These duties cannot be waived, and a lease that waives your duty to deliver or maintain a habitable unit is void in its entirety. One tenant's damage does not excuse repairs owed to other tenants.

title: Tenant Remedies for Untenantable Conditions
bodyText: If the unit becomes untenantable from fire, water or other casualty or a health hazard, or you substantially violate your repair duties in a way that materially affects health or safety, the tenant may move out unless you promptly repair (or even if you do, when the repair would impose undue hardship), owes no rent after the unit became untenantable, and gets back rent paid in advance for that period. A tenant who stays has rent reduced to the extent they lose normal use, but may not withhold all rent. Wisconsin has no repair-and-deduct statute, and these remedies do not apply if the tenant caused the condition.

title: Smoke and Carbon Monoxide Detectors
bodyText:
One- and two-unit buildings: you must install a working smoke detector in the basement and on each floor level of each unit (not the attic or storage area), and a carbon monoxide detector in the same places (not the garage) unless the building has no attached garage, no fireplace and no fuel-burning appliance; the tenant maintains the detectors in the unit, but you must fix one within 5 days after a tenant or inspector gives you written notice that it does not work.

Buildings with 3 or more units: you must install and maintain smoke detectors in the basement and at the head of each stairway on each floor, plus one in or within 6 feet of each sleeping area of each unit (not in a kitchen); you maintain common-area detectors and tenants maintain those in their units, subject to the same 5-day repair rule, with forfeitures of up to $50 a day.

Carbon monoxide detectors are required near the sleeping areas of units that contain a fuel-burning appliance; of other units in a building that contains one, such as a central boiler or water heater, unless there is no opening between the appliance and the unit or a detector is installed between them or on the ceiling of the appliance room; of units served by a fuel-burning forced-air furnace; and of units near an attached garage (with listed exceptions, and none at all if every fuel-burning appliance in the building is a warrantied sealed-combustion unit), and you must maintain them and repair or replace one within 5 days after a tenant's written notice.

title: Locks and Rekeying
bodyText: Wisconsin has no general rule requiring you to rekey between tenants or to supply particular locks. The exception: when a tenant gives you a certified copy of a qualifying injunction, release condition or criminal complaint involving domestic abuse, child abuse, sexual assault or stalking, you must change the locks, or let the tenant change them, within 48 hours, at the tenant's cost (if the person named is also a tenant of the unit, only when the document orders that person to stay away from the residence or not to contact the requesting tenant); a tenant you let change the locks must give you a key within a reasonable time.

title: Water Heater Temperature
bodyText: If a unit has its own water heater serving only that unit, set the thermostat no higher than 125 degrees Fahrenheit before each new tenant moves in, or at the lowest setting if that is higher than 125 degrees.

title: Heat
bodyText: Wisconsin has no statewide minimum indoor temperature for rentals, but heat matters three ways: you must disclose before signing if the heating cannot keep all living areas at 67 degrees Fahrenheit or is unsafe; if you agreed to supply heat, you must keep the heating equipment in repair; and a local housing code may set its own standard.

title: Pests, Bed Bugs and Mold
bodyText: Wisconsin has no specific disclosure for bed bugs, other pests or mold. But you must disclose, before signing, conditions you know of or could find by reasonable inspection that are a substantial hazard to the tenant's health or safety, and an infestation or excessive mold is a habitability problem for local inspection programs. If the tenant caused an infestation, the tenant must pay for or carry out the remediation.

title: Radon
bodyText: Wisconsin has no radon testing or disclosure requirement for residential rentals.

title: Lead Paint in Wisconsin Rentals
bodyText: For housing built before 1978 you must give the federal lead disclosure and pamphlet. Wisconsin adds no separate lease disclosure, but its health department and local health officers can order lead hazard reduction when a child is lead poisoned or a hazard is found, and Wisconsin has voluntary certificates of lead-free and lead-safe status. Work that disturbs paint must follow Wisconsin's lead-safe renovation rules, including giving the owner and an adult occupant the Renovate Right pamphlet no more than 60 days before renovation.

title: Drug Lab Contamination
bodyText: Wisconsin has no statute requiring landlords to disclose former methamphetamine labs or other drug contamination. A local ordinance aimed at illegal drug manufacturing can still require landlords to pass on information, and a substantial health hazard must be disclosed before signing.

title: Flood Disclosure
bodyText: Wisconsin requires no flood-zone or flood-history disclosure to residential tenants. Flood disclosures in Wisconsin apply to sellers, not landlords.

title: Questions About the Sex Offender Registry
bodyText: You have no duty to volunteer sex offender registry information. If someone asks you in connection with a rental, you must disclose what you actually know, but you are immune from liability if you promptly give the person written notice that they can get registry information from the Department of Corrections, including the Department's telephone number and internet site.

title: Deaths and Crimes on the Property
bodyText: Wisconsin has no statute requiring landlords to disclose a death, crime or other psychological stigma connected with a rental.

title: Condemned Premises
bodyText: You may not rent or advertise a unit that has been placarded and condemned, or for which you have received a notice of intent to condemn or an order to raze or repair, until all the required repairs are complete. Known uncorrected code violations that threaten health or safety must also be disclosed before signing.

title: Military Installation and Airport Zones
bodyText: Wisconsin requires no disclosure to tenants about nearby military installations or airport zones.

title: Cable and Video Service Access
bodyText: The owner or manager of a multiunit dwelling may not prevent or interfere with a video service provider serving a resident who subscribes. The provider must consult you about attachment points and wiring, install safely with minimal aesthetic impact, and pay for any building repairs its work requires.

title: Disability Accommodations and Modifications
bodyText: You must allow a tenant with a disability to make reasonable modifications at the tenant's expense when needed for full enjoyment of the housing, and, where it is reasonable, you may condition interior modifications on the tenant's agreement to restore the unit at the end of the tenancy, other than reasonable wear and tear. You may not raise the usual security deposit; if needed, you may negotiate reasonable payments into an interest-bearing escrow account, not more than the restoration cost, with the interest going to the tenant. You must also make reasonable accommodations in rules, policies, practices and services unless the accommodation would impose an undue hardship. Assistance animals have their own rules.

title: Tenant's Right to Exclusive Possession
bodyText: Until the lease ends or a periodic tenancy is terminated, and so long as the tenant is not in default, the tenant has the right to exclusive possession of the unit, subject only to your limited entry rights. Wisconsin has no separate statutory covenant of quiet enjoyment for leases.

title: Entering a Tenant's Unit
bodyText: You may enter only to inspect, make repairs, or show the unit to prospective tenants or buyers, at reasonable times and on at least 12 hours' advance notice unless the tenant agrees to less. No notice is needed if the tenant requests or agrees to the entry knowing the time, in a health or safety emergency, or if the tenant is absent and you reasonably believe entry is needed to protect the premises. Always announce yourself before entering. Any other entry right must be in a NONSTANDARD RENTAL PROVISIONS document.

title: Fire Sprinklers and Grills
bodyText: Wisconsin requires no sprinkler disclosure to tenants; sprinkler requirements for buildings come from the state commercial building and fire codes. By statute, those rules must require an automatic sprinkler system or 2-hour fire resistance in every multifamily dwelling with more than 20 units (or above the statute's floor-area limits), a city, village, town or county may set lower thresholds by ordinance, and the state may not require sprinklers in a one- or two-family dwelling. The state fire code also bars storing grill fuel on a balcony in buildings other than one- and two-family dwellings.

title: Pools at Rental Properties
bodyText: A pool or whirlpool serving a housing development, an apartment complex with 3 or more dwelling units, a condominium complex or a housing complex with a homeowners' association is a public pool under DATCP's rules and needs a license and must meet those rules. A pool serving fewer than 3 residences is not.

title: Window Guards
bodyText: Wisconsin has no window-guard or window-fall-prevention requirement for residential rentals.

title: Wisconsin Disclosure Checklist
bodyText:
Before signing and before taking any deposit: give the lease and written rules to review; disclose known uncorrected code violations and listed habitability conditions; disclose if water, heat or electricity is not included in rent and how shared charges are split; tell an applicant about any credit-report or background-check charge before ordering it; disclose non-rent charges with any rent quote; and give the check-in notice before taking a deposit.

At or before signing: name the manager and owner with a Wisconsin service address (not required for an owner-occupied building of 4 or fewer units), and identify any NONSTANDARD RENTAL PROVISIONS document.

In the lease or an addendum: the Notice of Domestic Abuse Protections.

At move-in: the check-in sheet.

If you will not store property left behind: written notice at signing and renewal.

Where they apply: an environmental continuing obligation that tenants must maintain goes in the lease; for registered lead-safe property, the lead-safe pamphlet and hazard-reporting form before the tenancy starts ("Wisconsin Lead Notices"); for an electric cooperative account with a project charge, the agreement notice and recorded notice before signing ("Electric Cooperative Account Charge" clause); in buildings of 5 or more units, the local recycling notice at signing and every six months ("Recycling Notices for 5+ Unit Buildings"); and notice to residents whenever pesticide is applied ("Notice When Pesticides Are Applied").

Federal lead disclosure for pre-1978 housing.

title: Notices for Unpaid Rent
bodyText:
For a month-to-month or week-to-week tenant, a year-to-year tenant, or a lease of one year or less, you may give a 5-day notice to pay or vacate.

A month-to-month tenant in default may instead get a 14-day notice to vacate with no chance to pay. Under a lease of one year or less, or a year-to-year tenancy, if the tenant was given a 5-day notice and then pays late again within one year, a 14-day notice to vacate ends the tenancy.

A lease of more than one year needs a 30-day notice to pay. The notice must be in writing and served by a method the statute allows; a wrong amount does not invalidate it unless it was intentionally wrong or the tenant paid or offered what they believed was due.

title: Notices for Other Lease Violations
bodyText: For a breach other than rent, a tenant under a lease of one year or less, or a year-to-year tenant, gets a 5-day notice to remedy the default or vacate; a tenant is complying if they promptly take reasonable steps to fix it or offer to pay adequate damages. A second breach within a year allows a 14-day notice to vacate with no cure. A month-to-month tenant can be given either the 5-day notice to remedy or a 14-day notice to vacate. Leases over one year need a 30-day notice to comply. Criminal activity and law-enforcement nuisance notices have their own 5-day no-cure rules.

title: Ending a Periodic Tenancy
bodyText: Unless you both agreed on another method or the tenant surrenders the unit, either side can end a month-to-month or other periodic tenancy only by written notice, at the end of a rental period, given at least 28 days before (or one full rental period if rent is paid more often than monthly). The notice must state the intent to end the tenancy and the termination date. A notice with a wrong date is generally effective on the first date that would have been proper. If a periodic tenant moves out without notice and stops paying, the tenancy ends as if notice had been given on the day you learn they left.

title: How to Serve a Notice
No Just-Cause Requirement
bodyText: Wisconsin does not require a reason to end a periodic tenancy with proper notice or to decline to renew a lease (manufactured home community operators are different: they may end or refuse to renew a resident's tenancy only on listed grounds, including other good cause). But you may not end or refuse to renew a tenancy in retaliation or for a discriminatory reason, a lease that lets you do so because the tenant called police, health or safety services is void in its entirety, and a tenant has a defense if you knew or should have known the tenant is a victim and the eviction is based on conduct related to domestic abuse, sexual assault or stalking by a non-guest or a guest they have excluded. Cities, villages, towns and counties may not impose eviction moratoriums.

title: The Wisconsin Eviction Process
bodyText: After the notice period ends, you file a small claims eviction. The summons return date is 5 to 25 days after issuance (at least 20 days for a nonresident), and if the tenant appears and contests, a trial must be held within 30 days after the return date. If you win, the court orders judgment and a writ of restitution, which only the sheriff executes; a writ received by the sheriff more than 30 days after issuance cannot be executed. Either side may demand a jury by the time issue is joined, and appeals must be started within 15 days. Accepting rent after filing does not by itself require dismissal. The court must pause the case for up to 10 working days if the tenant applies for emergency assistance before a writ is issued.

title: Eviction Records on the Court Website
bodyText: Wisconsin has no statute for sealing eviction records, but since July 1, 2025 the courts keep the files of eviction cases with no money judgment for only 2 years after the final order or judgment, or 10 years if a writ of restitution was granted; cases with a money judgment are kept 20 years. The public court website must show an eviction case for at least 10 years if a writ was granted and at least 2 years if it was dismissed with no money judgment docketed. Cities may not restrict your use of court records in screening.

title: Delays in an Eviction
bodyText: A Wisconsin court must pause an eviction case if the tenant applies for emergency assistance, until eligibility is decided and any payment arrives, for no more than 10 working days and not after the writ issues. At judgment, the court may stay the writ for up to 30 days for hardship, conditioned on the tenant paying all rent due and the value of occupancy during the stay. Service members' dependents on state active duty and foreclosed homeowners have separate stays.

title: No Self-Help Evictions
bodyText: You may not lock out, remove, or constructively evict a tenant, for example by shutting off heat, water or electricity, other than through a court eviction. A lease that authorizes eviction without a court is void in its entirety. Only the sheriff executes a writ of restitution.

title: Retaliation
bodyText: You may not raise rent, cut services, sue for possession, refuse to renew, or threaten any of these because a tenant complained in good faith to an elected official or a local housing code agency (DATCP's rule covers reports to any government agency), complained to you about repairs or code violations, or exercised a legal right; DATCP also protects tenants who join or organize a tenants' union. You may still evict for unpaid rent, the protection does not cover complaints about defects the tenant caused, and the tenant must show the action would not have happened but for the protected conduct. A lease that lets you take these steps because a tenant called police, health or safety services is void.

title: Property Left Behind
bodyText: If you give written notice at signing and at each renewal that you will not store items left behind, you may treat property left after move-out, or after an eviction if you tell the sheriff you will handle the property, as abandoned and dispose of it as you see fit, except that prescription medication and medical equipment must be held 7 days, and manufactured homes, mobile homes and titled vehicles need advance notice to the tenant and any known secured party. Without that notice you must follow the older 2009 version of the statute. Property left by a trespasser must be held 7 days.

title: Property After an Eviction
bodyText: When the sheriff executes a writ, the sheriff removes the tenant and, unless you choose otherwise, removes the tenant's property. You may have to advance the removal cost, which is added to the judgment; storage after the sheriff delivers the property to safekeeping is the tenant's expense. As an alternative, when delivering the writ you may tell the sheriff that you will remove and store or dispose of the property yourself under the abandoned-property statute; if you did not give the will-not-store notice, you must then follow the 2009 version of that statute.

title: Holdover Damages
bodyText: If a tenant stays without your consent after the lease ends, after a termination notice, or after an agreed termination, you may recover your actual damages, and at minimum twice the daily rental value for each day they stay (rental value is at least the rent last payable). Wisconsin sets that minimum by statute, so the lease does not need its own holdover rate.

title: Duty to Rerent
bodyText: If a tenant leaves early or is evicted, you can recover rent and damages only after crediting what you could earn by reasonable efforts to rerent, meaning the steps you would normally take under local practice. You may also recover reasonable listing and advertising costs. A lease that accelerates rent on default or waives your duty to mitigate is void in its entirety.

title: Attorney Fees and Costs
bodyText: A Wisconsin lease may not require the tenant to pay your attorney fees or costs for any dispute; a lease that does is void in its entirety. Fees that pass your collection or notice-service costs on to the tenant are risky because they may be treated the same way, so the clause library does not include them. You can recover only the costs and fees a court awards by statute, which in an eviction is $10 plus the statutory amount on any damages recovered. When suing over a worthless check, a separate statute allows exemplary damages and reasonable attorney fees, together capped at $500 per check.

title: Lease Terms That Void the Whole Lease
bodyText: A Wisconsin residential lease is void and unenforceable in its entirety if it: lets you raise rent, cut services, evict or refuse to renew, or threaten to, because the tenant called police, health or safety services; allows eviction without a court; accelerates rent or waives your duty to mitigate; requires the tenant to pay your attorney fees or costs; allows confession of judgment; says you are not liable for your own negligence; makes the tenant liable for injuries beyond their control or for damage from natural disasters or people other than the tenant and the tenant's guests or invitees; waives your duty to keep the unit habitable; allows ending a tenancy based solely on a crime of which the tenant or someone lawfully living with them was the victim; or allows termination for a crime committed in relation to the rental property unless the lease includes the Notice of Domestic Abuse Protections.

title: DATCP Enforcement and Double Damages
bodyText: DATCP's residential rental rules are orders under Wisconsin's trade-practices law. A tenant who suffers a money loss because you violated them, including the deposit, disclosure and prohibited-term rules, can recover twice the loss plus costs and reasonable attorney fees, and the State can seek forfeitures. The tenant must show the violation actually caused a money loss. In 2026 the Wisconsin Supreme Court held that the Consumer Act's debt-collection prohibitions do not govern a residential lease with rent payable monthly; for other payment arrangements, get advice before collecting arrears.

title: Jury Trials in Evictions
bodyText: In a Wisconsin eviction either side may demand a jury, by filing a written demand and paying the fee at or before joinder of issue; otherwise the right is waived. Wisconsin's constitution lets a jury be waived 'in the manner prescribed by law', which the state supreme court has said is not limited to statutes. No Wisconsin statute addresses a lease jury waiver and its enforceability is unsettled, so the clause library does not include one.

title: No Landlord Lien on Tenant Property
bodyText: Wisconsin abolished the landlord's right to seize a tenant's property for rent. You have no lien on or right to hold a tenant's property except under specific statutes or an express agreement, and DATCP requires that agreement to be signed or initialed by the tenant at the initial lease in a separate document titled "NONSTANDARD RENTAL PROVISION" that you discuss with the tenant before signing. The clause library does not offer such an agreement.

title: Domestic Abuse, Sexual Assault and Stalking
bodyText: A tenant facing an imminent threat of serious physical harm, or who is a victim of sexual assault, may end the tenancy by written notice with a certified copy of a qualifying injunction, release condition or criminal complaint, and owes no rent after the end of the month following the later of the notice or move-out, subject to your duty to rerent. You may end the tenancy of an offending tenant who threatens another tenant, on a 5-day written notice, if the offending tenant is named in such an order or complaint. Every lease must include the Notice of Domestic Abuse Protections.

title: Victim Status and Evictions
bodyText: Status as a victim of domestic abuse, sexual assault or stalking is a protected class in Wisconsin housing. A tenant has a defense to eviction if you knew or should have known they were a victim and the eviction is based on that abuse by a non-guest, or by a guest they sought an injunction against or told you in writing, after receiving a notice, will no longer be their guest. Cities may not charge fees for police calls about these crimes.

title: When a Tenant Dies
bodyText: When a residential tenant dies, the tenancy ends 60 days after you learn of the death or at the end of the lease term, whichever is earlier; a periodic tenancy ends 60 days after you learn of it. The estate owes no rent after that, subject to your duty to rerent. Any other adult tenant remains liable. You may not contact the tenant's family members to collect rent they do not owe.

title: Service Members
bodyText: Besides the federal Servicemembers Civil Relief Act, Wisconsin protects members of the Wisconsin National Guard or state defense force ordered to state active duty for 30 days or more. A member who signed a lease before entering state active duty may end it by written notice delivered personally or by first-class mail; for monthly rent, termination is effective 30 days after the next rent due date. Evicting the family of a member on state active duty from a dwelling whose rent does not exceed the federal limit requires a court order, and on the member's application the court must stay the case for up to 90 days unless the member's ability to pay is not materially affected.

title: When Tenants May End a Lease Early
bodyText: Wisconsin lets a tenant end a lease early only in specific situations: a threat of serious physical harm or sexual assault with qualifying court papers, the tenant's death, state active military duty (plus federal military protections), and an untenantable unit you do not promptly repair, or whose repair would impose undue hardship. Otherwise a tenant who leaves early remains liable for rent, reduced by what you can recover by reasonable efforts to rerent.

title: Criminal Activity and Nuisance Terminations
bodyText:
You may end a tenancy on a 5-day written notice, without a chance to cure, if the tenant, a household member or a guest engages in criminal activity threatening other tenants, neighbors or you and your staff, or in drug manufacturing or distribution on or near the premises.

The notice must state its basis, describe the activity, its date and the people involved, tell the tenant they may seek help from a lawyer, a volunteer legal clinic or a tenant resource center, and state their right to contest the allegations in court.

No arrest or conviction is needed, but the rule does not apply to a tenant who is the victim.

A property owner may also give a 5-day notice to vacate after police or the district attorney give written notice that a drug or criminal-gang nuisance exists in the unit or was caused by the tenant on the owner's property; that notice must state its basis and the tenant's right to contest the termination in an eviction action.

A lease that allows termination for a crime committed in relation to the rental property is void in its entirety unless it includes the Notice of Domestic Abuse Protections.

title: Condominium Conversions
bodyText: Before converting a residential building to condominiums, you must give each tenant written notice. For 60 days after delivery, the tenant has the first right to buy their unit if it is offered for sale, and for 120 days the tenant cannot be required to vacate unless they breach the lease or fail to pay rent. A tenant may waive these rights in writing.

title: Foreclosure and Tenants
bodyText: A residential tenant may not be named as a defendant in a Wisconsin foreclosure unless the tenant has a lien or ownership interest. If a tenant is later evicted because a foreclosure sale ended the tenancy, the eviction complaint must say so. Federal law may give tenants additional notice rights after foreclosure.

title: Squatters and Unauthorized Occupants
bodyText: Wisconsin has no special fast-track for removing squatters from a rental; someone who is not a tenant can be removed through police if the circumstances meet the criminal-trespass standard, or through an eviction action, which may be brought against any person not entitled to possession. Property a trespasser leaves must be held 7 days before you dispose of it.

title: Automatic Renewal Notices
bodyText: An automatic renewal clause can't be enforced against a tenant unless you give separate written notice calling attention to it. Wisconsin's statute counts the 15-to-30-day window back from the tenant's deadline to give notice of nonrenewal; DATCP's rule counts it back from the renewal's effective date. Send the notice in both windows, or one notice that falls within both, and serve it by a method the statute allows.

title: Tenancies at Will
bodyText: A tenant at will holds with your permission without a lease and without periodic rent. A tenancy at will, like a periodic tenancy, ends only by 28 days' written notice unless the parties agreed otherwise. A tenant at will may not assign or sublet without your consent.

title: Subletting and Assignment
bodyText: A tenant at will or a periodic tenant (week-to-week, month-to-month, or any period shorter than year-to-year) needs your consent to sublet or assign. Any other tenant may transfer unless the lease expressly restricts it, so state the restriction in the lease. If the lease restricts transfer, consenting to one transfer is not consent to later ones, and the original tenant stays liable unless you release them.

title: No Waiver of Collection Exemptions
bodyText: A lease cannot waive a tenant's exemptions of personal property from collection: in Wisconsin a contractual waiver of those exemption rights made before judgment is void. The debtor must claim an exemption at seizure or within a reasonable time after, before the property is sold.

title: Showing the Lease and Rules Before Signing
bodyText: A written lease and any written rules must be given to a prospective tenant to review before the lease is signed and before you accept any earnest money or security deposit. Give the tenant copies when the lease is signed. If the lease provides for it, copies may be delivered electronically.

title: When a Lease Must Be in Writing
bodyText: A lease for more than one year must be in writing and signed, stating the rent, the start and end dates and the premises. If a tenant moves in under an unenforceable longer lease and pays monthly rent, they become a month-to-month tenant. An agreement to end a lease more than one year early must be in writing signed by both parties.

title: Changes in Ownership or Management
bodyText: When the person who collects rent and manages the property, or the owner or service address you disclosed, changes, mail or deliver written notice to tenants within 10 business days. (This does not apply to an owner-occupied building of 4 or fewer units.) A buyer takes over the lease obligations, and the seller stays liable unless released.

title: Local Rental Inspections
bodyText: Wisconsin limits local rental inspections: a city, village, town or county may inspect on a complaint, under state or federal law, or through a district-based inspection program, and may charge inspection fees only within statutory caps (which may rise yearly by inflation or 2 percent), with no program-inspection fee if no habitability violation is found or one is corrected within the period allowed. A program may not inspect a property less than 8 years old, and a property with no violation, or a corrected one, may not be reinspected under the program for at least 5 years. Local rules also cannot add security-deposit or move-in or move-out inspection requirements.

title: Local Rental Registration
bodyText: Wisconsin bars local rental licensing and certification. A municipality may require only a simple registration listing one owner or contact person's name, address, phone number and email, and outside Milwaukee may charge only a one-time fee reflecting actual costs, up to $10 per building, plus up to $10 per building to register a change of ownership, management or contact information. No local occupancy or transfer-of-tenancy fee is allowed. State business registration is a separate matter: an out-of-state LLC or corporation that does business in Wisconsin must register with the Department of Financial Institutions and may not maintain an eviction until it does (Wis. Stat. §§ 183.0902, 180.1502; see "Nonresident Landlords Must Name a Wisconsin Agent").

title: Tenants' Right to Call for Help
bodyText: A lease that lets you raise rent, cut services, evict, refuse to renew, or threaten to, because a tenant contacted police, health or safety services is void in its entirety, and acting that way invites a retaliation claim. Cities, villages, towns and counties may not charge an owner or occupant a fee for the owner's or occupant's own police call about domestic abuse, sexual assault or stalking.

title: No State Lease Form
bodyText: Wisconsin does not prescribe a residential lease form. The only lease text it prescribes word for word is the Notice of Domestic Abuse Protections, and Wisconsin sets no type-size or formatting rules for residential leases (a manufactured home community site agreement must set out its terms conspicuously). Some optional terms must sit in a separate document with a set title: NONSTANDARD RENTAL PROVISIONS (deposit withholding, entry) or NONSTANDARD RENTAL PROVISION (a lien or right to hold the tenant's property).

title: Requiring Renter's Insurance
bodyText: Wisconsin has no statute limiting a landlord's requirement that tenants carry renter's insurance. A lease may require it.

title: Wisconsin Fair Housing
bodyText: Wisconsin's fair housing law covers more classes than federal law: sex, race, color, sexual orientation, disability, religion, national origin, marital status, family status, status as a victim of domestic abuse, sexual assault or stalking, lawful source of income, age (18 and older) and ancestry. A narrow exemption covers choosing someone to share your own unit. Violations can bring damages and forfeitures up to $10,000 for a first offense.

title: Lawful Source of Income
bodyText: Wisconsin prohibits discrimination based on lawful source of income. Apply the same screening standards to income from wages, benefits, support or other lawful sources.

title: What You May Ask Applicants
bodyText: You may ask applicants about family status and marital, financial and business status, but not about race, color, disability, sexual orientation, ancestry, national origin, religion, creed, or status as a victim of domestic abuse, sexual assault or stalking. You may ask about age only to verify eligibility for qualifying senior housing. You may not ask for or require access to, or the login for, an applicant's social media or other personal internet accounts (public information is fine).

title: Tenant Screening in Wisconsin
bodyText: Cities and counties may not restrict your use of an applicant's income, occupation, rental history, credit information, public court records including arrests and convictions, or identity documents, or limit how far back you look. State and federal fair housing law still apply, so use consistent written criteria. A landlord who gives a reference about a former tenant at the request of a prospective landlord or the tenant is presumed to act in good faith and is immune from civil liability unless they knowingly gave false information or acted maliciously.

title: Immigration Status
bodyText: Wisconsin has no statute on landlords asking about or acting on a tenant's immigration status. National origin and ancestry are protected classes, so apply any identity or status checks uniformly.

title: Foreign Ownership of Land
bodyText: Nonresident aliens, foreign corporations, and entities more than 20% foreign-owned may not hold more than 640 acres of Wisconsin land, with exceptions. The limit rarely affects residential landlords, and Wisconsin has no separate foreign-adversary rule for rental property.

title: Assistance Animals in Wisconsin
bodyText: You may not refuse to rent, evict, charge extra or harass a tenant with a disability because of a trained assistance animal or an emotional support animal. For a trained assistance animal you may ask for reliable documentation unless the disability is readily apparent or known (and only for the need if just the disability is apparent). For an emotional support animal you may ask for documentation of the disability and the need from a licensed health professional. You may deny an animal if the documentation is not provided, if the specific animal poses a direct threat or would cause substantial physical damage that cannot be reduced, or if it would impose an undue financial and administrative burden or fundamentally alter your services. The tenant is responsible for sanitation and damage caused by the animal.

title: False Emotional Support Animal Claims
bodyText: A person who intentionally misrepresents a disability or the need for an emotional support animal to obtain housing, and a health professional who misrepresents a patient's need, faces a forfeiture of at least $500 in Wisconsin.

title: Pet Deposits and Pet Rent
bodyText: Wisconsin has no cap on pet rent or pet deposits. A pet deposit is part of the security deposit and must be returned or accounted for under the same 21-day rules, and pet damage is deductible as tenant damage. You may not charge any pet fee or deposit for an assistance animal.

title: Towing From Rental Property
bodyText: You may have an unauthorized vehicle towed from your property right away if the area is properly posted with clearly visible notice that it is private property and unauthorized vehicles may be removed; otherwise only after a parking citation or a repossession judgment. Only a towing service may remove it, at your request, and the towing service must first notify local police. DOT caps the basic tow at $150 and storage at $25 a day outdoors or $35 indoors, with limited extra charges for special equipment or long travel and a municipal service fee of up to $35 (plus a matching towing-service fee). A vehicle reported stolen may not be towed this way. Booting is allowed only where a local ordinance permits it.

title: Electric Vehicle Charging
bodyText: Wisconsin has no law giving tenants a right to install electric vehicle chargers or requiring landlords to provide them.

title: Firearms and Rental Property
bodyText: Wisconsin's trespass law lets the occupant, not a landlord who has leased the residence, bar visitors from carrying firearms inside a residence. In a multi-unit building, the owner may bar non-residents from carrying firearms in common areas and grounds, except parking areas where the firearm stays in a vehicle. No Wisconsin statute addresses lease clauses restricting tenants' own firearms.

title: Flags and Political Signs
bodyText: Wisconsin's flag protections bind homeowners' associations, housing cooperatives and condominium associations, not landlords. Political signs are different: during an election campaign period a tenant has the same right as an owner to put a sign with a political message in any area the tenant occupies exclusively, and the lease decides which areas are exclusive. Local governments may regulate only the size, shape or placement of signs for safety, and signs over 11 square feet. Your lease may set reasonable rules for common areas and for other displays.

title: Solar Devices
bodyText: Wisconsin limits local governments' restrictions on solar energy systems, but has no law giving tenants a right to install solar devices, including portable balcony units.

title: Cameras and Doorbell Cameras
bodyText: Wisconsin has no statute on tenants installing doorbell or security cameras. Criminal law forbids installing a surveillance device, including a peephole, in a private place to observe a person nude without consent, so keep landlord cameras to common areas.

title: Repairing Damage the Tenant Caused, and Being Reimbursed
bodyText:
If the tenant's acts or inaction damage the premises, including by an insect or other pest infestation, Wisconsin lets you choose who fixes it: you may let the tenant repair or remediate the damage and redecorate, or do the work yourself and require the tenant to reimburse your reasonable cost (Wis. Stat. § 704.07(3)(a)).

Your cost is presumed reasonable unless the tenant proves otherwise, and it can include materials or labor you provide yourself and, at a reasonable hourly rate, your time buying or providing materials, supervising your agent or hiring a contractor. The statute calls this a reimbursement; it does not make the cost rent.

When the tenant moves out you may withhold from the security deposit amounts reasonably necessary for tenant damage, waste or neglect, but never for normal wear and tear (Wis. Stat. § 704.28(1)(a), (3)). Entering the unit to do the work follows Wisconsin's ordinary entry rules ("Entering a Tenant's Unit").

These rules apply to every residential tenancy whatever the lease says: an agreement to waive them is void (Wis. Stat. § 704.07(1)).

title: No Blank-Space Rule
bodyText: Wisconsin imposes no statutory requirement that a written residential lease have every blank completed. Several Wisconsin rules still turn on what the lease and the papers given at signing say: the domestic abuse protections notice must be in the lease or an addendum (Wis. Stat. § 704.14); the names and addresses of the person who manages the premises and of the owner or person authorized to accept legal papers must be disclosed in writing at or before signing (Wis. Admin. Code ATCP § 134.04(1)); and a written lease and rules must be shown to the prospective tenant before signing and before any earnest money or deposit is accepted, with copies given at signing (Wis. Admin. Code ATCP § 134.03(1)). A blank left in a required statement is a missing statement. Fill in every blank before signing, as good practice rather than a statutory duty.

title: Arbitration Clauses in Wisconsin Leases
bodyText: Wisconsin's Arbitration Act makes a written agreement to arbitrate future disputes arising out of a contract valid and enforceable, subject to the ordinary defenses to any contract, and it does not exclude residential leases (Wis. Stat. § 788.01). No Wisconsin statute or rule specifically allows or bans arbitration in an ordinary residential lease; the one narrow rule is for a home sold in foreclosure and leased back to the homeowner, where a contract term requiring arbitration of disputes under the foreclosure-reconveyance statute is void at the homeowner's option (Wis. Stat. § 846.40(7); "Rules a Lease Cannot Change"). The library does not offer an arbitration clause for Wisconsin, because of the risk if a court disagrees with you: a residential lease is void and unenforceable in its entirety if it authorizes removing a tenant other than by a court eviction under chapter 799, or requires the tenant to pay your attorney fees or costs in any legal action or dispute under the lease (Wis. Stat. § 704.44(2m), (4m)), and DATCP's rule repeating that list (Wis. Admin. Code ATCP § 134.08(2), (4)) lets a tenant with a money loss from a violation recover twice the loss plus costs and attorney fees (Wis. Stat. § 100.20(5); "DATCP Enforcement and Double Damages"). Whether an arbitration clause, or an arbitrator's award of costs or fees under one, counts as such a term has not been decided in any Wisconsin source the library has read; a clause that reached eviction would plainly be one. If you still want to arbitrate money disputes, have a lawyer draft your own clause, keep possession (eviction) actions in court, and do not make the tenant pay your arbitration costs or fees. A search of the Wisconsin Statutes, Administrative Code, Constitution and 2025 session laws found no other rule on arbitration of residential tenancy disputes.

title: Penalties for Using a Prohibited Lease Term
bodyText: Wisconsin has no separate penalty for knowingly or deliberately using a lease that contains a prohibited term; the void-lease rule, the tenant's double-damages claim and the civil forfeiture below do not depend on whether you knew. A lease that contains any term on Wisconsin's prohibited list is void and unenforceable in its entirety, not just the term (see "Lease Terms That Void the Whole Lease"). The same list is a DATCP trade-practice rule, so a tenant who suffers a money loss because of the violation can sue for twice the loss plus costs and reasonable attorney fees; DATCP or a district attorney can seek a civil forfeiture of $100 to $10,000 for each violation; and a person who refuses, neglects or fails to obey the rule can be fined $25 to $5,000 or jailed for up to one year for each offense (see "DATCP Enforcement and Double Damages"). A search of the Wisconsin Statutes, Administrative Code, Constitution and 2025 session laws found no added penalty keyed to knowing use. Have every lease form checked against the list before you use it.

title: Rules a Lease Cannot Change
bodyText: Wisconsin has no single rule declaring every tenant right non-waivable. Many of the default rules in Wisconsin's landlord-tenant chapter (for example on access, alterations, fixtures and property left behind) apply only when there is no inconsistent provision in a writing signed by both you and the tenant. But a lease cannot change these: (1) the prohibited terms, any one of which makes the whole lease void and unenforceable (see "Lease Terms That Void the Whole Lease"); (2) your repair and untenantability duties and the tenant's remedies, which an agreement may not waive (see "Repair Duties Cannot Be Waived"); (3) the statutory termination notices, which a lease for one year or less or a periodic tenancy may not shorten or replace, and the criminal-activity termination rule, which no lease may vary (see "Waiving or Shortening Termination Notices"); and (4) DATCP's residential rental rules (deposits, check-in, disclosures, entry, late fees, no self-help), which bind you whatever the lease says except where a rule itself allows a separate signed NONSTANDARD RENTAL PROVISIONS document. A search of the Wisconsin Statutes, Administrative Code, Constitution and 2025 session laws found no general non-waiver rule beyond these. One narrower rule covers a home sold and leased back: when a homeowner in foreclosure sells to a foreclosure purchaser who leases or conveys an interest back, any waiver of the statute regulating that deal (written contract, cancellation right, fair lease terms, a stay of eviction) is void, except a waiver of the 5-day cancellation right in a handwritten statement signed by all parties holding title, allowed only when the foreclosure sale is within those 5 business days.

title: Repair Duties a Lease Cannot Modify
bodyText: A Wisconsin lease cannot waive or shift your repair duties. Any agreement to waive them, including one in the lease, is void, and a lease that waives your duty to deliver or maintain a habitable unit is void and unenforceable in its entirety (see "Repair Duties Cannot Be Waived"). There is no exception for a property without a well or utility water. What the lease can do: (1) say which services you furnish, since your duty to repair service equipment covers services you have expressly or impliedly agreed to furnish, such as heat and water; (2) give the tenant ordinary maintenance tasks, such as lawn care, snow removal or keeping the unit clean (see "Tenant Maintenance & Cleanliness" clause, "Landscaping & Irrigation" clause, "Snow Removal" clause); and (3) require routine cleaning, which a 2013 attorney general opinion (OAG 4-13, as summarized in the annotation to Wis. Stat. § 704.07; opinion not read) says is not a repair duty. Separately, where no local housing code applies, the law itself makes the tenant keep furnished plumbing, wiring and equipment in working order when the repair cost is minor in relation to the rent, and the tenant pays for damage the tenant causes.

title: When a Repair Problem Is Serious Enough
bodyText: Wisconsin ties a tenant's statutory repair remedies to how serious the problem is. The tenant may move out, unless you promptly repair, only if the unit becomes untenantable from fire, water or other casualty or a condition hazardous to health, or if your failure to make repairs is a substantial violation materially affecting the tenant's health or safety. Rent is reduced only while a condition materially affects health or safety or substantially affects the use and occupancy of the unit, and only to the extent the tenant loses normal use; the tenant may not withhold all rent while staying. A local ordinance on rent abatement must use the same threshold. Lesser defects are still your duty to repair, but they do not trigger these remedies (see "Tenant Remedies for Untenantable Conditions"). Before signing, you must disclose uncorrected code violations you know of that present a significant threat to health or safety, and listed conditions such as no hot or cold running water (see "Code Violations and Habitability Conditions" clause).

title: No Habitability Presumptions
bodyText: Wisconsin has no statute or administrative rule creating a presumption about habitability, such as a presumption that a unit with a code violation is uninhabitable, that a delay in repairs is bad faith, or that an action you take after a tenant's complaint is retaliatory. A search of the Wisconsin Statutes, Administrative Code, Constitution and 2025 session laws found none. Under Wis. Stat. § 704.45 a tenant who claims retaliation must show by a preponderance of the evidence that your action would not have happened but for the retaliation; the separate DATCP retaliation rule (Wis. Admin. Code ATCP § 134.09(5)) states no presumption either (see "Retaliation"). The presumptions that do exist in Wisconsin rental law run the other way: when the tenant damages the unit and you do the repair, your cost is presumed reasonable unless the tenant proves otherwise, and a tenant who signs or initials a NONSTANDARD RENTAL PROVISIONS item is rebuttably presumed to have agreed to it. One lead rule works both against and for you: failing to comply on time with a lead hazard reduction order is prima facie evidence of negligence in a later injury suit, and complying creates a rebuttable presumption that you used reasonable care as to lead poisoning or exposure caused after compliance by the hazards the order covered (for interim control work, only while that work is reasonably expected to reduce or eliminate the hazard) (Wis. Stat. § 254.166(2m); "Lead Paint in Wisconsin Rentals").

title: No Required Habitability Statement in the Lease
bodyText: Wisconsin has no statute or administrative rule requiring the lease itself to state that you will deliver or keep the unit fit for habitation, and none prescribing habitability wording. A search of the Wisconsin Statutes, Administrative Code, Constitution and 2025 session laws found none. Your repair duties apply whether or not the lease mentions them, and a lease that waives them is void in its entirety (see "Repair Duties Cannot Be Waived"). The library's "Maintenance & Repairs" clause states your duties in the statute's terms. What Wisconsin does require in writing before the lease is signed is the disclosure of known code violations and listed habitability conditions ("Code Violations and Habitability Conditions" clause).

title: Liability Waivers and Indemnity Clauses
bodyText: A Wisconsin lease is void and unenforceable in its entirety if it says you are not liable for property damage or personal injury caused by your own negligent acts or omissions, or if it makes the tenant liable for personal injury from causes clearly beyond the tenant's control or for property damage caused by natural disasters or by anyone other than the tenant and the tenant's guests or invitees (see "Lease Terms That Void the Whole Lease"). So do not use a general release, "hold harmless" or broad indemnity clause; a damage clause should reach only the tenant and the tenant's guests or invitees (see "Damage Caused by Tenant" clause). These bars do not affect ordinary maintenance the tenant owes by law or takes on in a written agreement (see "Tenant Maintenance & Cleanliness" clause). The statutes do give you narrow protections of their own: immunity when you answer a sex offender registry question and give the written notice the statute describes (see "Sex Offender Registry Notice" clause); immunity for a good-faith tenancy reference to another landlord; no civil liability for changing locks as the domestic abuse lock-change rule requires; for the owner of a one- or two-family dwelling or of an apartment or other residential building, no liability for a false carbon monoxide alarm from a reasonably maintained detector or for a detector failure caused by someone else's tampering or by a faulty detector you reasonably maintained; and no liability under the personal Internet account law for not asking a tenant or applicant for access to their accounts. A search of the Wisconsin Statutes, Administrative Code, Constitution and 2025 session laws found no other landlord immunity, for example for removing a tenant's property or acting on a police notice.

title: No Eviction Fees or Penalties in the Lease
bodyText: Do not put an eviction fee, filing or service charge, or a fixed penalty for being evicted in a Wisconsin lease. A lease that requires the tenant to pay attorney fees or costs you incur in any legal action or dispute arising under the lease is void and unenforceable in its entirety, not just the term; you may recover only the costs and attorney fees a court awards under the court-costs statutes (see "Attorney Fees and Costs"). A lease is also void if it lets you bring an eviction because the tenant contacted police, health or safety services, or allows eviction other than through the courts (see "Lease Terms That Void the Whole Lease"). Wisconsin has no statute on penalty or liquidated-damages clauses in a residential lease; the statutory limits on agreed damages apply to sales and leases of goods, not housing. Apart from DATCP's rule on late rent fees and penalties (Wis. Admin. Code ATCP § 134.09(8); see "Late Fees in Wisconsin"), a search of the Wisconsin Statutes, Administrative Code, Constitution and 2025 session laws found no other rule. Cautious course: charge nothing for an eviction except what the court awards.

title: Waiving or Shortening Termination Notices
bodyText: Whether a Wisconsin lease can change the statutory termination notices depends on the tenancy. Lease of one year or less, year-to-year and month-to-month or week-to-week tenancies: a lease provision for termination contrary to the statute (for example a shorter pay-or-vacate notice, no chance to cure, or a waiver of notice) is invalid; use the statutory 5-day and 14-day notices (see "Notices for Unpaid Rent", "Notices for Other Lease Violations"). Lease for more than one year: the statute's 30-day notice to pay or comply applies, but a lease provision for termination contrary to it is not invalidated by that rule. Any lease: a provision contrary to the criminal-activity termination rule is invalid. Ending a periodic tenancy without breach takes written notice of at least 28 days (or one rent period if rent is paid more often than monthly) at the end of a rental period, unless the parties expressly agreed on another method and the agreement is proved by clear and convincing evidence; the library keeps the statutory notice (see "Ending a Month-to-Month Tenancy" clause, "Ending a Periodic Tenancy"). Notices are given by the methods the statute lists.

title: Confession of Judgment
bodyText: A Wisconsin lease may not authorize you or your agent to confess judgment against the tenant (that is, to have a judgment entered without a lawsuit the tenant can defend) in any action arising under the lease. A lease that does is void and unenforceable in its entirety, not just the term (see "Lease Terms That Void the Whole Lease"). Separately, any authorization in a note signed after June 18, 1972 for a creditor to confess judgment for the debtor is void, so a separate promissory note signed by the tenant that authorizes a confessed judgment does not work either; treat any other confession document signed with the lease as part of the rental agreement, which would make the whole lease void. To recover possession or money, file an eviction or small claims action and let the tenant answer (see "The Wisconsin Eviction Process").

title: Shortening the Notice for Showings
bodyText: In Wisconsin you may enter to show the unit to prospective tenants or buyers only at reasonable times and on at least 12 hours' advance notice (see "Entering a Tenant's Unit"). Notice can be shorter in only two ways that the lease body cannot supply: the tenant, when told of a particular proposed entry, agrees to a shorter time, or the tenant, knowing the proposed time, asks for or agrees to the entry in advance. A standing agreement for shorter showing notice (for example same-day showings during the last month of the lease) is entry under circumstances the rule does not otherwise allow, so it must go in a separate written document entitled "NONSTANDARD RENTAL PROVISIONS" that you specifically identify and discuss with the tenant before the lease is signed; use the library's entry document for it ("Nonstandard Rental Provisions: Entry" clause) and have the tenant sign or initial it. Whatever the notice, announce yourself before entering and identify yourself on request.

title: Deposit Rights a Lease Cannot Waive
bodyText: Wisconsin has no statute or rule stating in so many words that a tenant cannot waive deposit rights, and a search of the Wisconsin Statutes, Administrative Code, Constitution and 2025 session laws found none. In practice the lease cannot change them. You may withhold only for the reasons the law lists (tenant damage, waste or neglect; unpaid rent; unpaid landlord-provided or municipal utility charges; unpaid municipal permit fees), plus reasons in a separate signed NONSTANDARD RENTAL PROVISIONS document, and never for normal wear and tear (see "Use of Security Deposit" clause, "Nonstandard Rental Provisions: Deposit Withholding" clause). You must return the balance, with a written statement of anything withheld, within 21 days after the dates the law sets (see "Returning the Deposit Within 21 Days"). So a lease clause saying the tenant forfeits the deposit (for example for leaving early or for not giving notice), or agreeing to a longer return period, does not work, and acting on it is a DATCP violation for which the tenant can recover twice the loss plus costs and attorney fees (see "Penalties for Deposit Violations"). Accepting part of an earnest money refund does not waive the rest.

title: Casualty and Mitigation Rules Cannot Be Waived
bodyText:
Neither of Wisconsin's rules on these points can be waived by the lease.

Mitigation: if a tenant leaves early or is evicted, you recover rent and damages only after crediting what reasonable efforts to rerent would bring, and a lease that accelerates rent on default or otherwise waives your duty to mitigate is void and unenforceable in its entirety (see "Duty to Rerent"). You may still agree in advance to accept a surrender for a fixed fee (see "Early Termination" clause).

Casualty: the tenant's rights when fire, water or other casualty makes the unit untenantable (to move out unless you promptly repair, to stop owing rent, to a rent reduction while staying), which do not apply when the tenant's own negligence or improper use caused the damage, are part of the repair statute, and any agreement to waive that statute in a residential tenancy, including one in the lease, is void; Wisconsin has no rule letting an express written agreement override them (see "Tenant Remedies for Untenantable Conditions").

The statute gives the landlord no casualty termination right of its own, so the library offers one by contract (see "Landlord Termination After Casualty" clause); it does not take away any tenant right.

title: Liquidated Damages in a Lease
bodyText:
Apart from late rent fees, Wisconsin has no statute or administrative rule governing liquidated damages in a residential lease.

A late rent fee or late rent penalty, a sum agreed in advance for paying late, may be charged only if the rental agreement specifically provides it, only after applying any rent prepayments, and never on an unpaid late fee (Wis. Admin. Code ATCP § 134.09(8); see "Late Fees in Wisconsin").

For any other agreed damages, a search of the Wisconsin Statutes, Administrative Code, Constitution and 2025 session laws found none; the statutory limits on agreed damages apply to sales and leases of goods, not housing.

What the statutes do limit: a lease that accelerates rent on default or waives your duty to mitigate is void in its entirety (see "Duty to Rerent"); a lease may not make the tenant pay your attorney fees or costs (see "Attorney Fees and Costs"); deductions from the deposit are limited to the listed reasons and actual, reasonable amounts (see "Use of Security Deposit" clause); and from an earnest money deposit you may keep only your actual costs and damages, with lost rent only after reasonable efforts to mitigate.

Cautious course: recover actual damages, and use a fixed sum only as the price of an agreed early termination (see "Early Termination" clause), not as a penalty for breach.

title: Tenant Remedies When You Breach
bodyText: Wisconsin's main remedies for a tenant when you fail to keep the unit in repair are in the repair statute: if the unit becomes untenantable, or a substantial violation of your repair duties materially affects health or safety, the tenant may move out unless you promptly repair and owes no further rent, or may stay and pay reduced rent, but may not withhold all rent while staying (see "Tenant Remedies for Untenantable Conditions"). A tenant who loses money because you violated DATCP's rental rules (for example failing to deliver possession on time, entering unlawfully, or mishandling the deposit) can sue for twice the loss plus costs and attorney fees (see "DATCP Enforcement and Double Damages").
