Two health statutes add more: if a court finds you have not complied with a state lead hazard order for a rented dwelling, it may order the occupants to pay their rent into escrow until you comply; and a tenant of a building that violates the municipal building code's health or safety provisions or a local health order may petition the municipality, and if it does not act within 20 days sue directly, to have the property declared a nuisance or health hazard, which can lead to a court-appointed receiver collecting the rents (this does not apply to an owner-occupied one- or two-family dwelling). Bringing that action is not just cause for eviction. Wisconsin has no repair-and-deduct statute and no general rent-withholding or escrow statute; a search of the Wisconsin Statutes, Administrative Code, Constitution and 2025 session laws found none.

title: How Tenants Request Repairs
bodyText: Wisconsin has no statute or administrative rule setting a form or method for a tenant's ordinary repair request, and none saying that a lease accepting oral or electronic requests waives anything. A search of the Wisconsin Statutes, Administrative Code, Constitution and 2025 session laws found none. Your repair duties run whether or not a request is written, and the tenant's untenantability remedies and the retaliation protection for complaining to you about repairs do not depend on written notice, so a lease term requiring written requests helps you keep records but does not cut down those rights. The library's "Maintenance & Repairs" clause asks the tenant to notify you promptly in writing. One written-notice rule does exist: when an occupant gives you written notice that a smoke detector or carbon monoxide detector is not working (or a CO detector has been removed by someone else), you must fix it within 5 days after receiving the notice (see "Smoke and Carbon Monoxide Detectors").

title: No Right to End a Lease Over Repair Costs
bodyText: Wisconsin has no statute or administrative rule letting a landlord (or a tenant) end a residential lease because repairs would cost more than a set amount or a share of the property's value. A search of the Wisconsin Statutes, Administrative Code, Constitution and 2025 session laws found none. Your repair duties continue whatever they cost, and a lease that waives them is void in its entirety (see "Repair Duties Cannot Be Waived"). After a fire, water or other casualty the tenant may move out if you do not promptly repair, and the library offers a landlord termination right after a casualty you did not cause, by contract (see "Landlord Termination After Casualty" clause). The repair-cost thresholds that do exist serve municipal raze orders: a finding by the municipal governing body, building inspector or designated officer that repairs would cost more than 50 percent of the building's (adjusted) assessed value makes repair presumed unreasonable, which supports an order to raze, not a lease termination.

title: Shifting Maintenance Duties to the Tenant
bodyText:
Wisconsin does not let a residential lease shift any of your statutory repair duties to the tenant: keeping the areas you control and the equipment for services you agreed to furnish in reasonable repair, making necessary structural repairs, repairing furnished plumbing, wiring and equipment (where no local housing code applies), and complying with any local housing code.

An agreement to waive them, including one in the lease, is void, and a lease that waives your duty to maintain the premises is void in its entirety (see "Repair Duties Cannot Be Waived"). There is no listed duty a lease may shift on a precondition, and no rule that consideration or a conspicuous writing makes a shift valid.

What a lease can do is give the tenant ordinary maintenance by agreement, such as cleaning, lawn care and snow removal (see "Tenant Maintenance & Cleanliness" clause, "Landscaping & Irrigation" clause, "Snow Removal" clause); no separate writing or consideration is required for that.

By statute, where no local housing code applies, the tenant also keeps furnished plumbing, wiring and equipment in working order when the repair cost is minor in relation to the rent, and the tenant pays for damage the tenant causes (see "Damage Caused by Tenant" clause). For broader repair agreements see "Agreements for the Tenant to Do Repairs".

title: Agreements for the Tenant to Do Repairs
bodyText: Wisconsin lets a tenant take on ordinary maintenance in the lease or another written agreement, and sets no special formalities for it: no separate document, no stated consideration, no good-faith recital, and no single-family limit. A search of the Wisconsin Statutes, Administrative Code, Constitution and 2025 session laws found no such requirement. The library covers the common tasks with "Tenant Maintenance & Cleanliness", "Landscaping & Irrigation" and "Snow Removal". The library does not offer a broader agreement for the tenant to do repairs or remodeling, because Wisconsin voids any agreement to waive your statutory repair duties, and a lease that waives your duty to maintain the premises is void in its entirety; a list of tenant repairs that strays into those duties (structural repairs, the equipment for services you furnish, furnished plumbing, wiring and appliances, or anything a local housing code requires of you) could put the whole lease at risk (see "Shifting Maintenance Duties to the Tenant"). You may add your own written agreement for specific minor tasks (for example replacing furnace filters or light bulbs), stating what you give in return, that the work does not reduce your repair duties, and that parts the tenant installs at your cost belong to you and may not be removed.

title: Unconscionable Lease Terms
bodyText: Wisconsin has no unconscionability statute written for residential leases. Its unconscionability statutes cover sales of goods, leases of goods, consumer credit transactions and time-shares; the Consumer Act's version applies to consumer credit transactions, and in 2026 the Wisconsin Supreme Court held that the Act's debt-collection rules do not govern a residential lease with rent payable monthly (see "DATCP Enforcement and Double Damages"). A court may still apply the general contract doctrine of unconscionability to a lease term, which requires both an absence of meaningful choice and terms unreasonably favorable to one side. In practice the specific rules do the work: Wisconsin's list of prohibited terms voids the whole lease (see "Lease Terms That Void the Whole Lease"), and the repair duties cannot be waived. No statute declares any particular lease clause enforceable notwithstanding unconscionability, and none lets a court revise a running lease because it has become excessively burdensome. A search of the Wisconsin Statutes, Administrative Code, Constitution and 2025 session laws found no other rule.

title: Carpet Cleaning at Move-Out
bodyText: A Wisconsin lease may require the tenant to pay for routine carpet cleaning, and doing so does not void the lease, because routine cleaning is not one of your statutory repair duties. But DATCP's rules sharply limit how you collect it: you may not collect the cost in advance (any prepayment beyond one month's rent is a security deposit), and you may not deduct routine carpet cleaning or routine painting from the security deposit, since the deposit cannot be withheld for normal wear and tear, even by a NONSTANDARD RENTAL PROVISIONS document. You may deduct cleaning or repair costs only for damage beyond normal wear and tear that the tenant caused (see "Use of Security Deposit" clause). Because a lease clause could be enforced only by a separate claim against the tenant, and a clause that routes the cost through the deposit would violate the DATCP rules, the library does not offer a carpet-cleaning clause; you may add your own that requires cleaning without touching the deposit or collecting in advance.

title: When the 21 Days Start
bodyText:
In Wisconsin the 21 days to return a security deposit (with a written statement of anything withheld) do not depend on a surrender notice, key return or forwarding address from the tenant.

They run from: the end of the lease, if the tenant moves out on that date; the end of the lease or, if you rerent sooner, the start of the new tenancy, if the tenant moves out or is evicted early; or the date you learn the tenant has moved out or the sheriff has removed the tenant, if the tenant leaves after the lease ends (see "Returning the Deposit Within 21 Days").

Wisconsin has no statute or rule conditioning the return on the tenant's notice or forwarding address.

Ask for a forwarding address and mail the deposit to it or to the last address you have: if you otherwise comply, you are not in violation just because the post office cannot deliver it.

title: No Posted Deposit Standards Rule
bodyText: Wisconsin has no statute or administrative rule requiring you to post or hand out the standards you use to set security deposits, however many units you have, and no cap on the amount (see "No Security Deposit Cap"). What does limit you is fair housing law: you may not exact different or more stringent price, terms or conditions for renting because of a protected characteristic (see "Wisconsin Fair Housing"), and when a tenant with a disability makes a reasonable modification at the tenant's expense, you may not increase the customarily required security deposit (you may negotiate a restoration escrow instead, within the statute's limits). Apply one written deposit policy to everyone in the same situation. Milwaukee, Madison and other municipalities may have their own rules.

title: No Fast-Track Deposit Procedure
bodyText: Wisconsin has no statute or administrative rule setting a fast-track procedure for security deposit disputes, or letting you settle the deposit early, for example when a tenant abandons the unit. A search of the Wisconsin Statutes, Administrative Code, Constitution and 2025 session laws found none. The ordinary rule applies: return the deposit, less only lawful deductions and with a written statement of each, within 21 days after the date the law sets; if the tenant leaves early, that date is the end of the lease or, if you rerent sooner, the start of the new tenancy (see "Returning the Deposit Within 21 Days", "When the 21 Days Start"). If you and the tenant disagree, either side may sue in small claims court. The lease may let you send the deposit accounting and refund documents electronically (see "Electronic Delivery of Documents" clause).

title: No Separate Notice for Nonrefundable Fees
bodyText: Wisconsin has no statute or administrative rule requiring a nonrefundable fee to be disclosed in a separate notice or document, or separately signed or initialed. A search of the Wisconsin Statutes, Administrative Code, Constitution and 2025 session laws found none. The question rarely arises, because Wisconsin has no nonrefundable deposit: everything a tenant pays as security for the tenant's obligations, and any rent prepaid beyond one month, is a refundable security deposit subject to the 21-day return rules, whatever you call it (see "Nonrefundable Deposits and Fees"). A true fee for a service may be charged, but you must disclose every non-rent charge whenever you quote the rent, and you may not misstate it (see "Disclosing Non-Rent Charges"); listing each fee in the lease is the safe course. The separate documents Wisconsin does require are NONSTANDARD RENTAL PROVISIONS (for example for deposit deductions beyond the standard list), not fee notices.

title: Penalties for Skipping the Check-In Notice
bodyText:
Before you accept a security deposit, Wisconsin requires you to tell the tenant in writing that, by a deadline at least 7 days after the tenancy starts, the tenant may inspect the unit and report preexisting damage and may ask for a list of the physical damages or defects charged to the previous tenant's deposit (see "Check-in and Preexisting Damage" clause, "Check-in Notice and Previous Damage List").

Wisconsin attaches no special penalty to leaving that notice out: you do not lose the right to withhold from the deposit, and there is no fixed multiple of the deposit.

But the notice is a DATCP rule, so a tenant who loses money because of the violation can sue for twice the loss plus costs and reasonable attorney fees, and DATCP or a district attorney can seek forfeitures (see "Penalties for Deposit Violations").

Without the notice and the tenant's report, you will also find it harder to prove that damage happened during the tenancy.

A city, village, town or county may not add deposit or move-in or move-out inspection requirements beyond DATCP's rules.

title: Fees for Services You Do Not Provide
bodyText: Wisconsin has no statute or administrative rule that specifically bars charging a fee for a service you do not provide (for example an amenity, trash pickup or a utility the tenant does not receive). A search of the Wisconsin Statutes, Administrative Code, Constitution and 2025 session laws found none. DATCP's rules cover most of the ground anyway: to induce someone to rent, you may not misrepresent the amount of rent or non-rent charges or fail to disclose, whenever you quote rent, any non-rent charge that will increase the total the tenant pays (see "Disclosing Non-Rent Charges"); a promise before the lease to clean, repair or improve must be in writing with a completion date, and you must keep it (see "Promised Cleaning and Repairs" clause); and utility charges not included in rent must be disclosed before the lease, with the basis for allocating them where units are not separately metered (see "Utility Charge Allocation" clause). A tenant who loses money because you violated these rules can sue for twice the loss plus costs and attorney fees. Charge only for services you actually provide, and stop the charge if the service ends.

title: No Late Fee Cap
bodyText: Wisconsin has no statute or administrative rule capping a residential late fee, as a percentage of rent or a dollar amount, and none setting a grace period; the same is true for manufactured home communities. A search of the Wisconsin Statutes, Administrative Code, Constitution and 2025 session laws found none. The limits that apply are DATCP's: you may charge a late fee only as the lease specifically provides, you must first apply any prepaid rent, and you may never charge a fee for not paying a late fee (see "Late Fees in Wisconsin"). The only figure in the statutes is for self-service storage space, not dwellings: a late fee of $20 or 20 percent of the monthly rent, whichever is greater, is presumed reasonable there. Keep a residential late fee in line with your real cost of late payment.

title: Statutory Caps on Charges
bodyText: Wisconsin caps very few of the charges an ordinary residential landlord makes. The caps that apply: an applicant may be charged only your actual cost, up to $25, for a nationwide consumer credit report, and nothing if the applicant gives you one less than 30 days old; a nonresident applicant may be charged your actual cost, up to $25, for a background check (see "Application and Screening Charges"); unpaid amounts carry the 5 percent legal rate of interest unless a higher lawful rate is clearly stated in writing (see "Interest on Unpaid Amounts"); and towing from your lot is limited to the state's towing and storage rates (see "Towing From Rental Property"). There is no cap on the security deposit, late fees, returned-payment fees, pet deposits or pet rent, or other fees for an ordinary rental (see "No Security Deposit Cap", "No Late Fee Cap", "Pet Deposits and Pet Rent"), and no rent control (see "No Local Rent Control in Wisconsin"). Manufactured home community site rentals are different: the security deposit may not exceed 2 months' rent or $750, whichever is less, and a water and sewer deposit may not exceed $75. A search of the Wisconsin Statutes, Administrative Code, Constitution and 2025 session laws found no other cap.

title: Listing Fees in the Lease
bodyText:
Wisconsin has no statute or administrative rule requiring an ordinary residential lease to list every fee, to show rent and fees as one total, or to give notice before adding a fee, and none capping a markup on a third-party-billed service or barring a common-area fee.

But you must disclose every non-rent charge that will increase what the tenant pays whenever you quote the rent, you may not misstate any charge, you may charge a late fee only as the lease specifically provides, and utility charges not included in rent must be disclosed before the lease (see "Disclosing Non-Rent Charges", "Utility Charge Allocation" clause).

Use the library's "Fees and Charges" list to put every fee in the lease.

Manufactured home community site leases are different: DATCP requires the rental agreement to state each charge not included in the rent.

title: Government Fines and Tenants
bodyText:
Wisconsin has no statute or administrative rule that bars you from passing a government fine or nuisance abatement cost on to a tenant, or that limits a pass-through to fines the tenant caused.

So a pass-through exists only if the lease creates it: use the optional "Fines Caused by Tenant" clause, which reaches only violations by the tenant or the tenant's guests or invitees and never a fine for a condition you are responsible for, such as a repair you must make.

You may not deduct the amount from the security deposit unless a signed NONSTANDARD RENTAL PROVISIONS document allows it, and the clause must never pass on your attorney fees or legal costs, which would void the lease.

Condominium association fines work differently: when a tenant's violation of the declaration, bylaws or association rules results in a fine, the tenant is liable for it, and you as unit owner become liable only if the association gives the required notice and the tenant does not pay within 30 days (see "Homeowner / Condominium Association Compliance" clause).

title: Passing Local Rental Fees to Tenants
bodyText: State law sharply limits the fees a Wisconsin city, village, town or county may charge you as a rental owner. Outside a 1st class city (Milwaukee), registration may carry only a one-time fee reflecting actual cost, up to $10 per building, and a one-time fee of up to $10 for registering a change of ownership, management or contact information. Inspection fees under a local inspection program are capped and may be charged only when a habitability violation is found and not corrected in time, and no local government may impose an occupancy or transfer-of-tenancy fee. No Wisconsin statute bars or authorizes passing such a fee on to a tenant. The library does not offer a pass-through clause: the registration fees are small and one-time, and an inspection fee arises only when an inspector finds a habitability violation at your property (for a program inspection, only one you did not correct in time), which should not be shifted to the tenant. If you choose to pass on a registration fee, you may add your own clause stating the amount, and you must disclose it whenever you quote the rent (see "Disclosing Non-Rent Charges"). Manufactured home community site tenants are different: a monthly municipal permit fee is assessed against the tenant, and an unpaid one may be withheld from the deposit when you become liable for it. Milwaukee, Madison and other municipalities may have their own rules.

title: Charging for Detector Tampering
bodyText:
Wisconsin has no statute or administrative rule setting or permitting a fee you may charge a tenant for removing, disabling or tampering with a smoke or carbon monoxide detector.

Tampering with an installed carbon monoxide detector is itself prohibited for any person, and in a residential building it can be punished by a fine of up to $10,000 or up to 9 months in jail for a first offense and is a felony after that.

The library's "Smoke and Carbon Monoxide Detectors" clause has the tenant agree not to tamper with any detector.

If the tenant or the tenant's guests or invitees damage or disable a detector, you may recover your reasonable actual cost of repair or replacement as tenant-caused damage (see "Damage Caused by Tenant" clause); the library does not offer a fixed tampering fee, because a set charge not tied to actual cost may be attacked as a penalty and no statute authorizes one.

title: Collection Fees
bodyText: Do not put a collection fee in a Wisconsin lease. A lease that requires the tenant to pay attorney fees or costs you incur in any legal action or dispute arising under the lease is void and unenforceable in its entirety, and a fee for collecting past-due rent or damages, including a percentage charged by a collection agency, is the kind of cost that rule reaches; the library therefore offers no collection-fee clause (see "Attorney Fees and Costs"). You may recover the costs and fees a court awards. If you hand a debt to a collection agency, the agency must be licensed by the state; the cautious course is that the agency collects only what the tenant owes you, plus what a court awards. In 2026 the Wisconsin Supreme Court held that the Consumer Act's debt-collection prohibitions do not govern a residential lease with rent payable monthly (see "DATCP Enforcement and Double Damages").

title: Fees for Preparing or Serving Notices
bodyText: Do not charge a Wisconsin tenant a fee for preparing or serving a notice, such as a 5-day notice to pay rent or vacate or a notice to remedy a breach. No Wisconsin statute or rule authorizes such a fee, and a lease that requires the tenant to pay costs you incur in any legal action or dispute arising under the lease is void and unenforceable in its entirety; a notice that starts the eviction process is part of that dispute, so the library offers no notice-service-fee clause (see "Attorney Fees and Costs", "No Eviction Fees or Penalties in the Lease"). A notice fee could also make the amount in a pay-or-vacate notice wrong: Wisconsin keeps a notice with an incorrect amount valid unless the misstatement is intentional or the tenant paid or offered what the tenant believes is due, but an amount you added on purpose puts the notice at risk. A search of the Wisconsin Statutes, Administrative Code, Constitution and 2025 session laws found no rule authorizing the fee. You recover only the costs a court awards.

title: Late Fees for Subsidized Tenants
bodyText: Wisconsin has no statute or administrative rule setting a special late-fee rule for tenants whose rent is partly paid by a subsidy or voucher. A search of the Wisconsin Statutes, Administrative Code, Constitution and 2025 session laws found none. Wisconsin's general late-fee rules apply: a late fee only as the lease specifically provides, prepaid rent applied first, and no fee on a late fee (see "Late Fees in Wisconsin"). For a Housing Choice Voucher (Section 8) tenancy, federal rules add that the family is not responsible for the part of the rent covered by the housing assistance payment, and the housing agency's failure to pay is not the tenant's lease violation and is not grounds to end the tenancy during the lease term (see "Federal Rules for a Housing Choice Voucher Lease"). So charge a late fee, if the lease provides one, only on the tenant's own share and only when the tenant's share is late.

title: Passing Tax and Insurance Increases to Tenants
bodyText:
Wisconsin has no statute or administrative rule on lease clauses that pass property tax or insurance increases on to a residential tenant: none requires the clause to state the tenant's exact share, refund an abatement, or limit deposit deductions for it.

So a pass-through exists only if the lease creates it: use the optional "Tax and Insurance Increases" clause, which states the tenant's percentage, requires the bill and calculation, and refunds a share of any reduction, and disclose it whenever you quote the rent (see "Disclosing Non-Rent Charges").

Do not have the tenant pay the property tax bill directly: a tenant who pays the property taxes may recover them from you with interest of 1 percent a month, and may deduct them from rent unless the lease says otherwise.

An unpaid tax share is not one of the standard deposit deductions, so withholding it from the deposit needs a NONSTANDARD RENTAL PROVISIONS document (see "Nonstandard Rental Provisions: Deposit Withholding" clause).

title: No Veterans Rental Incentive
bodyText: Wisconsin has no statute or administrative rule giving landlords a tax credit, fee waiver or other incentive for renting to veterans, and none requiring or regulating a veterans' rent discount or preference in private rental housing. A search of the Wisconsin Statutes, Administrative Code, Constitution and 2025 session laws found none. Wisconsin's veterans housing provisions are of other kinds: veterans housing loans financed through the state housing authority, county veterans housing programs, and public housing authority projects for veterans. If you offer veterans a discount, state it in the lease as a rent concession (see "Rent Concessions" clause), and apply it consistently. Service members have federal and state termination and other rights (see "Service Members").

title: Rent Collection and Repair Duties
bodyText: Wisconsin has no rule like the uniform act's that whoever receives the rent takes on the landlord's repair duties regardless of a lease, assignment, deed or security instrument. A search of the Wisconsin Statutes, Administrative Code, Constitution and 2025 session laws found none. The rules that do apply: your repair duties cannot be waived by any agreement with the tenant (see "Repair Duties Cannot Be Waived"); if you sell or transfer your interest, the lease covenants bind your successor for breaches while the successor holds the interest, and you are not released from your own lease obligations unless the lease or an express release says so (see "Changes in Ownership or Management"); and if you assign the rents to a lender, the lender may collect them after your default without becoming a mortgagee in possession with that liability, a tenant who pays the lender on notice is credited as if paying you, and the assignment does not change the rights and duties between you and the tenant. So you remain responsible for repairs even while a lender collects the rent.

title: Rent Paid in Installments
bodyText:
Wisconsin law lets the lease decide when and how rent is paid; no statute or rule addresses splitting the monthly rent into installments.

You may agree to installments using the optional "Rent Paid in Installments" clause, stating each amount and due date. Each installment is rent due on its date, so a missed one supports the usual 5-day notice to pay or vacate, or a 30-day notice under a lease for more than one year (see "Notices for Unpaid Rent"), and a late fee applies only as the lease specifically provides.

Be careful with a month-to-month tenancy: the period of a periodic tenancy is normally shown by the interval between rent-paying dates, so weekly payments could make it a week-to-week tenancy, which either side can end on notice equal to one week.

State the rent as a monthly amount payable in installments to show you intend a month-to-month tenancy, but know that the notice rule turns on how often rent is payable, so installments due more often than monthly may still allow notice equal to the installment interval; the text does not settle this, so in a month-to-month tenancy offer installments only if you accept that risk.

title: Rent Changes During the Lease Term
bodyText:
In Wisconsin, rent can change during a fixed-term lease only as the lease itself provides.

Use the optional "Scheduled Rent Changes" clause for set increases or an index adjustment, or the optional "Mid-Term Rent Increase" clause for an increase on written notice with a right for the tenant to leave instead (see "Raising Rent in Wisconsin").

Wisconsin has no retaliation safe harbour that depends on such a clause, and no rule measuring your notice against the notice the lease requires of the tenant.

Whatever the lease says, you may not raise rent where the increase would not happen but for retaliation for a tenant's good-faith complaint or exercise of a legal right, and a lease that lets you raise rent because the tenant called police, health or safety services is void in its entirety.

While your unit is the subject of an actual or anticipated nuisance receivership action, you also may not raise that tenant's rent if the tenant shows the increase would not have happened but for the action and that no nuisance was found, that the tenant was found not to cause it, or that the increase is not necessary to abate it (Wis. Stat. § 823.23(4)(b)).

Manufactured home community site rentals follow separate DATCP rules that bar most increases during the term.

title: No Rent Reporting Rules
bodyText: Wisconsin has no statute or administrative rule on rent reporting: nothing requires you to offer positive rent reporting or a tenant to join a reporting program, nothing bars you from reporting on-time or late rent to a credit bureau, and nothing requires advance notice to the tenant before you report. A search of the Wisconsin Statutes, Administrative Code, Constitution and 2025 session laws found none. If you or a service you use reports rent to a consumer reporting agency, federal credit reporting law governs the accuracy of what is reported; report only accurate, undisputed amounts and correct errors promptly. The Wisconsin Consumer Act's collection rules, which include limits on reporting disputed debts, do not govern a residential lease with rent payable monthly (see "DATCP Enforcement and Double Damages").

title: Counterclaims and Rent Payments in an Eviction
bodyText: Wisconsin does not require a tenant to pay rent into court to defend an eviction, to demand a jury, or while the case is pending, and it has no compulsory counterclaim rule. A search of the Wisconsin Statutes, Administrative Code, Constitution and 2025 session laws found none. In an eviction the tenant may answer orally or in writing (in writing if the tenant disputes your title) and may counterclaim; any claim related to the rented property counts as arising from the same transaction, and such a related counterclaim above the small claims limits moves the whole case to regular civil procedure (an unrelated one above the limits is dismissed) (see "The Wisconsin Eviction Process"). Rent payments come in at three later points: a court that stays the writ for hardship, for up to 30 days, must condition the stay on the tenant paying all rent and charges due at judgment plus the reasonable value of occupancy during the stay; a tenant who appeals the judgment for possession and wants the appeal to stop the eviction must file an undertaking guaranteeing rent and other damages while the appeal is pending, payable to you at once on default (see "Delays in an Eviction"); and, separately, a court may order rent paid into escrow when an owner fails to comply with a state lead hazard order (see "Tenant Remedies When You Breach").

title: No Lockouts for Unpaid Rent
bodyText: No. A Wisconsin landlord may not lock out a tenant who is behind on rent, even with advance notice, an opt-in lease clause or a promise of key access on request. You may not exclude, forcibly evict or constructively evict a tenant other than through a court eviction, and a lease that authorizes eviction or exclusion other than by the court eviction procedure is void and unenforceable in its entirety, not just the clause (see "No Self-Help Evictions"). Cutting off or substantially reducing heat, water or electricity to force a tenant out is constructive eviction, and doing it in retaliation is separately prohibited. The route for unpaid rent is a written notice to pay or vacate and, if the tenant does neither, an eviction action; only the sheriff removes a tenant, under a writ of restitution (see "Notices for Unpaid Rent", "The Wisconsin Eviction Process").

title: Rent Certificates and Property Tax in Rent
bodyText: Wisconsin does not require you to tell tenants what part of the rent goes to property tax, in the lease or by an annual statement. The state's homestead credit instead treats a fixed share of rent as property tax (25 percent of rent, or 20 percent if heat is included). But when a tenant claims that credit, the Department of Revenue's rules have the tenant and the landlord complete its "Rent Certificate" form: you fill in the rent paid, subtract the reasonable value of any food, medical or other personal services you provide, and check whether heat was included. You may not charge a fee for supplying the information. If you refuse, the tenant may file with rent receipts and an unsigned certificate marked "Landlord Refuses to Sign", and the department may examine records and require testimony to check the claim. A tenant who pays the property tax bill on your property may recover it from you with interest of 1 percent a month (see "Passing Tax and Insurance Increases to Tenants").

title: Demanding Rent for a Unit With Code Problems
bodyText: Wisconsin has no statute or administrative rule that bars you from demanding or collecting rent, or from serving a notice to pay rent or vacate, only because a unit has code violations or is in poor repair. Narrower rules do cut off or reduce rent. (1) Condemned premises: 'No landlord may rent or advertise for rent any premises which have been placarded and condemned for human habitation' (Wis. Admin. Code ATCP § 134.09(1)), and the same bar covers premises on which a notice of intent to placard and condemn or a raze order has been received, until the required repairs are done ("Condemned Premises"). Under the razing statute, 'Any person who rents, leases or occupies a building which has been condemned for human habitation, occupancy or use under subd. 1. shall be fined not less than $5 nor more than $50' or jailed, for each week (Wis. Stat. § 66.0413(1)(br)2.). (2) Untenantable premises: if the unit becomes untenantable or a substantial repair violation materially affects health or safety and the tenant stays, 'rent abates to the extent the tenant is deprived of the full normal use of the premises' (Wis. Stat. § 704.07(4)); a tenant who justifiably moves out owes no rent after the premises became untenantable, but a tenant who stays may not withhold all rent ("Tenant Remedies for Untenantable Conditions"). (3) Lead orders: if you fail to comply with a lead-hazard order, 'the circuit court may order the occupants of the affected dwelling or premises to withhold rent in escrow until the owner of the dwelling or premises complies with the order' (Wis. Stat. § 254.30(1)(b)). (4) Nuisance receivership: a court-appointed receiver may 'charge and collect rents derived from the residential property' (Wis. Stat. § 823.23(3)(a)1.). Milwaukee, Madison and other municipalities may have their own rules; a local rent-abatement ordinance may allow abatement only for conditions that materially affect health or safety or substantially affect use and occupancy (Wis. Stat. § 704.07(5)).

title: Your Remedies When a Tenancy Ends on Default
bodyText: Once you have ended the tenancy with the notice Wisconsin law requires ("Notices for Unpaid Rent", "Notices for Other Lease Violations"), your remedies are these. Possession: only through a small claims eviction action; eviction actions use the small claims procedure 'regardless of the amount of rent claimed therein' (Wis. Stat. § 799.01(1)(a)), and a lease that authorizes removal other than by judicial eviction is void ("No Self-Help Evictions"). Rent and damages with possession: you 'may join with the claim for restitution of the premises any other claim against the defendant arising out of the defendant’s possession or occupancy of the premises' (Wis. Stat. § 799.40(2)), stated separately in the complaint (Wis. Stat. § 799.41(1)); if you win, the court orders restitution and enters judgment on the joined claim (Wis. Stat. § 799.44(1)). Rent and damages after the tenant leaves or is removed: if the tenant 'is removed for failure to pay rent or any other breach of a lease, the landlord can recover rent and damages except amounts which the landlord could mitigate' (Wis. Stat. § 704.29(1)), and the recovery 'is reduced by the net rent obtainable by reasonable efforts to rerent the premises' (Wis. Stat. § 704.29(2)(b)), plus reasonable listing and advertising costs ("Duty to Rerent"). A lease cannot accelerate the remaining rent or waive mitigation ("Lease Terms That Void the Whole Lease"). A tenant who stays after the termination date owes holdover damages. A money claim alone (for example, rent after the tenant has moved out) uses the small claims procedure where 'the amount claimed is $10,000 or less' for actions begun before January 1, 2027, and '$15,000 or less' for actions begun on or after that date (Wis. Stat. § 799.01(1)(d); 2025 Wis. Act 105 (SB 787)); a larger claim is outside the small claims chapter. Costs and attorney fees come only as a court awards them, never from a lease term ("Attorney Fees and Costs").

title: Who Can Accept Eviction Papers for the Tenant
bodyText: Wisconsin has no statute or administrative rule on a lease naming a person to accept a termination notice or the eviction summons for the tenant. The general rules: in a small claims eviction, the general rules on 'the mode and manner of service of process' apply (Wis. Stat. § 799.12(1)), with personal or substituted service or, where the circuit court's rule allows, mail service, which must be by certified mail in eviction cases (Wis. Stat. § 799.12(2), (3)). Personal jurisdiction may also be obtained by serving 'an agent authorized by appointment or by law to accept service of the summons for the defendant' (Wis. Stat. § 801.11(1)(d)). Whether a term in your own lease counts as such an appointment is not settled by any statute, and a summons served on someone the court finds was not authorized can leave you without a valid judgment, so this library does not offer a clause appointing a person to accept service for the tenant; you may add your own clause, but do not rely on it in place of the usual methods. Termination notices are served by the methods in Wis. Stat. § 704.21 ("How to Serve a Notice"). Two statutes do name an agent. A party to a residential tenancy who is not a Wisconsin resident 'shall designate an agent to accept service of process in this state for an action involving the tenancy', in a writing filed with the department of financial institutions (Wis. Stat. § 704.22(1), (2)); this binds a nonresident tenant as well as a nonresident landlord ("Nonresident Landlords Must Name a Wisconsin Agent"). And a participant in the address confidentiality program 'certifies the department to be the program participant’s designated agent for service of process' (Wis. Stat. § 165.68(3)(b)4.g.), so the Department of Justice may be served for that tenant. A person who has received the participant's notification form may not 'intentionally disclose to another person the actual address of a program participant' (Wis. Stat. § 165.68(5)(c)), while an eviction complaint must identify the real property (Wis. Stat. § 799.41(1)). No statute says how the two fit; before filing against a program participant, ask the clerk of court how to submit the property description so the address is not made public (a participant may ask the clerk to keep records revealing the actual address private, Wis. Stat. § 66.0504(2)(a)), and see "Keeping a Victim's Information and Address Private".

title: No Possession Bond in Wisconsin
bodyText: Wisconsin has no statute or administrative rule providing an end-of-term possession bond, a bond that lets you take possession before judgment, or a confessed judgment for possession. A search of the Wisconsin Statutes, Administrative Code, Constitution and 2025 session laws found none. Possession comes only from a judgment and writ of restitution in a small claims eviction ("The Wisconsin Eviction Process"). Do not put a confessed-judgment or bond-for-possession term in the lease: a residential rental agreement is void and unenforceable if it 'Authorizes the landlord or an agent of the landlord to confess judgment against the tenant in any action arising under the rental agreement' (Wis. Stat. § 704.44(5m); Wis. Admin. Code ATCP § 134.08(5)), or if it 'Authorizes the eviction or exclusion of a tenant from the premises, other than by judicial eviction procedures as provided under ch. 799' (Wis. Stat. § 704.44(2m)); see "Lease Terms That Void the Whole Lease". Bonds appear only after judgment and only by court order: a court that stays the writ for hardship 'may further require the defendant, as a condition of such stay, to give a bond in such amount and with such sureties as the court directs' (Wis. Stat. § 799.44(3)), and a tenant's appeal does not stay the judgment for restitution 'unless the appellant serves and files with the notice of appeal an undertaking to the plaintiff' covering costs and the rent and damages accruing during the appeal (Wis. Stat. § 799.445). A foreclosed homeowner's eviction stay is granted 'without the imposition of a bond' (Wis. Stat. § 846.40(9)(a)).

title: Paying to Stop a Nonpayment Termination
bodyText: A Wisconsin tenant's chance to pay and stay comes during the notice period, not after. Under a 5-day notice to pay or vacate, the tenancy is terminated only 'if the tenant fails to pay accordingly' (Wis. Stat. § 704.17(2)(a); the same words govern month-to-month and week-to-week tenants, Wis. Stat. § 704.17(1p)(a)); under a lease of more than one year, 'all rent due must be paid on or before the date specified in the notice' (Wis. Stat. § 704.17(3)(a)). For these notices 'rent' includes past-due late fees (Wis. Stat. § 704.17(1g)). Some notices give no chance to pay at all (the 14-day notices; "Notices for Unpaid Rent"). Wisconsin has no statute or administrative rule that lets a tenant redeem or reinstate a tenancy by paying after it has been terminated, before judgment or after it, and none that requires special wording before you accept a partial payment. A search of the Wisconsin Statutes, Administrative Code, Constitution and 2025 session laws found none. If you accept money after the notice, the eviction 'may not be dismissed because the landlord accepts past due rent or any other payment from the tenant after serving notice of default or after commencing the action' (Wis. Stat. § 799.40(1m)), and an earlier waiver is no defense ("Accepting Rent After a Notice"); still, say in writing when you accept a payment that it does not reinstate the tenancy, since a landlord who permits the tenant 'to remain in possession contrary to such notice' is treated differently under Wis. Stat. § 704.17(2)(a). Payment can delay possession in two ways: the court must stay the case while an emergency-assistance application is decided, for no more than 10 working days (Wis. Stat. § 799.40(4)(a)), and a hardship stay of the writ of up to 30 days 'shall be conditioned upon the defendant paying all rent or other charges due and unpaid at the entry of judgment' and the value of occupancy during the stay (Wis. Stat. § 799.44(3); "Delays in an Eviction"). Neither restores the tenancy. Federal law may lengthen notice on covered properties ("Federal 30-Day Notice to Vacate for Federally Backed Properties").

title: Default, Forfeiture and the Tenant's Chance to Cure
bodyText: In Wisconsin a tenant's default does not by itself end the tenancy; your written notice under Wis. Stat. § 704.17 does, if the tenant does not comply in time ("Notices for Unpaid Rent", "Notices for Other Lease Violations"). A lease clause that ends or forfeits the tenancy on default some other way does not work in most residential leases: 'provisions in the lease or rental agreement for termination contrary to this section are invalid except in leases for more than one year' (Wis. Stat. § 704.17(5)(a)), and termination terms contrary to the criminal-activity rules are invalid in every lease (Wis. Stat. § 704.17(5)(b)). Once a proper notice expires, 'the tenant is not entitled to possession or occupancy of the premises after the date of termination specified in the notice' (Wis. Stat. § 704.17(4)), but termination does not release the tenant from rent: if the tenant 'is removed for failure to pay rent or any other breach of a lease, the landlord can recover rent and damages' less what you could mitigate, 'unless the landlord has expressly agreed to accept a surrender of the premises and end the tenant’s liability' (Wis. Stat. § 704.29(1); "Duty to Rerent"). The tenant's protection against forfeiture is the cure period in the notice: a tenant is 'deemed to be complying with the notice if promptly upon receipt of such notice the tenant takes reasonable steps to remedy the default and proceeds with reasonable diligence', or offers adequate damages (Wis. Stat. § 704.17(2)(b)), and pays rent by the notice date ("Paying to Stop a Nonpayment Termination"). Wisconsin has no statute or administrative rule giving a court power to relieve a residential tenant from forfeiture after the tenancy is terminated. A search of the Wisconsin Statutes, Administrative Code, Constitution and 2025 session laws found none. The one-year period to pay after judgment in Wis. Stat. § 704.31 applies only to leases of 30 years or more under which the tenant built improvements worth more than $50,000.

title: Late Benefit or Voucher Payments and Eviction
bodyText: Wisconsin has no statute or administrative rule that gives a tenant a defense to a nonpayment eviction, or a continuance, because a social security, other government benefit or rent-subsidy payment arrived late. The nearest rule is the emergency-assistance stay: 'The court shall stay the proceedings in a civil action of eviction if the tenant applies for emergency assistance under s. 49.138, except that no stay may be granted under this paragraph after a writ of restitution has been issued', and the stay 'may not remain in effect for more than 10 working days' (Wis. Stat. § 799.40(4)(a); "Delays in an Eviction"). The usual nonpayment notice rules still apply, and a tenant who pays all rent due by the notice date keeps the tenancy ("Paying to Stop a Nonpayment Termination"). Separately, refusing to rent because a tenant's income comes from a lawful source such as benefits can be housing discrimination ("Lawful Source of Income"), and federally assisted housing has its own program rules.

title: What a Notice to Vacate Can Add
bodyText: Wisconsin has no statute or administrative rule on extra terms in a notice to vacate or a move-out form, and none that bars repairs or alterations to a unit while an ordinary notice to vacate is running. A search of the Wisconsin Statutes, Administrative Code, Constitution and 2025 session laws found none. A notice ending a periodic tenancy needs only to be in writing and 'substantially inform the other party to the landlord-tenant relation of the intent to terminate the tenancy and the date of termination' (Wis. Stat. § 704.19(4)); nonpayment, breach, nuisance and criminal-activity notices have the contents set by Wis. Stat. § 704.17 ("Notices for Unpaid Rent", "Notices for Other Lease Violations", "Criminal Activity and Nuisance Terminations"). A notice is one-sided and cannot add obligations the lease does not contain; put anything new in a separate signed agreement, and never one that waives a right a lease may not waive ("Lease Terms That Void the Whole Lease"). Two conversion statutes protect the tenancy during a notice period. When a building is converted to time-shares, 'The terms of a residential tenancy may not be altered during the notice period required under sub. (1)' (120 days), and failing to give that notice 'is a defense to an action for possession' (Wis. Stat. § 707.50(1m)(b), (c)). On a condominium conversion, 'A tenant may not be required to vacate the property during the 120-day period immediately following the date of delivery of the notice' unless the tenant breaches the lease or fails to pay rent (Wis. Stat. § 703.08(2); "Condominium Conversions"); the tenant may waive that right to remain, and the first right of purchase, only in writing (Wis. Stat. § 703.08(3)). While any notice is running, keep up your repair duties ("Repair Duties Cannot Be Waived") and avoid any act that could look like retaliation.

title: Minors as Tenants and in Evictions
bodyText: In Wisconsin 'Minor' means 'a person who has not attained the age of 18 years' (Wis. Stat. § 990.01(20)), and an adult is a person who has reached 18 (Wis. Stat. § 990.01(3)). Wisconsin has no statute or administrative rule on whether a minor may sign an ordinary residential lease, on emancipating a minor to contract, or on naming a tenant's minor children as eviction defendants. A minor's general power to avoid contracts (the defense of infancy) is case law, so the cautious course is to lease only to adults and, if a minor must be a party, to have a parent or guardian sign as tenant or guarantor. The one statutory exception is narrow: a 17-year-old unaccompanied youth is presumed competent to contract for admission to a shelter facility or transitional living program, and 'The defense of infancy does not apply to any contract with a minor' meeting that section (Wis. Stat. § 48.9875(2), (3)); it does not cover ordinary rentals. You do not need to name the tenant's children in an eviction: the sheriff executing the writ removes 'the defendant and all other persons found upon the premises claiming under the defendant' (Wis. Stat. § 799.45(2)(a)). If you do sue a minor, service on a minor under 14 must also be made 'upon a parent or guardian having custody of the child' (Wis. Stat. § 801.11(2)(a)), while 'A minor 14 years of age or older who is not adjudicated incompetent and not otherwise under guardianship is not a person under disability' for service (Wis. Stat. § 801.11(2)).

title: When a Tenant Files for Bankruptcy
bodyText: Wisconsin has no statute or administrative rule on what happens to an eviction, a writ of restitution or a lease when the tenant files for bankruptcy; federal bankruptcy law controls. Under federal law the filing operates as a stay of, among other things, 'any act to obtain possession of property of the estate or of property from the estate or to exercise control over property of the estate' (FEDERAL: 11 U.S.C. § 362(a)(3)), so stop the eviction and do not deliver the writ to the sheriff until the stay is lifted or an exception applies. Two exceptions matter to landlords. First, the stay does not reach 'the continuation of any eviction, unlawful detainer action, or similar proceeding by a lessor against a debtor involving residential property in which the debtor resides as a tenant under a lease or rental agreement and with respect to which the lessor has obtained before the date of the filing of the bankruptcy petition, a judgment for possession' (FEDERAL: 11 U.S.C. § 362(b)(22)), unless within the federal time limits the tenant certifies that state law would let the tenant cure the entire monetary default after judgment, deposits the next 30 days' rent with the bankruptcy clerk and then certifies the cure (FEDERAL: 11 U.S.C. § 362(l)). Wisconsin has no statute letting a tenant cure after judgment ("Paying to Stop a Nonpayment Termination"), but whether a certification is good is for the bankruptcy court; you may object, and the court must hold a hearing within 10 days. Second, an eviction based on endangerment of the property or illegal use of controlled substances is excepted if you file and serve the certification the statute describes (FEDERAL: 11 U.S.C. § 362(b)(23), (m)). In a chapter 7 case, 'if the trustee does not assume or reject an executory contract or unexpired lease of residential real property' within 60 days after the order for relief (or extra time the court allows), 'such contract or lease is deemed rejected' (FEDERAL: 11 U.S.C. § 365(d)(1)). Get bankruptcy advice before acting.

title: Barring a Person From the Property
bodyText: Wisconsin's trespass statutes let an owner or occupant tell a person to stay off the land. A person who 'Enters or remains on any land of another after having been notified by the owner or occupant not to enter or remain on the premises' is subject to a Class B forfeiture (Wis. Stat. § 943.13(1m)(b)), and a person 'has received notice' if 'notified personally, either orally or in writing, or if the land is posted' as the statute describes (Wis. Stat. § 943.13(2)(am)). An owner or occupant may also give consent 'for a specified purpose or subject to specified conditions' (Wis. Stat. § 943.13(3m)). So you may give a written no-trespass notice to a non-tenant who has caused trouble in the common areas and call the police if the person returns. Your notice does not override your tenant's own right to admit guests to the unit the tenant occupies: entering a dwelling is a crime only if done 'without the consent of some person lawfully upon the premises' (Wis. Stat. § 943.14(2)), and a tenant's guests were held not to be trespassers while the tenant had not been given a termination notice (Johnson v. Blackburn, 220 Wis. 2d 260 (Ct. App. 1998), as summarized in the annotation to Wis. Stat. § 704.17). In employer-provided housing, 'Any authorized occupant of employer-provided housing shall have the right to decide who may enter, confer and visit with the occupant in the housing area the occupant occupies' (Wis. Stat. § 943.13(5)). If a tenant keeps admitting a barred person who endangers others, your remedy is a lease-violation or criminal-activity notice ("Notices for Other Lease Violations", "Criminal Activity and Nuisance Terminations"), never a lockout. The library offers no barred-person lease covenant for Wisconsin; you may add your own, but keep it tied to conduct that threatened health, safety or property, exempt emergency responders and anyone the tenant must admit by law, never penalize a tenant for calling for help ("Tenants' Right to Call for Help") and never use it against a victim of the barred person ("Victim Status and Evictions"). Milwaukee, Madison and other municipalities may have their own rules.

title: Who May Appear in Court for an LLC or Corporation Landlord
bodyText: Evictions are small claims actions in Wisconsin ("The Wisconsin Eviction Process"), and in small claims an entity landlord may appear without a lawyer through its own people. Under Wis. Stat. § 799.06(2) a person 'may appear in his, her, or its own proper person or by an attorney', and 'a person is considered to be acting in his, her, or its own proper person if the appearance is by a member, as defined in s. 183.0102 (11), agent, or authorized employee of the person, or by an agent of the member or an authorized employee of the agent' (Wis. Stat. § 799.06(2)); the eviction itself may be brought by the person entitled to possession 'or by that person’s agent authorized in writing' (Wis. Stat. § 799.40(1)), so give your property manager a written authorization. An assignee of a claim may not appear through a full-time employee who is not a lawyer (Wis. Stat. § 799.06(2)). Outside small claims the general rule applies: appearing 'as agent, representative or attorney, for or on behalf of any other person, or any firm, partnership, association or corporation in any action or proceeding' in a court of record is practicing law (Wis. Stat. § 757.30(2)), and the annotations report that a nonlawyer may not file an appeal for a corporation except that Wis. Stat. § 799.06(2) allows a nonlawyer employee to appear in a small claims appeal (Jadair Inc. v. United States Fire Insurance Co., 209 Wis. 2d 187 (1997), and Holz v. Busy Bees Contracting, Inc., 223 Wis. 2d 598 (Ct. App. 1998), as summarized in the annotations to Wis. Stat. § 757.30 and Wis. Stat. § 799.06; opinions not read); hire a lawyer for anything beyond small claims. Before filing, check the entity's standing to sue. An out-of-state LLC 'doing business in this state may not maintain an action or proceeding in this state unless it has registered to do business in this state' (Wis. Stat. § 183.0902(2)), and an out-of-state corporation that needs a certificate of authority 'may not maintain a proceeding in any court in this state until it obtains' one (Wis. Stat. § 180.1502(1)); its leases and title stay valid (Wis. Stat. § 183.0902(3); Wis. Stat. § 180.1502(4)), and 'Owning, without more, property' is not doing business (Wis. Stat. § 183.0905(1)(j); Wis. Stat. § 180.1501(2)(i)), so whether renting it out is depends on the facts ("Nonresident Landlords Must Name a Wisconsin Agent"). Wisconsin has no general assumed-name or trade-name filing requirement and no bar on suing under an unfiled business name; a search of the Wisconsin Statutes, Administrative Code, Constitution and 2025 session laws found none, though some licensing laws ask for trade names. Sue and sign leases in the entity's legal name. A nonresident landlord must name a Wisconsin agent for service (Wis. Stat. § 704.22; "Nonresident Landlords Must Name a Wisconsin Agent", "Landlord and Agent Identification" clause).

title: Deadlines for Suing Over Rent or Damage
bodyText: Wisconsin's general limitation periods are in Wis. Stat. ch. 893. A suit for unpaid rent or other money owed under the lease is 'an action upon any contract, obligation, or liability, express or implied' and 'shall be commenced within 6 years after the cause of action accrues or be barred' (Wis. Stat. § 893.43(1)); each missed installment probably starts its own period. A suit for damage to the property 'not arising on contract' also has 6 years (Wis. Stat. § 893.52(1)); a claim for injury to a person has 3 years (Wis. Stat. § 893.54(1m)). Once you have a judgment, an 'action upon a judgment or decree of a court of record' must be brought within 20 years after entry (Wis. Stat. § 893.40). Partial payments: the annotation to Wis. Stat. § 893.43 reports that a partial payment made before the period runs 'tolls the statute and sets it running from the date of payment' (St. Mary’s Hospital Medical Center v. Tarkenton, 103 Wis. 2d 422 (Ct. App. 1981), as summarized in the annotation to Wis. Stat. § 893.43; opinion not read), and the chapter keeps the effect of 'a payment of any principal or interest made by any person' (Wis. Stat. § 893.48). A promise to pay restarts the period only if it is 'contained in some writing signed by the party to be charged thereby' (Wis. Stat. § 893.45), and a payment by one co-tenant does not extend the period against the others (Wis. Stat. § 893.49). Do not count on the outer limit: deposit and notice rules run on much shorter clocks ("Returning the Deposit Within 21 Days"), and a lease term shortening the tenant's time to sue is not offered by this library.

title: Actual Notice and Agreed Notice Methods
bodyText:
Wisconsin's landlord-tenant chapter lists how notices must be served: notice by the landlord 'must be given under this chapter by one of the following methods' (Wis. Stat. § 704.21(1)), and the tenant's notices have their own list (Wis. Stat. § 704.21(2); "How to Serve a Notice").

Actual notice is the safety valve: 'If notice is not properly given by one of the methods specified in this section, but is actually received by the other party, the notice is deemed to be properly given; but the burden is upon the party alleging actual receipt to prove the fact by clear and convincing evidence' (Wis. Stat. § 704.21(5)), and such a notice is given 'The day of actual receipt by the other party' (Wis. Stat. § 704.19(7)(e)).

So a text message or e-mail that the tenant actually read can count, but only if you can prove receipt to that high standard; never rely on it for a termination notice.

A lease cannot make an electronic method the way to serve a notice to pay or vacate or to remedy or vacate, and this library does not rely on one for any notice ending a tenancy: Wisconsin's electronic transactions chapter does not apply to a notice of 'Default, acceleration, repossession, foreclosure, or eviction, or the right to cure, under a credit agreement secured by or a rental agreement for a primary residence of an individual' to the extent federal law excludes it (Wis. Stat. § 137.12(2r)(b); FEDERAL: 15 U.S.C. § 7003(b)(2)(B)), and the items a lease may allow electronically are listed in Wis. Stat. § 704.10 ("Electronic Delivery of Documents" clause).

A periodic tenancy may also end by another method if 'The parties have agreed expressly upon another method of termination and the parties’ agreement is established by clear and convincing proof' (Wis. Stat. § 704.19(2)(a)1.), but lease terms on termination for nonpayment or breach that are contrary to Wis. Stat. § 704.17 are invalid except in leases of more than one year (Wis. Stat. § 704.17(5)(a)), and terms contrary to Wis. Stat. § 704.17(3m) are invalid in any lease (Wis. Stat. § 704.17(5)(b)).

A tenant may give notice to 'any person who has been receiving rent or managing the property as the landlord’s agent' (Wis. Stat. § 704.21(2)(a)), so make sure your managers pass notices on.

The general definition of notice in Wis. Stat. § 401.202 belongs to the Uniform Commercial Code, not to residential leases.

title: Which Notices Must Be in Writing
bodyText: Every notice that ends or threatens to end a Wisconsin tenancy must be written. For nonpayment, breach, nuisance and criminal-activity notices, 'Notice must be in writing and given as specified in s. 704.21' (Wis. Stat. § 704.17(4)); a periodic tenancy or tenancy at will 'can be terminated by either the landlord or the tenant only by giving to the other party written notice complying with this section' (Wis. Stat. § 704.19(2)(a)), and that notice 'must be in writing, formal or informal' (Wis. Stat. § 704.19(4)). The automatic-renewal reminder must be 'written notice in the same manner as specified in s. 704.21' (Wis. Stat. § 704.15; "Automatic Renewal Notices"). Serve them by a Wis. Stat. § 704.21 method ("How to Serve a Notice", "Actual Notice and Agreed Notice Methods"). Agreements are different: 'An agreement to terminate a tenancy more than one year prior to the expiration date specified in a valid written lease is not enforceable unless it is in writing signed by both parties', but any other agreement to end a lease early, or to end a periodic tenancy without the statutory notice, 'may be either oral or written' (Wis. Stat. § 704.03(4)), and an agreement not in a writing signed by both parties 'must be proved by clear and convincing evidence' (Wis. Stat. § 704.03(5)). A lease for more than a year must itself meet the writing requirements of Wis. Stat. § 704.03(1) ("When a Lease Must Be in Writing"). Put every agreement to end a tenancy in a signed writing anyway. Other written-notice duties appear in their own rows: the deposit withholding statement ("Returning the Deposit Within 21 Days"), the landlord identity disclosure ("Landlord and Agent Identification" clause) and the domestic abuse termination notice ("Domestic Abuse, Sexual Assault and Stalking").

title: Proceedings Against the Property
bodyText:
Wisconsin has no statute or administrative rule requiring a tenant to tell you about a lawsuit, foreclosure or other proceeding or claim against the property.

The duty can come only from the lease, and the library's optional clause does that ("Notice of Proceedings Against the Property" clause).

Two statutes protect your position anyway. 'No act of a tenant in acknowledging as landlord a person other than the tenant’s original landlord or the latter’s successors in interest can prejudice the right of the original landlord or the original landlord’s successors to possession of the premises' (Wis. Stat. § 704.13).

And in a foreclosure, 'the complaint may not name a tenant of residential real property as a defendant unless the tenant has a lien or ownership interest in the real property' (Wis. Stat. § 802.03(9)), so a residential tenant will usually not be served with foreclosure papers at all ("Foreclosure and Tenants", "Federal Tenant Protections After Foreclosure").

title: Working With Police and Reporting Duties
bodyText: Wisconsin has no statute or administrative rule requiring a landlord to join a crime-free housing program, or to cooperate with police or hand over tenant information on a bare police request without a court order. A court order is different: when a court order under Wis. Stat. § 968.36(5)(b) directs it, a 'landlord, custodian or other person shall furnish the investigative or law enforcement officer forthwith all information, facilities and technical assistance necessary' to install a pen register or trap and trace device, is reasonably compensated, and cannot be sued for complying (Wis. Stat. § 968.37(1), (2), (3), (4)). A search of the Wisconsin Statutes, Administrative Code, Constitution and 2025 session laws found none; Milwaukee, Madison and other municipalities may have their own programs. Law enforcement figures in landlord-tenant law in three ways. First, under Wis. Stat. § 704.17(1p)(c), (2)(c) and (3)(b), police reports can support a termination: if you receive written notice from a law enforcement agency or from the office of the district attorney that a drug-house or criminal-gang nuisance under Wis. Stat. § 823.113(1) or (1m)(b) exists in the unit or was caused by the tenant on your property, you may give a 5-day notice to vacate that states its basis and the tenant's right to contest it ("Criminal Activity and Nuisance Terminations"). Second, your lease may not punish a tenant for calling for help: a lease that lets you raise rent, cut services, sue for possession or refuse to renew 'because a tenant has contacted an entity for law enforcement services, health services, or safety services' is void (Wis. Stat. § 704.44(1m); "Tenants' Right to Call for Help"). Third, one reporting duty binds everyone, landlords included: 'Any person who knows that a crime is being committed and that a victim is exposed to bodily harm shall summon law enforcement officers or other assistance or shall provide assistance to the victim' (Wis. Stat. § 940.34(2)(a)), unless doing so would endanger the person or others are already summoning help (Wis. Stat. § 940.34(2)(d)); a violation is a Class C misdemeanor (Wis. Stat. § 940.34(1)(a)). Licensed private detectives and security staff have a broader duty to report crimes (Wis. Stat. § 940.34(2)(b), (c)). Unclaimed deposits may have to be reported under the unclaimed property law ("Deposits You Cannot Return").

title: Construction Liens and Tenant Improvements
bodyText:
In Wisconsin a contractor or supplier who improves land and gives the required notices has a lien 'on all interests in the land belonging to its owners' (Wis. Stat. § 779.01(3)). 'Owner' means 'the owner of any interest in land who, personally or through an agent, enters into a contract, express or implied, for the improvement of the land' (Wis. Stat. § 779.01(2)(c)).

When your tenant hires the work, the tenant is the owner of its own leasehold interest, so the lien reaches that interest; under the statute's text your interest is exposed mainly if the tenant contracted as your agent (an annotation also reports a tenant's unpaid contractor recovering for unjust enrichment from a landlord who had not paid the tenant for the improvements: S&M Rotogravure Service, Inc. v. Baer, 77 Wis. 2d 454 (1977), as summarized in the annotation to Wis. Stat. § 779.02; this point is unsettled here), and outside a few listed relationships 'there shall be a similar presumption against agency in all other cases' (Wis. Stat. § 779.01(2)(c)).

Wisconsin has no statute or administrative rule creating a notice of nonresponsibility or giving a lease term the power to keep your interest free of liens.

So: require your consent before any alteration (Wis. Stat. § 704.05(3); "No Alterations" clause), do not hire or pay the tenant's contractors yourself, and consider the optional clause "No Liens From Tenant's Work", under which the tenant pays its contractors, tells them in writing that you are not paying, and has any lien released. Do not add a term making the tenant pay your attorney fees or court costs over a lien ("Lease Terms That Void the Whole Lease").

title: Special Districts and Assessments
bodyText: Wisconsin has no statute or administrative rule requiring you to tell a tenant, or state in the lease, that the property lies in a business improvement district, tax incremental district, lake or sanitary district or other special district, or that it carries special assessments. A search of the Wisconsin Statutes, Administrative Code, Constitution and 2025 session laws found none. The taxes and special assessments on the property are yours. If you pass any district or assessment charge on to the tenant, put it in the lease, and you must disclose it whenever you state the rent: a landlord may not, to induce a rental, 'Fail to disclose, in connection with any representation of rent amount, the existence of any non-rent charges which will increase the total amount payable by the tenant during tenancy' (Wis. Admin. Code ATCP § 134.09(9)(a)3.; "Disclosing Non-Rent Charges"). The special-assessment questions on the real estate condition report are for sellers, not landlords (Wis. Stat. § 709.03).

title: Changing Rent or Terms of a Month-to-Month Tenancy
bodyText: Wisconsin has no statute or administrative rule setting a notice period for changing the rent, fees, rules or other terms of a month-to-month or other periodic tenancy, and none that treats a change as a termination. During a fixed term you may change terms only as the lease allows, and new rules bind the tenant only as "Rules and Regulations" clause provides. For a periodic tenancy the cautious course is to give written notice of the change, served by a Wis. Stat. § 704.21 method, at least as long before it takes effect as the notice that would end the tenancy: a periodic tenancy ends 'only at the end of a rental period' (Wis. Stat. § 704.19(2)(b)1.), on 'At least 28 days’ notice' or, where rent is payable more often than monthly, notice 'at least equal to the rent-paying period' (Wis. Stat. § 704.19(3)); see "Raising Rent in Wisconsin". The same notice works for raising a fee the lease already provides; any non-rent charge must have been disclosed before the rental ("Disclosing Non-Rent Charges"). If a fixed-term lease renews automatically, changed renewal terms do not cure the separate renewal-reminder requirement: the reminder must be given 'at least 15 days but not more than 30 days prior to the time specified for the giving of such notice to the lessor' (Wis. Stat. § 704.15), and DATCP's rule counts the same window back from the renewal's 'stated effective date' (Wis. Admin. Code ATCP § 134.09(3)); give the reminder within both windows ("Automatic Renewal" clause, "Automatic Renewal Notices"). Never change terms in retaliation. Manufactured home community sites follow separate DATCP rules (Wis. Admin. Code ch. ATCP 125).

title: Seasonal and Short-Term Rentals
bodyText: Wisconsin has no statute or administrative rule specific to seasonal tenancies. A search of the Wisconsin Statutes, Administrative Code, Constitution and 2025 session laws found none. A rental for a season with fixed start and end dates is an ordinary lease, 'an agreement, whether oral or written, for transfer of possession of real property ... for a definite period of time' (Wis. Stat. § 704.01(1)); it ends on its expiration date without a termination notice, and a tenant who stays on is a holdover ("Holdover" clause, "Holdover Damages"). If the lease renews automatically for the next season, the renewal reminder rules apply (Wis. Stat. § 704.15; Wis. Admin. Code ATCP § 134.09(3); "Automatic Renewal Notices"). The heating disclosure covers 'all seasons of the year in which the dwelling unit may be occupied' (Wis. Admin. Code ATCP § 134.04(2)(b)2.; "Heat"). Very short stays are treated as lodging, not tenancies under the DATCP rental rules: those rules do not apply to 'A dwelling unit, such as a dwelling unit in a hotel, motel or boarding house, that is being rented only by tourist or transient occupants' (Wis. Admin. Code ATCP § 134.01(4)). Under Wis. Stat. § 66.1014(2)(d)2., a person who 'maintains, manages, or operates a short-term rental', meaning a dwelling offered for rent 'for fewer than 30 consecutive days' (Wis. Stat. § 66.0615(1)(dk)), 'for more than 10 nights each year' must get a DATCP tourist rooming house license and any local license (Wis. Stat. § 66.1014(2)(d)2.). A city, village, town or county 'may not enact or enforce an ordinance that prohibits the rental of a residential dwelling for 7 consecutive days or longer', though for rentals of more than 6 but fewer than 30 days it may cap the total at no fewer than 180 days within any 365-day period, and a person who rents the person's residential dwelling 'shall notify the clerk of the political subdivision in writing when the first rental within a 365-day period begins' (Wis. Stat. § 66.1014(2)(a), (d)1.). Room and sales taxes on short stays are covered in "Sales Tax and Rent". Seasonal manufactured home sites are outside the manufactured home community rules (Wis. Admin. Code ATCP § 125.01) and outside this row.

title: Small-Landlord Exemptions and Unit Thresholds
bodyText: Wisconsin has no statute or administrative rule that sets a landlord's duties, or exempts a landlord, by the number of units the landlord owns, and none limiting purchases of homes by large investors. A search of the Wisconsin Statutes, Administrative Code, Constitution and 2025 session laws found none. The thresholds that exist turn on the building, not the portfolio. (1) Fair housing: Wisconsin's open housing law has no small-landlord exemption; the legislature 'hereby extends the state law governing equal housing opportunities to cover single-family residences that are owner-occupied' (Wis. Stat. § 106.50(1)). Its main exclusion is for choosing a roommate: it does not apply 'to a decision by an individual as to the person with whom he or she will, or continues to, share a dwelling unit', except a residence occupied by more than 5 persons, and advertising rules still apply (Wis. Stat. § 106.50(5m)(em)). The federal Fair Housing Act does exempt, except from its advertising rule, a single-family house rented by an owner who owns no more than three and uses no broker, and 'rooms or units in dwellings containing living quarters occupied or intended to be occupied by no more than four families living independently of each other, if the owner actually maintains and occupies one of such living quarters as his residence' (FEDERAL: 42 U.S.C. § 3603(b)(1), (2)); Wisconsin's law still applies to those rentals ("Wisconsin Fair Housing"). (2) Landlord identification: the duty to disclose the manager and the person authorized to accept service 'does not apply to an owner-occupied structure containing no more than 4 dwelling units' (Wis. Admin. Code ATCP § 134.04(1)(c); "Landlord and Agent Identification" clause). (3) Construction liens: a contractor need not give the owner the lien notice where 'more than 4 family living units are to be provided or added' by a wholly residential project (Wis. Stat. § 779.02(1)(c)), so on smaller jobs the notice protects you ("Construction Liens and Tenant Improvements"). (4) Detector and meter rules differ by building size ("Smoke and Carbon Monoxide Detectors", "Separate Electric Meters").

title: Penalties for Denying an Assistance Animal
bodyText: Wisconsin has no criminal penalty aimed at a landlord who denies a service or emotional support animal. A search of the Wisconsin Statutes, Administrative Code, Constitution and 2025 session laws found none. Denial is handled as housing discrimination, with civil penalties. If an individual with a disability has a disability-related need for an animal individually trained to do work or perform tasks, under Wis. Stat. § 106.50(2r)(bg)1. 'it is discrimination for a person to refuse to rent or sell housing to the individual, cause the eviction of the individual from housing, require extra compensation from the individual as a condition of continued residence in housing, or engage in the harassment of the individual because he or she keeps such an animal' (Wis. Stat. § 106.50(2r)(bg)1.); the same rule covers emotional support animals (Wis. Stat. § 106.50(2r)(br)1.). You may ask for reliable documentation and may deny the animal only on the grounds the statute lists (Wis. Stat. § 106.50(2r)(bg)2., 4., (br)2., 4.; "Assistance Animals in Wisconsin", "Service and Assistance Animals" clause). On a finding of discrimination the department may order damages and assess a forfeiture; against a respondent with no prior violation the hearing examiner 'may assess a forfeiture against a respondent who is not a natural person in an amount not exceeding $10,000' (Wis. Stat. § 106.50(6)(h)2.), with higher maximums of $25,000 (one prior adjudged act in the preceding 5 years) and $50,000 (2 or more in the preceding 7 years) (Wis. Stat. § 106.50(6)(h)2.); against an individual with no prior adjudged act the maximum is $10,000, the $25,000 and $50,000 tiers apply only to prior acts with an offense date before September 1, 1992, and the statute states no figure for an individual with a later prior act (Wis. Stat. § 106.50(6)(h)3.), plus attorney fees (Wis. Stat. § 106.50(6)(i)). In court the tenant may recover 'damages, including punitive damages', costs and reasonable attorney fees (Wis. Stat. § 106.50(6m)(a)). The public-accommodation service-animal rule, with forfeitures of $100 to $1,000 for a first willful violation (Wis. Stat. § 106.52(4)(d)1.), covers places such as 'lodging establishments' (hotels, bed and breakfasts and tourist rooming houses) (Wis. Stat. § 106.52(1)(e)1.); whether it also reaches the common areas of an apartment building is not settled by statute, so treat a common-area denial as covered. Tenants who falsely claim a disability or need face their own forfeiture ("False Emotional Support Animal Claims"). Federal fair housing law also bars disability discrimination (FEDERAL: 42 U.S.C. § 3604).

title: Student Housing
bodyText: Wisconsin has no statute or administrative rule giving privately owned student housing its own landlord-tenant rules, and no student exemption from the tenant protections. A private landlord renting to students follows the ordinary rules. The exclusions run the other way, for housing a school itself operates: DATCP's rental rules do not apply to 'A dwelling unit operated by a public or private institution if occupancy is incidental to detention or the provision of medical, geriatric, educational, counseling, religious or similar services' (Wis. Admin. Code ATCP § 134.01(1)), or to 'A dwelling unit owned and operated by government, or a subdivision or agency of government' (Wis. Admin. Code ATCP § 134.01(7)), such as public university residence halls. A privately owned or master-leased student building is not institution-operated housing in that sense, so treat it as an ordinary rental ("Which Rentals Wisconsin's Rules Cover"), except for fire safety: a 'private student residential building' (Wis.
