Stat. § 101.14(4)(b)1m.; privately owned and operated, capacity of at least 100, at least 80 percent students, with residence-hall attributes such as a food service plan or resident advisor) must have an automatic fire sprinkler system on each floor under the department's rules if its construction began on or after January 7, 2006, or, if it is over 60 feet tall and its construction began before that date, by January 1, 2014 (Wis. Stat. § 101.14(4)(b)1m., 3.e., f.; "No Sprinkler Disclosure"). Student status is not among the protected classes in the open housing law (Wis. Stat. § 106.50(1)), but the listed classes, including age, marital status, family status and lawful source of income, all apply, and Wisconsin has no small-landlord or student-housing exemption from that law ("Small-Landlord Exemptions and Unit Thresholds", "Wisconsin Fair Housing"). Leases to groups of students usually rely on joint and several liability ("Joint & Several Liability" clause) and, where a student is under 18, on a parent's signature ("Minors as Tenants and in Evictions"). Madison and other college towns may have their own rules.

title: Family Child Care in a Rental
bodyText: Wisconsin has no statute or administrative rule requiring a landlord to allow a tenant to run a family child care home, or setting conditions (such as insurance or liability terms) for one. A search of the Wisconsin Statutes, Administrative Code, Constitution and 2025 session laws found none. The statewide rule binds municipalities, not landlords: 'No municipality may prevent a family child care home from being located in a zoned district in which a single-family residence is a permitted use', and a municipality may not set standards different from the state licensing standards (Wis. Stat. § 66.1017(2)); a family child care home is 'a dwelling licensed as a child care center by the department of children and families under s. 48.65 where care is provided for not more than 12 children' (Wis. Stat. § 66.1017(1)(a)). Whether a tenant may operate one in your unit is therefore a matter for the lease: a residential-use clause ("Residential Use Only" clause) can require your written consent for a business, and you may set reasonable conditions in that consent, such as proof of the state license and liability insurance. Apply the same policy to every tenant and never base a decision on family status or another protected class ("Wisconsin Fair Housing"). A tenant who runs child care in the unit may still not use the premises 'in such manner as to interfere unreasonably with use by another occupant of the same building' (Wis. Stat. § 704.05(3)).

title: Keeping a Victim's Information and Address Private
bodyText: Wisconsin has no statute or administrative rule that sets a general duty for landlords to keep confidential what a tenant tells them about domestic abuse, sexual assault or stalking, or the documents a tenant gives them. A search of the Wisconsin Statutes, Administrative Code, Constitution and 2025 session laws found none. Treat that information as confidential anyway and share it only as needed to act on it. Three rules do apply. (1) Screening: you may ask applicants about family, marital, financial and business status, but 'not concerning race, color, disability, sexual orientation, ancestry, national origin, religion, creed, status as a victim of domestic abuse, sexual assault, or stalking' (Wis. Stat. § 106.50(5m)(f)1.; "What You May Ask Applicants"). (2) Address confidentiality program: a victim certified by the Department of Justice gets an assigned address, and 'No person who has received a notification form from a program participant may refuse to use the assigned address for the program participant, may require a program participant to disclose his or her actual address, or may intentionally disclose to another person the actual address of a program participant' (Wis. Stat. § 165.68(5)(c)); 'A person who intentionally releases information in violation of this section is guilty of a misdemeanor' (Wis. Stat. § 165.68(7)). The participant has also made the department 'the program participant’s designated agent for service of process' (Wis. Stat. § 165.68(3)(b)4.g.), so you may serve court papers there ("Who Can Accept Eviction Papers for the Tenant"). (3) Court records: on a participant's written request, a clerk of court or other local clerk 'may not disclose any record in his or her possession that would reveal the program participant’s actual address, except pursuant to a court order' (Wis. Stat. § 66.0504(2)(a)). Before filing an eviction that must describe the premises, ask the clerk how to keep the address out of the public file. In housing assisted under a federal covered housing program, information a victim submits 'shall be maintained in confidence by the public housing agency or owner or manager and may not be entered into any shared database or disclosed to any other entity or individual', except with the person's written consent, for an eviction proceeding or as law requires (FEDERAL: 34 U.S.C. § 12491(c)(4)); that rule does not reach other rentals.

title: Deposit Return After a Domestic Abuse Termination
bodyText: Wisconsin has no special deposit-return rule for a tenant who ends the tenancy under the domestic abuse, sexual assault or stalking statute (Wis. Stat. § 704.16; "Domestic Abuse, Sexual Assault and Stalking"). A search of the Wisconsin Statutes, Administrative Code, Constitution and 2025 session laws found none. The general 21-day rule applies ("Returning the Deposit Within 21 Days"): you must return the deposit, less lawful withholdings, 'within 21 days after' one of the triggers in Wis. Stat. § 704.28(4), and for a tenant who leaves before the lease's termination date the trigger is 'the date on which the tenant’s rental agreement terminates or, if the landlord rerents the premises before the tenant’s rental agreement terminates, the date on which the new tenant’s tenancy begins' (Wis. Stat. § 704.28(4)(b)). The statute does not say on which date a Wis. Stat. § 704.16 termination takes effect; it says only that the tenant 'shall not be liable for any rent after the end of the month following the month in which he or she provides the notice or removes from the premises, whichever is later' (Wis. Stat. § 704.16(2), (2m)). The cautious course is to treat the tenancy as ending no later than that date and return the deposit within 21 days after it, or within 21 days after a new tenant's tenancy begins if you rerent sooner; you may withhold rent the tenant owes up to that date (Wis. Stat. § 704.28(1)(b)) and the other standard items, never normal wear and tear ("Use of Security Deposit" clause). No statute says how one deposit is divided when one co-tenant leaves under Wis. Stat. § 704.16 and others stay; the abuser's lease obligations continue (Wis. Stat. § 704.16(4)(c)2. says nothing in the lock-change rule relieves that tenant 'from any obligation under a rental agreement'), so the cautious course is to hold the deposit for the continuing tenancy unless the tenants agree in writing to divide it, and to tell the leaving tenant so in writing.

title: Changing Locks for a Victim Tenant
bodyText: Wisconsin requires a lock change on request for a victim tenant (summary in "Locks and Rekeying"). 'At the request of a residential tenant who provides the landlord with a certified copy of a document specified in sub. (1) (b) 1. to 7. or (1m) (a) or (b), a landlord shall change the locks to the tenant’s premises', and this applies 'regardless of whether sub. (1) or (1m) applies', that is, whether or not the tenant is also ending the tenancy (Wis. Stat. § 704.16(4)(a)). The qualifying documents are the injunctions, release conditions and criminal complaints listed in "Documents That Qualify a Victim Tenant". You must 'have the locks changed, or may give the tenant permission to change the locks, within 48 hours after receiving a request and certified copy', and 'The tenant shall be responsible for the cost of changing the locks'; if the tenant changes them, the tenant must give you a key within a reasonable time (Wis. Stat. § 704.16(4)(b)). Where the person named in the document is also a tenant of the unit, you need not change the locks unless the document is an injunction directing that person 'to avoid the residence of the tenant requesting that the locks be changed' or a release condition ordering no contact (Wis. Stat. § 704.16(4)(c)1.), and the lock change does not relieve that person of the lease or any other liability to you (Wis. Stat. § 704.16(4)(c)2.). 'A landlord is not liable for civil damages for any action taken to comply with this subsection' (Wis. Stat. § 704.16(4)(d)). Outside this rule, never lock out a co-tenant on your own; removal is only by court eviction ("No Self-Help Evictions"). When a co-tenant's acts put the victim tenant at imminent threat of serious physical harm and that co-tenant is named in a qualifying injunction, release condition or criminal complaint, you may end that offending tenant's tenancy on a written 5-day notice stating its basis and the right to contest it (Wis. Stat. § 704.16(3)(b); "Domestic Abuse, Sexual Assault and Stalking"), but if that tenant stays, you still need an eviction judgment to remove them. The rule was amended by 2025 Wis. Act 90 (effective March 8, 2026) to cover the sexual-assault documents.

title: Where Wisconsin's Protection-Order Laws Are
bodyText: Wisconsin's protection-order statutes have not been moved or renumbered; the citations in Wisconsin's domestic abuse rows are current. The injunction statutes are in Wis. Stat. ch. 813: domestic abuse restraining orders and injunctions (Wis. Stat. § 813.12, injunctions under its subsection (4)), child abuse restraining orders and injunctions (Wis. Stat. § 813.122), restraining orders and injunctions for individuals at risk (Wis. Stat. § 813.123) and harassment restraining orders and injunctions (Wis. Stat. § 813.125, injunctions under its subsection (4)). The related criminal statutes are stalking (Wis. Stat. § 940.32) and domestic abuse arrests (Wis. Stat. § 968.075). These are the statutes the lease-termination and lock-change rule cites (Wis. Stat. § 704.16; "Domestic Abuse, Sexual Assault and Stalking", "Changing Locks for a Victim Tenant", "Documents That Qualify a Victim Tenant") and that the eviction defense cites (Wis. Stat. § 106.50(5m)(dm)2.a., which lists injunctions 'under s. 813.12, 813.122, 813.123, or 813.125'; "Victim Status and Evictions"). The termination rule itself was amended by 2025 Wis. Act 90, effective March 8, 2026, which moved the sexual-assault criminal complaint from Wis. Stat. § 704.16(1)(b)5. to the new Wis. Stat. § 704.16(1m)(b); a lease or form that still cites Wis. Stat. § 704.16(1)(b)5. should be updated. 2025 Wis. Act 149 amended parts of Wis. Stat. § 813.12, Wis. Stat. § 813.123 and Wis. Stat. § 813.125 without renumbering the injunction subsections.

title: Documents That Qualify a Victim Tenant
bodyText: Wisconsin's termination and lock-change rights turn on a certified copy of a court or charging document, not a self-statement. For the imminent-threat termination, Wis. Stat. § 704.16(1)(b) requires notice 'and with a certified copy of any of the following': an injunction under Wis. Stat. § 813.12(4) protecting the tenant; an injunction under Wis. Stat. § 813.122 protecting the tenant's child; an injunction under Wis. Stat. § 813.125(4) protecting the tenant or child based on stalking; 'A condition of release under ch. 969 ordering the person not to contact the tenant'; a criminal complaint alleging stalking of the tenant or child; or a criminal complaint filed after the person's arrest for a domestic abuse offense against the tenant (Wis. Stat. § 704.16(1)(b)1.-4., 6., 7.), and the tenant or child must face 'an imminent threat of serious physical harm' if the tenant stays (Wis. Stat. § 704.16(1)(a)). For the sexual-assault termination, no separate threat finding is needed: the tenant gives notice with a certified copy of a Wis. Stat. § 813.125(4) injunction based on sexual assault or a criminal complaint alleging sexual assault of the tenant or child (Wis. Stat. § 704.16(1m)(a), (b)). The lock-change right uses the same lists, 'a certified copy of a document specified in sub. (1) (b) 1. to 7. or (1m) (a) or (b)' (Wis. Stat. § 704.16(4)(a)), but when the named person is a co-tenant only a stay-away injunction or no-contact release condition requires the change (Wis. Stat. § 704.16(4)(c)1.; "Changing Locks for a Victim Tenant"). Your own termination of an offending tenant requires that the offending tenant be 'the named offender' in one of a parallel list of injunctions, release conditions or criminal complaints (Wis. Stat. § 704.16(3)(b)2.a.-g.). Wis. Stat. § 704.16 sets no time limit on how recent the document must be and does not accept a letter from an advocate or a self-certification. The eviction defense for victims needs no certified copy: it turns on what you 'knew or should have known' (Wis. Stat. § 106.50(5m)(dm)), and where the abuser was the tenant's invited guest, also on the tenant having sought an injunction or, after a Wis. Stat. § 704.17 notice, given you a written statement that the person will no longer be a guest and not invited the person back since (Wis. Stat. § 106.50(5m)(dm)1., 2.; "Victim Status and Evictions"). In housing assisted under a federal covered housing program, the federal certification form, a signed statement from a victim service provider, attorney or medical or mental health professional, or a police or court record also qualify for federal protections (FEDERAL: 34 U.S.C. § 12491(c)(3)).

title: Tenant Illness, Incapacity or Move to Care
bodyText: Wisconsin has no statute or administrative rule that ends a tenancy, or lets a tenant end a lease early, because the tenant becomes ill, loses capacity, or moves to a nursing home, assisted living or other care facility. A search of the Wisconsin Statutes, Administrative Code, Constitution and 2025 session laws found none. A tenant in that situation stays liable for rent under the lease, reduced by what you can recover by reasonable efforts to rerent (Wis. Stat. § 704.29; "Duty to Rerent"), and a periodic tenancy ends on the ordinary notice ("Ending a Periodic Tenancy"). The statutory early-termination rights are listed in "When Tenants May End a Lease Early". The closest rule is death: 'if a residential tenant dies, his or her tenancy is terminated' on the earlier of 60 days after you learn of the death or the end of the lease term, the estate owes no rent after that, and another adult tenant stays bound (Wis. Stat. § 704.165(1)(a), (2), (3); "When a Tenant Dies"). You may agree to release a tenant who must move to care, and a lease may offer that option; if you do, put the release in a signed writing (Wis. Stat. § 704.03(4)). A tenant with a disability may also ask for a reasonable accommodation in your rules or policies, which could include an early release (Wis. Stat. § 106.50(2r)(b)4.; "Disability Accommodations and Modifications").

title: Ending a Lease After a Disaster or Environmental Event
bodyText: Wisconsin has no statute or administrative rule that ends a residential tenancy, or gives the landlord a right to end it, because of a flood, storm, contamination, declared emergency or other environmental event. A search of the Wisconsin Statutes, Administrative Code, Constitution and 2025 session laws found none. The tenant's side is statutory: if the premises 'become untenantable because of damage by fire, water, or other casualty or because of any condition hazardous to health' (Wis. Stat. § 704.07(4)), the tenant may move out unless you promptly repair, and may move out anyway if the repair period would impose undue hardship on the tenant; while the tenant stays and the condition materially affects health or safety or substantially affects use and occupancy, rent abates to the extent the tenant is deprived of full normal use (not in full); a tenant who justifiably leaves owes no rent after the premises became untenantable and gets back rent paid in advance for that period, and none of this applies if the damage was caused by the tenant's negligence or improper use (Wis. Stat. § 704.07(4); "Tenant Remedies for Untenantable Conditions"). Your side is contractual: a landlord termination right after a casualty exists only if the lease reserves it, and the library's optional clause covers "fire, water, or other casualty" not caused by you ("Landlord Termination After Casualty" clause); an environmental event that damages the property is a casualty under that clause. A lease may not make the tenant liable for 'Property damage caused by natural disasters or by persons other than the tenant or the tenant’s guests or invitees' (Wis. Stat. § 704.44(7)(b); "Lease Terms That Void the Whole Lease"). If the event leads to a government order to vacate or placard, you may not rent the unit until repairs are complete ("Condemned Premises").

title: Guarantors and Lease Renewals
bodyText:
Wisconsin has no statute or administrative rule specific to guaranties of residential leases: none limits a guarantor to the original term, requires a stated maximum or end date, caps what a guarantor may be asked to pay up front, or lets a guarantor insist that you sue the tenant first.

The general writing rule applies: 'Every special promise to answer for the debt, default or miscarriage of another person' is void unless it 'or some note or memorandum thereof, expressing the consideration, be in writing and subscribed by the party charged therewith' (Wis. Stat. § 241.02(1)(b)).

Whether a guaranty reaches a renewal, extension or month-to-month holdover, and whether a later rent increase releases the guarantor, turns on the guaranty's own words and on case law, so say it expressly.

The library's optional clause "Guaranty" states the consideration, a maximum amount, and whether renewals are covered.

A lease may not make the tenant pay your attorney fees or costs beyond what a court awards (Wis. Stat. § 704.44(4m); "Attorney Fees and Costs"); no statute says the same of a guarantor, but because a guaranty signed on the lease could be read as part of the rental agreement, the library's clause does not ask a guarantor to pay them either.

title: Long Leases: Length Limits and Signatures
bodyText: Wisconsin sets no maximum term for a residential lease. The one constitutional limit is for farmland: 'Leases and grants of agricultural land for a longer term than fifteen years in which rent or service of any kind shall be reserved.. are declared to be void' (Wis. Const. art. I, § 14). What a long lease needs is formality. Under Wis. Stat. § 704.03(1), a lease 'for more than a year' is not enforceable unless it meets the conveyance requirements of Wis. Stat. § 706.02 and states the rent, the start and end dates and the premises, or a signed writing with those terms is followed by the tenant's move-in (Wis. Stat. § 704.03(1); "When a Lease Must Be in Writing"). Leases of one year or less are outside the conveyance chapter (Wis. Stat. § 706.001(2)(c)). Under Wis. Stat. § 706.02 the lease must be 'signed by or on behalf of all parties, if a lease or contract to convey' (Wis. Stat. § 706.02(1)(e)), and, where it 'alienates any interest of a married person in a homestead', it must be 'signed, or joined in by separate conveyance, by or on behalf of each spouse' (Wis. Stat. § 706.02(1)(f)); lessors are grantors under the chapter (Wis. Stat. § 706.01(6)). So if you are married and lease out your home (the dwelling you live in, with up to 40 acres, Wis. Stat. § 706.01(7)) for more than a year, have your spouse sign too; the annotations report that the homestead signature cannot be waived by agency (Wangen v. Leum, 46 Wis. 2d 60 (1970), as summarized in the annotation to Wis. Stat. § 706.02). Check whether a lease of a home the owner no longer lives in is a homestead conveyance, and how Wisconsin's marital property law (Wis. Stat. ch. 766) affects who must sign; the cautious course for a married owner is to have both spouses sign any lease longer than one year. No seal or acknowledgment is required for the lease itself by these sections.

title: Initialing Lease Provisions
bodyText: Wisconsin has no statute or administrative rule requiring a tenant to initial lease clauses or notices, or making a lease notice ineffective because it was not initialed. A search of the Wisconsin Statutes, Administrative Code, Constitution and 2025 session laws found none. Initials matter in Wisconsin only for the separate NONSTANDARD RENTAL PROVISIONS documents. For deposit withholding, 'If the tenant signs his or her name, or writes his or her initials, by a nonstandard rental provision, it is rebuttably presumed that the landlord has specifically identified the nonstandard rental provision with the tenant and that the tenant has agreed to it' (Wis. Stat. § 704.28(2); Wis. Admin. Code ATCP § 134.06; "Nonstandard Rental Provisions: Deposit Withholding" clause). The entry provision carries the same presumption when the tenant 'signs or initials' it (Wis. Admin. Code ATCP § 134.09(2)(c); "Nonstandard Rental Provisions: Entry" clause). An agreement letting you hold a tenant's property 'is not effective unless signed or initialed by the tenant' (Wis. Admin. Code ATCP § 134.09(4)(b); "No Landlord Lien on Tenant Property"). For those documents, have the tenant initial next to each provision and sign the page. Elsewhere, the tenant's signature on the lease is enough; the Notice of Domestic Abuse Protections must be in the lease or an addendum but need not be initialed (Wis. Stat. § 704.14; "Notice of Domestic Abuse Protections" clause).

title: Renting to Registered Sex Offenders
bodyText: Wisconsin has no statute or administrative rule that limits whom a landlord may rent to because of sex offender registration: no duty to check whether an applicant or occupant is registered, no distance rule that binds landlords, and no crime of leasing a dwelling to two or more registrants. Residence limits that exist bind the offender or the state, not you: for example, the residency requirement for certain offenders under GPS tracking (Wis. Stat. § 301.48) and court-ordered placement on supervised release (Wis. Stat. § 980.08). Some municipalities have sex offender residency ordinances; state law bars enforcing such an ordinance 'that restricts or prohibits a person from providing housing to a sex offender against an individual who is released under s. 980.08 or against a person who provides housing to the individual' while the individual is on supervised release, living where ordered and complying with court orders (Wis. Stat. § 980.135). Your only statewide duty concerns questions: 'a landlord or his or her agent has no duty to disclose to any person in connection with the rental of real property' registry information unless asked, must disclose what you actually know if asked, and are immune if you promptly give written notice of how to reach the Department of Corrections (Wis. Stat. § 704.50; "Questions About the Sex Offender Registry", "Sex Offender Registry Notice" clause). Screening on criminal history is covered in "Tenant Screening in Wisconsin".

title: Housing You Provide to an Employee
bodyText: Apart from migrant workers, Wisconsin has no statute or administrative rule requiring a landlord who houses an employee to give a disclosure of occupancy and vacating terms, and none requires offering a rental agreement when the job ends. A search of the Wisconsin Statutes, Administrative Code, Constitution and 2025 session laws found none. What the law does say: (1) If the employee holds the unit under the employment contract rather than a lease, the employee may not be a tenant at all; ch. 704 provides that 'a person holding possession of real property under a contract of purchase or an employment contract is not a tenant under this chapter' (Wis. Stat. § 704.01(5)). (2) DATCP's rental rules do not apply to 'A dwelling unit which the landlord provides free of charge to any person, or which the landlord provides as consideration to a person whom the landlord currently employs to operate or maintain the premises' (Wis. Admin. Code ATCP § 134.01(5)), so a resident manager or caretaker housed as part of pay falls outside them. (3) An employee who is not a tenant still may not be removed by self-help; an eviction may be brought 'to remove therefrom any person who is not entitled to either the possession or occupancy of such real property' (Wis. Stat. § 799.40(1); "The Wisconsin Eviction Process"). (4) 'Any authorized occupant of employer-provided housing shall have the right to decide who may enter, confer and visit with the occupant in the housing area the occupant occupies' (Wis. Stat. § 943.13(5)). (5) Migrant labor camps have their own rules: the employer's written recruiting disclosure and signed work agreement must state the 'kind of housing and any charges in connection therewith' (Wis. Stat. § 103.915(1), Wis. Stat. § 103.915(4)(a)), and after the worker's employment ends, 'the employer may require a worker to vacate residence at the migrant labor camp operated by the employer upon final payment of wages' (Wis. Stat. § 103.926), and workers decide who may visit them (Wis. Stat. § 103.925). The cautious course is a separate written housing agreement that says whether the employee is a tenant, what rent (if any) is charged, and when and how the right to occupy ends with the job.

title: Renting the Same Unit Twice
bodyText: Wisconsin has no statute or administrative rule that speaks specifically to double-letting, that is, renting the same unit or room to two tenants for the same period. A search of the Wisconsin Statutes, Administrative Code, Constitution and 2025 session laws found none. The general rules cover it. 'No landlord shall fail to deliver possession of the dwelling unit to the tenant at the time agreed upon in the rental agreement, except where the landlord is unable to deliver possession because of circumstances beyond the landlord’s control' (Wis. Admin. Code ATCP § 134.09(6); "Possession Delay" clause), and renting a unit you have already promised to someone else is not beyond your control. Once the tenancy begins, 'the tenant has the right to exclusive possession of the premises' (Wis. Stat. § 704.05(2); "Tenant's Right to Exclusive Possession"). A landlord may not misrepresent 'the location, characteristics or equivalency of dwelling units' to induce a rental (Wis. Admin. Code ATCP § 134.09(9)(a)1.). A tenant who loses money because of a violation of the DATCP rules may sue for twice the loss, costs and attorney fees ("DATCP Enforcement and Double Damages"). Before signing a new lease, confirm that the prior tenant's tenancy will have ended (or that a holdover tenant has left) by the new start date.

title: Guests Displaced by a Disaster
bodyText: Wisconsin has no statute or administrative rule that lets a tenant shelter people displaced by a fire, flood, storm or declared emergency in spite of the lease's guest or occupancy limits, or that bars a landlord from enforcing those limits during a disaster. A search of the Wisconsin Statutes, Administrative Code, Constitution and 2025 session laws found none. Your lease's guest rules ("Guest Policy" clause, "Guest Policy (14-Day Limit)" clause) therefore apply as written, and so do any government occupancy limits; it is 'not discrimination based on family status to comply with any reasonable federal, state or local government restrictions relating to the maximum number of occupants permitted to occupy a dwelling unit' (Wis. Stat. § 106.50(5m)(e)). You may agree in writing to let a tenant host displaced relatives or friends for a stated period; doing so is good practice and avoids a lease-violation dispute. If you do enforce the guest limit, use the ordinary written notice to remedy or vacate ("Notices for Other Lease Violations"), and apply the same rule to every tenant ("Wisconsin Fair Housing"). A guest is not your tenant, but if the guest stays after the tenancy ends, removal is by court eviction ("Squatters and Unauthorized Occupants").

title: After a Fire, Flood or Declared Disaster
bodyText:
Wisconsin has no statute or administrative rule that ends a tenancy, suspends rent or adds landlord duties because a disaster or emergency has been declared.

The ordinary casualty rules decide what happens. 'If the premises are damaged by fire, water or other casualty, not the result of the negligence or intentional act of the landlord', your general repair duty under Wis. Stat. § 704.07(2) 'is inapplicable and either sub. (3) or (4) governs' (Wis. Stat. § 704.07(2)(c)).

Under sub. (4), if the unit becomes untenantable the tenant may move out unless you proceed promptly to repair (or even then, if the repair would impose undue hardship); a tenant who stays, where the condition materially affects health or safety or substantially affects use and occupancy, has rent reduced 'to the extent the tenant is deprived of the full normal use of the premises', and a tenant who justifiably moves out 'is not liable for rent after the premises become untenantable' and gets back rent paid in advance for that period; none of this applies if the damage was caused by the tenant's negligence or improper use (Wis. Stat. § 704.07(4); "Tenant Remedies for Untenantable Conditions").

The tenancy does not end by itself; it ends when the tenant justifiably moves out, by agreement, or under a casualty clause in the lease ("Landlord Termination After Casualty" clause, "Ending a Lease After a Disaster or Environmental Event").

A lease may not make the tenant pay for damage caused by natural disasters (Wis. Stat. § 704.44(7)(b)). If a placard or vacate order issues, you may not re-rent until repairs are done ("Condemned Premises").

During a period the governor certifies as one of abnormal economic disruption, 'No seller may sell, or offer to sell, in this state at wholesale or at retail, consumer goods or services at unreasonably excessive prices' (Wis. Stat. § 100.305(2)); whether a residential lease is a consumer good or service sold by a 'Seller' as defined there is not settled by the statute or Wis. Admin. Code ch. ATCP 106, so avoid sharp rent increases on new rentals during a declared emergency.

Needy families with children may get state emergency assistance 'in cases of fire, flood, natural disaster, homelessness or impending homelessness, or energy crisis' (Wis. Stat. § 49.138(1m)).

title: Alternate Housing During Repairs
bodyText: Wisconsin has no statute or administrative rule requiring a private landlord to provide or pay for a hotel or other alternate housing while a unit is repaired or is untenantable, whether or not the tenant asks. A search of the Wisconsin Statutes, Administrative Code, Constitution and 2025 session laws found none. The tenant's statutory remedies are to move out or to stay with reduced rent: if the premises become untenantable the tenant 'may remove from the premises unless the landlord proceeds promptly to repair or rebuild' (Wis. Stat. § 704.07(4)), a tenant who stays has rent abated 'to the extent the tenant is deprived of the full normal use of the premises' (Wis. Stat. § 704.07(4)), and a tenant who justifiably moves out owes no rent after the premises became untenantable; abatement applies only where the condition materially affects health or safety or substantially affects use and occupancy, and none of this applies if the tenant's negligence or improper use caused the damage (Wis. Stat. § 704.07(4); "Tenant Remedies for Untenantable Conditions"). Relocation payments in Wisconsin law are owed by a 'condemnor' (Wis. Stat. § 32.185): a body that acquires property for public purposes, or a 'displacing agency', which includes any person carrying out a program or project with public financial assistance that permanently displaces a tenant, including by rehabilitation or demolition (Wis. Stat. § 32.185; Wis. Stat. § 32.19(2)(e)1.; "Condemnation" clause). A private landlord repairing without public financial assistance owes none; if a repair or rehabilitation project uses public funds and will permanently displace a tenant, check the relocation rules (Wis. Admin. Code ch. Adm 92) before starting. You may offer temporary housing as a practical alternative to losing the tenant or the rent, but put any offer and who pays in writing. If you keep a tenant out of the unit for your own convenience, or cut services to force a move, that can be an unlawful exclusion or retaliation ("No Self-Help Evictions", "Retaliation").

title: Recording a Lease
bodyText: Wisconsin has no statute or administrative rule requiring you to record, register or file a residential lease with any public office. Recording is optional and matters only against a later buyer or lender. Wisconsin's conveyancing chapter does not cover a lease 'for a term limited to one year or less', 'except that instruments relating to such excluded transactions, if in recordable form, shall be entitled to record' (Wis. Stat. § 706.001(2)(c)). A longer lease is a conveyance, and an unrecorded conveyance 'shall be void as against any subsequent purchaser, in good faith and for a valuable consideration, of the same real estate or any portion of the same real estate whose conveyance is recorded first' (Wis. Stat. § 706.08(1)(a)). A buyer or lender is charged with notice 'arising from use or occupancy of the real estate by any person' when diligent inquiry of the occupants would have disclosed the interest and the occupancy is 'actual, visible, open and notorious' (Wis. Stat. § 706.09(2)(a)), so a tenant in possession usually gives notice of the lease; how that applies to a particular tenant is for the courts. Recording does not change the rights you and the tenant have against each other under Wisconsin's landlord-tenant chapter; a lease for more than one year must meet the writing rules ("When a Lease Must Be in Writing"). A municipality may not make you file leases with it: it may not require you to communicate any information about you or a tenant unless state or federal law requires it or it is required of all residential property owners (Wis. Stat. § 66.0104(2)(d)2.), and a local registration may ask only for one owner or contact name and contact details (Wis. Stat. § 66.0104(2)(e)4.; "Local Rental Registration"). Milwaukee, Madison and other municipalities may have their own rules.

title: No Good-Cause Notice in Wisconsin
bodyText: Wisconsin has no statute or administrative rule requiring good cause to end or decline to renew an ordinary residential tenancy, or requiring you to give the tenant a notice saying whether a good-cause law covers the unit or stating your reason. A month-to-month or other periodic tenancy ends on written notice that must 'substantially inform the other party to the landlord-tenant relation of the intent to terminate the tenancy and the date of termination' (Wis. Stat. § 704.19(4)), given at least 28 days ahead and at the end of a rental period ("Ending a Month-to-Month Tenancy" clause); no reason is required. Limits still apply: you may not refuse to renew a lease or bring an action for possession if 'the action or inaction would not occur but for the landlord’s retaliation against the tenant' for a good faith code complaint, a repair complaint or 'Exercising a legal right relating to residential tenancies' (Wis. Stat. § 704.45(1); "Retaliation"); a tenant's suit to have a building declared a nuisance or health hazard 'is not just cause for eviction' (Wis. Stat. § 254.595(8)); and the fair housing and domestic-abuse protections apply ("Wisconsin Fair Housing", "Victim Status and Evictions"). Under Wisconsin law, good cause is required only for a site in a manufactured home community (federal rules separately limit terminations of Housing Choice Voucher tenancies during the lease term, FEDERAL: 24 C.F.R. § 982.310(a)), where a tenancy 'may not be terminated, nor may the renewal of the lease be denied by the community operator, except upon' the listed grounds (Wis. Stat. § 710.15(5m)); those site rentals are outside this library. A municipality may not require you to communicate to tenants information that state or federal law does not require (Wis. Stat. § 66.0104(2)(d)1.a.), which reaches a local good-cause notice; whether state law also displaces a local good-cause rule itself is not settled by statute. Milwaukee, Madison and other municipalities may have their own rules.

title: No State Rights Guide to Hand Out
bodyText: Wisconsin has no statute or administrative rule requiring you to give a tenant a state-published guide to landlord and tenant rights and responsibilities, before signing or at renewal, or to get a signed acknowledgment that the tenant received one. A search of the Wisconsin Statutes, Administrative Code, Constitution and 2025 session laws found none. What Wisconsin does require is narrower: the domestic abuse protections notice in every lease ("Notice of Domestic Abuse Protections" clause), the check-in sheet at move-in ("Check-in and Preexisting Damage" clause) and the disclosures listed in "Wisconsin Disclosure Checklist". A municipality may not require you to give tenants information beyond those: no city, village, town or county may enact an ordinance that 'requires a landlord to communicate to tenants any information that is not required to be communicated to tenants under federal or state law' (Wis. Stat. § 66.0104(2)(d)1.a.), apart from ordinances aimed at the manufacture of illegal narcotics. You may hand tenants a guide of your choosing, but keep it separate from the lease and do not let it contradict the lease or the law. In federally assisted housing covered by the Violence Against Women Act, the housing provider must give the HUD notice of occupancy rights (see "No State Tenant Rights Statement").

title: No State Tenant Rights Statement
bodyText: Wisconsin has no statute or administrative rule requiring you to give a tenant a state agency's statement or summary of tenant rights, to attach one to the lease or have each tenant sign it, or that bars you from suing until you have given one. A search of the Wisconsin Statutes, Administrative Code, Constitution and 2025 session laws found none. The one statutory summary every Wisconsin lease must carry is the domestic abuse protections notice: 'A residential rental agreement shall include the following notice in the agreement or in an addendum to the agreement' (Wis. Stat. § 704.14), and the notice itself says 'A tenant is advised that this notice is only a summary of the tenant’s rights' (Wis. Stat. § 704.14(3)). The library prints it in every Wisconsin lease ("Notice of Domestic Abuse Protections" clause); no signature on each page is required. A municipality may not add its own required statement, because no ordinance may require you to communicate to tenants information that state or federal law does not require (Wis. Stat. § 66.0104(2)(d)1.a.; "No State Rights Guide to Hand Out"). Federal rule for covered assisted housing only: 'A covered housing provider must provide to each of its applicants and to each of its tenants the notice of occupancy rights and the certification form as described in this section' (FEDERAL: 24 C.F.R. § 5.2005(a)(1)), at admission, with any notice of eviction or termination of assistance, and at the other times that rule lists (FEDERAL: 24 C.F.R. § 5.2005(a)(2)); it does not reach private housing without federal assistance (FEDERAL: 34 U.S.C. § 12491).

title: Renting Homes in Single-Family Zones
bodyText: Wisconsin has no statute or administrative rule that limits renting a home in a single-family zone or makes renting depend on the owner living on the lot. State law runs the other way: 'a political subdivision may not enact or enforce an ordinance that prohibits the rental of a residential dwelling for 7 consecutive days or longer' (Wis. Stat. § 66.1014(2)(a)), and an inconsistent ordinance in effect on September 23, 2017 'does not apply and may not be enforced' (Wis. Stat. § 66.1014(2)(b)). A city, village, town or county may still regulate rentals in ways consistent with that rule (Wis. Stat. § 66.1014(2)(c)). For rentals of more than 6 but fewer than 30 consecutive days it may cap the total at no fewer than 180 days in any 365-day period, and you must notify the clerk in writing when the first such rental in a 365-day period begins (Wis. Stat. § 66.1014(2)(d)1.); a short-term rental for more than 10 nights a year needs a state tourist rooming house license and any local license the municipality requires (Wis. Stat. § 66.1014(2)(d)2.). A local rental registration may ask only for one owner or contact name and contact details (Wis. Stat. § 66.0104(2)(e)4.; "Local Rental Registration"). The court of appeals has held that an ordinance banning short-term rentals of some residential dwellings is preempted (Wisconsin Realtors Ass’n, Inc. v. City of Neenah, 2025 WI App 49, as summarized in the annotation to Wis. Stat. § 66.1014); how the statute applies to a particular zoning rule, such as an owner-occupancy condition, is for the courts. Milwaukee, Madison and other municipalities may have their own rules; check the local zoning code before renting.

title: Accessory Dwelling Units
bodyText:
Wisconsin has no statewide accessory dwelling unit statute: nothing in state law requires cities to allow accessory units, bars owner-occupancy conditions on them, or sets a minimum rental term for them.

Whether you may build or keep an accessory unit is a local zoning question.

Once a unit lawfully exists, the general rule applies: a city, village, town or county 'may not enact or enforce an ordinance that prohibits the rental of a residential dwelling for 7 consecutive days or longer' (Wis. Stat. § 66.1014(2)(a)), though it may limit rentals of more than 6 but fewer than 30 days ("Renting Homes in Single-Family Zones"); how that rule meets a local owner-occupancy condition is for the courts.

Renting an accessory unit is an ordinary residential tenancy under Wisconsin's landlord-tenant law.

If the unit shares water, heat or electricity with the main house and the charges are not in the rent, you must disclose before signing 'the basis on which charges for utility services will be allocated among individual dwelling units' (Wis. Admin. Code ATCP § 134.04(3); "Utility Charge Allocation" clause), and in a multi-unit building built after March 1, 1980 each dwelling unit needs its own electric meter unless an exception applies (Wis. Admin. Code PSC § 113.0803(1); "Separate Electric Meters").

The optional clause "The Premises Is an Accessory Dwelling Unit" records the lot layout, shared areas and shared utilities.

Milwaukee, Madison and other municipalities may have their own rules.

title: Local Health Rules for Rentals
bodyText: Wisconsin has no statute or administrative rule requiring you to give tenants a copy of local health-department rental regulations, on request or otherwise, or to refer tenants to a health district. A municipality may not add that duty: no ordinance may require you 'to communicate to tenants any information that is not required to be communicated to tenants under federal or state law' (Wis. Stat. § 66.0104(2)(d)1.a.). Local health officers do act on rental housing. If a local health officer finds a human health hazard on private property, the officer must notify 'the owner and the occupant of the property' (Wis. Stat. § 254.59) by registered mail and order it abated within 30 days, after which the officer must abate it, and the cost may be recovered from the person permitting the violation or charged as a special tax on the property; a person maintaining the hazard may be fined up to $300, imprisoned up to 90 days, or both (Wis. Stat. § 254.59(2)). A tenant of property that violates the municipal building code or a local board of health order may petition the municipality to sue to declare it a nuisance or human health hazard, and may sue directly if the municipality does not act within 20 days; a court may then appoint a receiver (Wis. Stat. § 254.595(1), (2); "Code Orders and Nuisance Receivership"). You may not retaliate against a tenant who 'Reported a violation of this chapter or a building or housing code to any governmental authority' (Wis. Admin. Code ATCP § 134.09(5)(a); "Retaliation"). Milwaukee, Madison and other municipalities may have their own rules.

title: Wisconsin Lead Notices
bodyText:
Beyond the federal lead disclosure and pamphlet for housing built before 1978 ("Lead-Based Paint Disclosure" clause), Wisconsin requires no state lead notice, certificate or packet with an ordinary lease.

Two narrower state rules can apply.

(1) Registered lead-safe property: if you hold a certificate of lead-safe status and the unit is occupied by someone other than you or your immediate family, then 'For tenancy of a dwelling unit under a rental agreement, the property owner shall ensure that a lead-safe information pamphlet under subd. 3. and a form under subd. 4. is delivered by personal, postal or delivery service to an adult occupant or other responsible occupant entering into a tenancy under a rental agreement' (Wis. Admin. Code DHS § 163.42(3)(b)2.a.).

The pamphlet comes from or is approved by the Department of Health Services, and the form lets the tenant report deteriorated paint and other potential lead hazards. Deliver them 'prior to the start of tenancy, entering into a rental agreement or accepting earnest money or a security deposit, whichever is later' (Wis. Admin. Code DHS § 163.42(3)(b)6.a.), and, for a certificate issued for 3 years or more, again at least every 13 months while the tenancy continues unless you post the pamphlet in each unit (Wis. Admin. Code DHS § 163.42(3)(b)7.). They may go out with the federal disclosure.

(2) Renovation: no more than 60 days before renovation work that disturbs paint in pre-1978 housing, the company doing the work must give the Renovate Right pamphlet to the owner and, if the unit is not owner-occupied, to an adult occupant, and must give written notice to affected units (Wis. Admin. Code DHS § 163.14(10)(a)).

See "Lead Paint in Wisconsin Rentals" for lead orders and certificates.

Milwaukee, Madison and other municipalities may have their own rules.

title: Code Orders and Nuisance Receivership
bodyText: Wisconsin lets local governments, and in some cases tenants, force repairs of substandard rental property through the courts, ending in a receiver who runs the building. (1) Nuisance or health hazard action: if property violates the health or safety provisions of a municipal building code or a local board of health order, the city, village or town may sue to declare it a nuisance or human health hazard; a tenant or class of tenants may petition the municipality to sue and may sue directly if it does not act within 20 days (Wis. Stat. § 254.595(1)). After judgment you have 60 days to eliminate the violation; if the judgment is not set aside, the court appoints a receiver who 'shall collect all rents and profits accruing from the property' and makes the repairs (Wis. Stat. § 254.595(2), (3)(a)). This does not apply to owner-occupied one- or two-family dwellings, and a tenant's action 'is not just cause for eviction' (Wis. Stat. § 254.595(7), (8)). (2) Receivership for residential nuisances: at least 60 days after written notice to owners and interested parties, a municipality may ask the court to appoint a receiver for residential property that is a nuisance (Wis. Stat. § 823.23(2)(a), (b)). The receiver may 'Take possession and control of the residential property including the right to enter into and terminate tenancies' and collect rents (Wis. Stat. § 823.23(3)(a)1.), and its court-approved unpaid costs become a lien with priority over most other liens (Wis. Stat. § 823.23(5)(b), (6)(c)). While an action is brought or anticipated, you may not raise rent, cut services, seek possession or refuse to renew if the tenant proves you would not have done so but for the action and also that no nuisance was found as to the unit, that the tenant did not cause it, or that your step is not necessary to abate it; and any notice of such an action must 'state the basis for the action and the right of the tenant to contest the action' (Wis. Stat. § 823.23(4)(b), (e)). (3) Health hazard orders: a local health officer may order a hazard abated within 30 days and charge the cost as a special tax on the property (Wis. Stat. § 254.59(2); "Local Health Rules for Rentals"). Local rental inspection programs are limited by state law ("Local Rental Inspections"), and you may not rent premises that are placarded and condemned or under a raze order until the required repairs are done ("Condemned Premises"). Milwaukee, Madison and other municipalities may have their own rules.

title: Code Variances and Tenants
bodyText: Wisconsin has no statute or administrative rule requiring you to tell tenants about, or attach to the lease, a variance, exception or waiver granted from a building, housing, health or fire code, with one exception that ends soon: if your property is served by its own public water system, you are its water supplier and, until January 1, 2027, must give public notice of operation under a drinking-water variance or exemption, repeated annually (Wis. Admin. Code NR § 809.953(1)(b)3., (2)(a)), and a community water system must give new customers, when service begins, a copy of the latest notice of 'the existence of a variance or exemption' (Wis. Admin. Code NR § 809.955(1)); from January 1, 2027, CR 25-069 removes the variance items from those rules. Variances exist: for one- and two-family dwellings under the uniform dwelling code, 'The department may grant a variance to a rule only if the variance does not result in lowering the level of health, safety and welfare established or intended by the rule' (Wis. Admin. Code SPS § 320.19), on a petition submitted through the municipality that enforces the code; petitions under other state building rules follow Wis. Admin. Code SPS § 303.01. A variance changes how a code requirement is met, not your duties to the tenant: before signing you must still disclose any uncorrected code violation you know of that presents a significant threat to the tenant's health or safety, and the listed habitability conditions (Wis. Admin. Code ATCP § 134.04(2); "Code Violations and Habitability Conditions" clause). A municipality may not require you to give tenants information that state or federal law does not require (Wis. Stat. § 66.0104(2)(d)1.a.). Milwaukee, Madison and other municipalities may have their own rules.

title: No Certificate of Occupancy Disclosure
bodyText: Wisconsin has no statute or administrative rule requiring you to tell a tenant whether the unit has a certificate of occupancy or occupancy permit, or to attach one to the lease. Local occupancy permits for new construction are a building-code matter between you and the municipality. A municipality generally may not make you hold a certificate or license to rent: no ordinance may require 'that a rental property or rental unit be certified, registered, or licensed' or that an owner 'obtain a certification or license related to owning or managing the residential rental property', except a registration limited to one owner or contact name and contact details (Wis. Stat. § 66.0104(2)(e)4.; "Local Rental Registration"). What you must disclose before signing is the condition of the unit: uncorrected building or housing code violations you know of that affect the unit or a common area and present a significant threat to the tenant's health or safety, and the listed habitability conditions (Wis. Admin. Code ATCP § 134.04(2); "Code Violations and Habitability Conditions" clause). You may not rent premises that have been placarded and condemned, or are under a raze or similar order, until the required repairs are done (Wis. Admin. Code ATCP § 134.09(1); "Condemned Premises"). Milwaukee, Madison and other municipalities may have their own rules.

title: No Occupancy Presumption Notice
bodyText: Wisconsin has no statute or administrative rule that presumes a tenant of a single-family home lacks lawful occupancy unless the lease is notarized, signed by a licensed property manager or lists the landlord's contact details, and none that requires a large-type notice about such a presumption on the first page of a lease. A search of the Wisconsin Statutes, Administrative Code, Constitution and 2025 session laws found none. A Wisconsin lease does not need to be notarized. A lease for more than a year is enforceable only if it meets the writing rules (Wis. Stat. § 704.03(1); "When a Lease Must Be in Writing"), and you must disclose in writing, at or before signing, who manages the property and who accepts legal papers for the owner, with an in-state address for service, unless the building is owner-occupied with no more than 4 units (Wis. Admin. Code ATCP § 134.04(1); "Landlord and Agent Identification" clause). Removing someone who is not a tenant is covered in "Squatters and Unauthorized Occupants".

title: Utility Shutoff Protections
bodyText:
Wisconsin's limits on shutting off residential electric, gas and water service are Public Service Commission rules for the utilities, and they protect occupants whoever holds the account.

Winter: for service that provides or affects the primary heat source, the cold weather rules apply 'during the period November 1 to April 15 in any year for all occupied residences' (Wis. Admin. Code PSC § 113.0304(2)(a); Wis. Admin. Code PSC § 134.0624(2)(a)), and 'A utility may disconnect only those households whose gross quarterly incomes are above 250% of the federal income poverty guidelines' and whose health and safety would not be endangered (Wis. Admin. Code PSC § 113.0304(4); Wis. Admin. Code PSC § 134.0624(4)); water service that is a necessary part of the heating system may not be disconnected in that period (Wis. Admin. Code PSC § 185.37(9)).

For lower-income and vulnerable households this works as a winter ban, not an added notice period.

Heat: 'The utility may not disconnect services in affected counties when a heat advisory, heat warning, or heat emergency issued by the national weather service is in effect' (Wis. Admin. Code PSC § 113.0301(16)); the water rule is the same (Wis. Admin. Code PSC § 185.37(8)(h)).

Medical emergencies postpone disconnection for up to 21 days on a physician's or official's statement (Wis. Admin. Code PSC § 113.0301(13)(a)).

Notice: at least 10 days' written notice to the customer (Wis. Admin. Code PSC § 113.0301(10)(a)); if the bill goes to a different address or to 'occupant', 'notice shall be posted at each individual dwelling unit of the service address not less than 5 days before disconnection', telling occupants they may apply to take over future bills (Wis. Admin. Code PSC § 113.0301(10)(b); Wis. Admin. Code PSC § 185.37).

For a jointly metered rental building in your name, the utility must first try to move the debt to your own home or office account (Wis. Admin. Code PSC § 113.0301(1)).

For you as landlord: service 'may not be disconnected or refused for any of the following reasons:... A utility to knowingly assist a landlord in the removal or eviction of a tenant from rental property' (Wis. Admin. Code PSC § 113.0301(8); Wis. Admin. Code PSC § 134.062(6)(g)); you may not constructively evict a tenant 'by any means including the termination or substantial reduction of heat, water or electricity to the dwelling unit' in retaliation (Wis. Admin. Code ATCP § 134.09(5)) or exclude a tenant except by court eviction (Wis. Admin. Code ATCP § 134.09(7)); and when a tenant ends service, you may ask for termination only by affirming 'that service termination will not endanger human health or life or cause damage to property' (Wis. Stat. § 196.643(1)).

See "Utility Accounts and Shutoffs", "Unpaid Municipal Utility Bills" and "Authorization for Notice of Electric Disconnection" clause.

title: Splitting Shared Utility Bills
bodyText:
Wisconsin lets you charge tenants a share of utilities that are not separately metered, but only with disclosure before signing: 'If individual dwelling units and common areas are not separately metered, and if the charges are not included in the rent, the landlord shall disclose the basis on which charges for utility services will be allocated among individual dwelling units' (Wis. Admin. Code ATCP § 134.04(3)), before entering into the lease or accepting earnest money or a security deposit ("Utility Charge Allocation" clause).

No Wisconsin statute or administrative rule makes such a term unenforceable, caps the allocation or prescribes a formula.

Related rules: 'If gas, electric or water service is measured jointly for 2 or more rental dwelling units, the owner shall maintain the account for gas, electric or water service in the name of the owner or in the name of the agent responsible for the collection of rent and the management of the rental dwelling units' (Wis. Stat. § 196.643(2)); each unit in a multi-unit residential building built after March 1, 1980 needs its own electric meter unless an exception applies (Wis. Admin. Code PSC § 113.0803(1); "Separate Electric Meters"); where individual metering is provided or required, common-area electric loads must be separately metered (Wis. Admin. Code PSC § 113.0802(3)); and the electric utility must inspect for joint metering when a tenant reasonably suspects being billed for equipment serving more than one unit, and may bill you for the inspection (Wis. Admin. Code PSC § 113.0802(4)).

Unpaid allocated charges may be taken from the deposit as 'Payment that the tenant owes under the rental agreement for utility service provided by the landlord but not included in the rent' (Wis. Stat. § 704.28(1)(c)).

For gas, no person may operate a 'master meter system', a gas pipeline system in an area such as a housing project or apartment complex through which the operator resells purchased gas to consumers who pay by meter 'or by other means such as rents' (Wis. Admin. Code PSC § 133.02(8); Wis. Admin. Code PSC § 135.018); if your property distributes gas that way, take advice before allocating gas charges.

For electricity and water, whether a landlord who meters and resells them to tenants becomes a regulated public utility is not settled by the definition in Wis. Stat. § 196.01(5)(a) without case law; the cautious course is to pass through only the utility's actual charges on the disclosed basis, with no markup or billing fee.

title: No Submetered Electric Regime
bodyText: Wisconsin has no statute or administrative rule setting a special regime for interrupting electric service that a landlord submeters or allocates to tenants. A search of the Wisconsin Statutes, Administrative Code, Constitution and 2025 session laws found none. Instead, each unit in a multi-unit residential building built after March 1, 1980 must have its own utility electric meter unless an exception applies (Wis. Admin. Code PSC § 113.0803(1); "Separate Electric Meters"), and where individual metering is provided or required, 'each customer or tenant is metered for his or her own consumption only' (Wis. Admin. Code PSC § 113.0802(3)). Whoever bills the tenant, you may not cut off or reduce service to force a tenant out: no landlord may 'constructively evict a tenant by any means including the termination or substantial reduction of heat, water or electricity to the dwelling unit' in retaliation (Wis. Admin. Code ATCP § 134.09(5)), or exclude a tenant other than by court eviction (Wis. Admin. Code ATCP § 134.09(7)). The utility's own shutoff protections are in "Utility Shutoff Protections"; the tenant's lease duty not to interrupt services is "Utility Service Continuity" clause.

title: Utility Account Transfers
bodyText: Wisconsin has no statute or administrative rule setting a deadline for a tenant to put utility accounts in the tenant's own name, or letting you cut off service the tenant has not transferred. A search of the Wisconsin Statutes, Administrative Code, Constitution and 2025 session laws found none. The library does not offer a clause letting you shut off untransferred service, because cutting service to an occupied unit risks an unlawful constructive eviction: no landlord may 'exclude, forcibly evict or constructively evict a tenant from a dwelling unit, other than by an eviction procedure specified under ch. 799' (Wis. Admin. Code ATCP § 134.09(7)), and a utility may not knowingly help a landlord remove a tenant ("Utility Shutoff Protections"). The rules that do apply: if gas, electric or water service 'is measured jointly for 2 or more rental dwelling units', the account must stay in your name or your managing agent's name (Wis. Stat. § 196.643(2)), so only separately metered service can be moved to the tenant. When a tenant ends service and no responsible party is identified, the utility may hold you responsible unless, within 15 days after its notice is mailed, you name the responsible party or ask for termination and affirm 'that service termination will not endanger human health or life or cause damage to property' (Wis. Stat. § 196.643(1)); a utility may not require proof of eviction to serve the unit in your name (Wis. Stat. § 196.643(4); "Utility Accounts and Shutoffs"). You may write your own clause requiring the tenant to open separately metered accounts in the tenant's name by a set date and to reimburse you the provider's actual charges for any period the account stayed in your name, provided it does not let you interrupt service, is not called rent and carries no late fee.

title: Utility Disclosures Before Signing
bodyText:
Wisconsin prescribes no utility disclosure form or attachment for a lease.

What it requires is a disclosure before signing: 'If charges for water, heat or electricity are not included in the rent, the landlord shall disclose this fact to the tenant before entering into a rental agreement or accepting any earnest money or security deposit from the prospective tenant', and if units and common areas are not separately metered and the charges are not in the rent, you must also disclose 'the basis on which charges for utility services will be allocated among individual dwelling units' (Wis. Admin. Code ATCP § 134.04(3); "Utility Charge Allocation" clause).

The disclosure may be in writing on any form, as long as it comes before the lease is signed or money is taken.

Before signing you must also disclose service conditions you know of or could find by reasonable inspection: no hot or cold running water, no electricity or an unsafe electrical system, heating that is unsafe or cannot keep living areas at 67°F, or plumbing or sewage disposal not in good operating condition (Wis. Admin. Code ATCP § 134.04(2)(b)1., 2., 3., 5., 6.; "Code Violations and Habitability Conditions" clause).

A search of the Wisconsin Statutes, Administrative Code, Constitution and 2025 session laws found no other required utility disclosure for leases (cost estimates or tariffs).

Prospective tenants can get usage history themselves: an electric or gas utility 'shall provide on request to current or prospective customers, tenants or property owners residential energy consumption information', the average for the prior 12 months or the highest and lowest amounts (Wis. Admin. Code PSC § 113.0501(5); Wis. Admin. Code PSC § 134.05(5)).

If the electric account is with an electric cooperative and carries a project electric account charge, a separate notice is required ("Efficiency Charges on the Electric Bill").

title: Efficiency Charges on the Electric Bill
bodyText:
Wisconsin has an on-bill charge that can follow a property's electric account, but only for electric cooperatives. A cooperative may finance energy efficiency, energy conservation, electric safety or emergency backup generation projects for a member or the member's landlord and recover the costs as a 'project electric account charge' on the electric bill (Wis. Stat. § 185.995(1)(c), (3)).

If the agreement is between the cooperative and you as landlord, the charge may go on the member's account only if 'the landlord and tenant consent in writing' (Wis. Stat. § 185.995(2)(d)); if the agreement is with a tenant member and is to bind later occupants, both you and the tenant must consent in writing (Wis. Stat. § 185.995(2)(e)2.).

The charge can pass to later owners or tenants only if the cooperative recorded a notice of electric account charge with the register of deeds before the change in tenancy (Wis. Stat. § 185.995(4), (5)).

Your duty: give each later tenant who will pay the electric bills notice of the written agreement and a copy of the notice of electric account charge before the lease is signed (Wis. Stat. § 185.995(6)).

If you do not, 'the subsequent lessee may void the lease and is entitled to the return of any deposits made under or with respect to the lease or may deduct from the lessee’s rent, for no more than one-half of the term of the lease, the amount of the charges for which the subsequent lessee is responsible under this subsection' (Wis. Stat. § 185.995(6)). Use "Electric Cooperative Account Charge" clause to record delivery.

Wisconsin has no rule on landlords submetering water for tenants outside manufactured home communities, whose operators' water and sewer billing rules (Wis. Admin. Code ch. SPS 326) are outside this library.

title: Getting Tenant Utility Usage Data
bodyText:
Wisconsin has no statute or administrative rule that lets a lease clause authorize a utility to release a tenant's energy usage data to you, or that requires building energy benchmarking.

Two rules already give owners some data. An electric or gas utility 'shall provide on request to current or prospective customers, tenants or property owners residential energy consumption information', either the 12-month average or the highest and lowest amounts, and doing so 'is neither a breach of customer confidentiality nor a guarantee or contract by the utility as to future consumption levels for the premises in question' (Wis. Admin. Code PSC § 113.0501(5); Wis. Admin. Code PSC § 134.05(5)).

A city, village or town utility 'may not release customer information to any person except with the consent of the customer obtained on a form specified' by the Public Service Commission, but it may release it to 'An owner of real property provided with municipal utility service or the owner’s designated agent or representative' (Wis. Stat. § 196.137(2), (2)(cr)).

For more detailed data from another utility, you need the tenant's consent in the form that utility requires; the optional clause "Energy Usage Data Authorization" has the tenant sign that release on request, limits your use of the data and lets the tenant withdraw without breaching the lease.

title: Utility Deposits and the Security Deposit
bodyText: Wisconsin has no separate rule for a utility deposit that a landlord collects; a search of the Wisconsin Statutes, Administrative Code, Constitution and 2025 session laws found none. Any money you hold for utility charges is part of the security deposit, which means 'the total of all payments and deposits given by a tenant to the landlord as security for the performance of the tenant’s obligations' (Wis. Admin. Code ATCP § 134.02(11)), so it is returned with the deposit within 21 days under the usual rules ("Return of Security Deposit" clause). The standard withholding list names utilities twice: you may withhold amounts reasonably necessary to pay 'Payment that the tenant owes under the rental agreement for utility service provided by the landlord but not included in the rent' and 'Payment that the tenant owes for direct utility service provided by a government-owned utility, to the extent that the landlord becomes liable for the tenant’s nonpayment' (Wis. Stat. § 704.28(1)(c), (d)). Utility charges outside those two items, such as a bill you chose to pay on a tenant's private utility account, can be withheld only under a signed NONSTANDARD RENTAL PROVISIONS document (Wis. Stat. § 704.28(2); "Nonstandard Rental Provisions: Deposit Withholding" clause). Deposits a tenant pays to the utility itself are the utility's to refund: on termination of residential electric service 'the utility shall credit the deposit, with accrued interest, to the customer’s final bill and return the balance within 30 days of issuing the final bill' (Wis. Admin. Code PSC § 113.0402(13)).

title: Which Fire and Building Codes Apply
bodyText: Which Wisconsin code reaches your rental depends on the building. (1) Buildings with 3 or more tenants are 'public buildings', a structure used 'by the public or by 3 or more tenants' (Wis. Stat. § 101.01(12)). Their use, operation and maintenance must comply with the state fire code, which incorporates 'NFPA 1, Fire Code — 2012, subject to the modifications specified in this chapter' (Wis. Admin. Code SPS § 314.001(1)); a municipality may instead enforce an equivalent alternate model fire code, and then owners need comply only with that ordinance (Wis. Admin. Code SPS § 314.001(2)). Their construction and alteration follow the commercial building code, which incorporates the 2021 International Building, Energy Conservation, Mechanical, Fuel Gas and Existing Building Codes with Wisconsin's modifications (Wis. Admin. Code SPS § 361.05; Wis. Admin. Code SPS § 361.02). So the fire code and the building code adopt different model codes and editions. (2) One- and two-family dwellings built on or after June 1, 1980 are under the uniform dwelling code (Wis. Admin. Code SPS § 320.02(1)(a); Wis. Admin. Code SPS § 320.03), which 'are not retroactive, except as specifically stated in a rule' (Wis. Admin. Code SPS § 320.02(4)), and a municipality 'may not adopt an ordinance on any subject falling within the scope of this code' (Wis. Admin. Code SPS § 320.02(2)(a)). (3) Elevators: 'No person may allow a conveyance to be operated on property owned by the person unless the person has received a permit' from the Department of Safety and Professional Services, issued after an inspection, for a one-year term and displayed on or in the conveyance or in the machinery room (Wis. Stat. § 101.983(2)(a), (c), (d)); this does not apply to 'elevators or dumbwaiters that serve individual residential dwelling units' (Wis. Stat. § 101.983(2)(e)). Smoke and carbon monoxide detector duties are statutory and apply to all rentals ("Smoke and Carbon Monoxide Detectors"); sprinklers are in "No Sprinkler Disclosure". The model codes themselves are not reproduced in Wisconsin's code. Milwaukee, Madison and other municipalities may have their own rules.

title: No Sprinkler Disclosure
bodyText: Wisconsin has no statute or administrative rule requiring you to tell tenants whether the building has a fire sprinkler system, and none offering private owners grants, loans or tax credits for sprinkler retrofits. Whether a building must have sprinklers is a building-code question. The commercial building code requires an automatic sprinkler system 'throughout all buildings with a Group R fire area' (Wis. Admin. Code SPS § 362.0903), except that a multifamily dwelling of not more than 4 units and 2 stories that is not on a community or municipal water system, and some townhouses, may use the lighter NFPA 13D sprinkler standard, and townhouses of not more than 2 stories with 2-hour separation walls may be built without sprinklers (Wis. Admin. Code SPS § 362.0903(5)(b) to (d), (10)); buildings more than 60 feet tall and student housing have their own rules (Wis. Admin. Code SPS § 362.0903(6), (7)). By statute the state must require a sprinkler system or 2-hour fire resistance in a multifamily dwelling with more than 20 dwelling units, more than 16,000 square feet of unit floor area, or common-area floor area above the limits for its construction type, and a county, city, village or town may enact ordinances 'that require an automatic fire sprinkler system or 2-hour fire resistance in every multifamily dwelling' within the statute's standards (Wis. Stat. § 101.14(4m)(am), (b)). One- and two-family dwellings are under the uniform dwelling code ("Which Fire and Building Codes Apply"). See also "Fire Sprinklers and Grills". Milwaukee, Madison and other municipalities may have their own rules.

title: Code Editions Adopted by Reference
bodyText: Wisconsin's building and fire rules incorporate outside codes by named edition, so the edition in the rule, not the newest one, is what applies until the rule is amended. The fire code incorporates 'NFPA 1, Fire Code — 2012' (Wis. Admin. Code SPS § 314.001(1)(a)); the commercial building code incorporates the 2021 International Building, Energy Conservation, Mechanical, Fuel Gas and Existing Building Codes (Wis. Admin. Code SPS § 361.05, as amended effective September 1, 2025); and the uniform dwelling code incorporates the dated standards listed in its tables (Wis. Admin. Code SPS § 320.24(2)), with alternate standards allowed only if 'equivalent to or more stringent than the standards incorporated by reference' and approved by the department (Wis. Admin. Code SPS § 320.24(3)(a)). When the department adopts a new edition, a new building is held to the code in effect for it, and the uniform dwelling code is 'not retroactive, except as specifically stated in a rule' (Wis. Admin. Code SPS § 320.02(4)). Wisconsin's landlord-tenant statute and the DATCP rental rules mostly state their own duties; the main exception is the repair statute, which makes compliance with any local housing code applicable to the premises a landlord duty (Wis. Stat. § 704.07(2)(a)5.), so the local code as currently in force applies. If a lease or a building rule refers to a code, name the code and edition, or say "as amended", so the reference does not freeze an old edition by accident. The incorporated model codes are not reproduced in Wisconsin's code.

title: Common-Area Lights and Tenant Meters
bodyText: In Wisconsin you may not wire common-area lights to a tenant's electric meter in a building where units are individually metered. The Public Service Commission's rule says that in multi-unit residential buildings 'where individual unit metering is provided, or required' (Wis. Admin. Code PSC § 113.0802(3)) the wiring 'shall be so installed or arranged so that each customer or tenant is metered for his or her own consumption only. Energy used by common area loads, for example, hallway lighting and heating, shall be separately metered and billed as appropriate under the utility’s filed tariff' (Wis. Admin. Code PSC § 113.0802(3)). Units in multi-unit residential buildings built after March 1, 1980 must be individually metered unless an exception applies (Wis. Admin. Code PSC § 113.0803(1); "Separate Electric Meters"). If a tenant reasonably suspects being billed for significant usage serving more than one unit, the utility must inspect and may bill you for the inspection (Wis. Admin. Code PSC § 113.0802(4)). So the library offers no clause making a tenant pay for shared-area lighting through the tenant's own service. Where the building is not individually metered and the charges are not in the rent, you must disclose before signing how utility charges will be allocated among units (Wis. Admin. Code ATCP § 134.04(3); "Utility Charge Allocation" clause). Keeping the lighting in the common areas working is your duty: you must 'Keep in a reasonable state of repair portions of the premises over which the landlord maintains control' (Wis. Stat. § 704.07(2)(a)1.), and the duty cannot be waived in a residential lease ("Repair Duties Cannot Be Waived"). Required lighting levels for hallways and exits come from the building codes. Milwaukee, Madison and other municipalities may have their own rules.

title: Stoves and Refrigerators
bodyText:
Wisconsin has no statute or administrative rule requiring you to supply a stove, range or refrigerator in a rental unit.

If you do furnish appliances, you must keep them working: unless the premises are subject to a local housing code, you must 'repair or replace any plumbing, electrical wiring, machinery, or equipment furnished with the premises and no longer in reasonable working condition' (Wis. Stat. § 704.07(2)(a)4.), except that the tenant must keep furnished equipment in reasonable working order 'if repair can be made at cost which is minor in relation to the rent' (Wis. Stat. § 704.07(3)(b)); where a local housing code applies, you must comply with it (Wis. Stat. § 704.07(2)(a)5.).

An appliance that cannot be used without a risk of fire or electrocution is a substantial violation materially affecting health or safety, entitling the tenant to rent abatement (Boelter v. Tschantz, 2010 WI App 18, as summarized in the annotation to Wis. Stat. § 704.07).

An agreement waiving these duties in a residential lease is void (Wis. Stat. § 704.07(1); "Repair Duties Cannot Be Waived"), so the library does not offer a clause excluding furnished appliances from your repair duty; list what you furnish in "Appliances & Equipment Included" clause.

If the tenant brings their own appliance, say so in the lease and on the check-in sheet so it is not treated as equipment furnished with the premises.

Milwaukee, Madison and other municipalities may have their own housing codes.

title: No Radiator Cover Rule
bodyText: Wisconsin has no statute or administrative rule requiring you to install steam radiator covers on request or to attach a radiator-cover rider to the lease. Radiator guards are required only in licensed child care centers, camps and similar facilities; that includes a family child care center a tenant runs in your unit, where the duty is the licensed provider's, not yours (Wis. Admin. Code DCF § 250.06(2)(a); "Family Child Care in a Rental"). Your general duties still apply: you must keep in reasonable repair the equipment you control that supplies heat (Wis. Stat. § 704.07(2)(a)2.; "Heat"), and a condition that is a substantial hazard to the tenant's health or safety must be disclosed before signing (Wis. Admin. Code ATCP § 134.04(2)(b)4.; "Code Violations and Habitability Conditions" clause). Covering an exposed steam radiator in a unit where young children live is a sensible precaution. Milwaukee, Madison and other municipalities may have their own rules.

title: No Balcony Inspection Rule
bodyText: Wisconsin has no statute or administrative rule requiring periodic inspection of balconies, decks or other exterior elevated elements of rental buildings. The building codes govern how balconies and decks are built: the uniform dwelling code reaches 'All garages, carports, porches, stoops, decks, balconies, stairways and similar structures' attached to a one- or two-family dwelling built on or after its effective date (Wis. Admin. Code SPS § 320.02(1)(g)), and the commercial building code governs larger buildings, including sprinkler protection for some balconies (Wis. Admin. Code SPS § 362.0903(9)). Keeping them safe afterward is part of your repair duty: you must 'Keep in a reasonable state of repair portions of the premises over which the landlord maintains control' and 'Make all necessary structural repairs' (Wis. Stat. § 704.07(2)(a)1., 3.), and a structural condition that is a substantial hazard must be disclosed before signing (Wis. Admin. Code ATCP § 134.04(2)(b)4.; "Code Violations and Habitability Conditions" clause). Having older wood balconies and decks checked on a regular schedule is good practice. Milwaukee, Madison and other municipalities may have their own rules.

title: Private Wells Serving Rentals
