bodyText: Wisconsin has no statute or administrative rule requiring you to test a private well that serves a rental, or to give tenants well test results. A search of the Wisconsin Statutes, Administrative Code, Constitution and 2025 session laws found none. Two rules can still reach you. (1) A well serving many people is a public water system: 'a system for the provision to the public of piped water for human consumption' with 'at least 15 service connections' or that 'regularly serves an average of at least 25 individuals daily at least 60 days out of the year' (Wis. Admin. Code NR § 809.04(67)). It is a community water system if it serves at least 15 connections used by year-round residents or at least 25 year-round residents, and a system serving 10 or more apartment units is presumed to be one (Wis. Admin. Code NR § 809.04(5)). The owner or operator is the 'water supplier' (Wis. Admin. Code NR § 809.04(91)) and must meet the Department of Natural Resources' monitoring and public notice rules, for example giving a Tier 2 public notice 'no later than 30 days after the public water system learns of the violation' (Wis. Admin. Code NR § 809.952(2)(a)); those notices are meant to reach people who do not pay the water bill, such as renters. (2) When a licensed pump installer or well driller works on a well, the installer must collect water samples for a certified laboratory and report the results (Wis. Admin. Code NR § 812.27(6); Wis. Admin. Code NR § 812.46), and must notify the well owner within 48 hours of learning the water exceeds the standards (Wis. Admin. Code NR § 812.27(7)). If you learn that well water is unsafe, it is a condition hazardous to health that you must disclose before signing (Wis. Admin. Code ATCP § 134.04(2)(b)4.; "Code Violations and Habitability Conditions" clause). Testing a rental's private well for bacteria and nitrate at least yearly is good practice.

title: Elevators and Other Shared Facilities
bodyText: Wisconsin has no statute or administrative rule listing building facilities, such as garage door openers, laundry rooms or intercoms, that a landlord must supply or maintain beyond the general repair duty. A search of the Wisconsin Statutes, Administrative Code, Constitution and 2025 session laws found none. The general duty covers what you do supply: you must 'Keep in a reasonable state of repair all equipment under the landlord’s control necessary to supply services that the landlord has expressly or impliedly agreed to furnish to the tenant, such as heat, water, elevator, or air conditioning' (Wis. Stat. § 704.07(2)(a)2.), and, except where the premises are subject to a local housing code (which you must then follow, Wis. Stat. § 704.07(2)(a)5.) and except for minor repairs the tenant must make under Wis. Stat. § 704.07(3)(b), repair or replace equipment furnished with the premises (Wis. Stat. § 704.07(2)(a)4.); the duty cannot be waived in a residential lease (Wis. Stat. § 704.07(1)). Specific facilities: an elevator, escalator or similar conveyance may not be operated on your property without a one-year operating permit issued after inspection and displayed on or in the conveyance or in the machinery room, except elevators or dumbwaiters that serve individual residential dwelling units (Wis. Stat. § 101.983(2); "Which Fire and Building Codes Apply"); a pool serving 3 or more units is a licensed public pool ("Pools at Rental Properties"); and smoke and carbon monoxide detectors have their own rules. Describe in the lease which shared facilities come with the unit ("Use of Property & Common Areas" clause, "Appliances & Equipment Included" clause).

title: Asbestos in Rental Buildings
bodyText: Wisconsin has no statute or administrative rule requiring you to notify or disclose to tenants that a building contains asbestos. A search of the Wisconsin Statutes, Administrative Code, Constitution and 2025 session laws found none. Asbestos work is regulated instead. An asbestos abatement company 'shall protect the health of occupants, visitors, workers, and any other persons near an asbestos abatement activity' (Wis. Admin. Code DHS § 159.21(1)), and when the structure is occupied or furnished, 'A written occupant protection plan shall be posted in plain view outside each regulated area', describing how occupants will be protected (Wis. Admin. Code DHS § 159.21(3)). Hire a company certified by the Department of Health Services for abatement work; the Department of Natural Resources' asbestos rules (Wis. Admin. Code ch. NR 447) also apply to renovation and demolition. Your general disclosure duty still applies: before entering into the lease or accepting any earnest money or security deposit, disclose conditions you know of or could find by reasonable inspection that 'constitute a substantial hazard to the health or safety of the tenant' (Wis. Admin. Code ATCP § 134.04(2)(b)4.; "Code Violations and Habitability Conditions" clause), such as damaged or crumbling asbestos material in the unit.

title: Bed Bug and Pest Cooperation
bodyText:
Wisconsin has no statute or administrative rule on bed bugs in rentals or on how a landlord and tenant must cooperate over pest treatment.

The general rules decide it. Treating an infestation is part of your repair duty unless the tenant caused it: 'If the premises are damaged, including by an infestation of insects or other pests, due to the acts or inaction of the tenant', you may let the tenant remediate it or do it yourself and recover your reasonable cost (Wis. Stat. § 704.07(3)(a); "Damage Caused by Tenant" clause).

Where a local ordinance makes it a violation, an infestation by rodents or insects is a 'habitability violation' for the purposes of local rental inspection programs (Wis. Stat. § 66.0104(1)(ah)8.), and an infestation you know of or could find by reasonable inspection that is a substantial hazard to the tenant's health or safety must be disclosed before entering into the lease or accepting any earnest money or security deposit (Wis. Admin. Code ATCP § 134.04(2)(b)4.; "Pests, Bed Bugs and Mold").

Entry for inspection and treatment follows the ordinary entry rule: at reasonable times with at least 12 hours' advance notice unless the tenant consents to a shorter time or to the entry, a health or safety emergency exists, or the tenant is absent and you reasonably believe entry is necessary to protect the premises from damage (Wis. Admin. Code ATCP § 134.09(2)).

The optional clause "Bed Bugs and Pest Treatment" asks the tenant to report suspected pests, allow treatment and follow preparation instructions.

Milwaukee, Madison and other municipalities may have their own rules.

title: Notice When Pesticides Are Applied
bodyText: Wisconsin requires written notice to residents whenever a pesticide (other than a germicide, sanitizer or disinfectant) is applied to a residential structure, including a rental building, and the duty falls on whoever makes the application, including you. 'A person making a residential application shall provide the following information in writing to residents at the time of the application' (Wis. Admin. Code ATCP § 29.55(3)(a)): who made the application and how to reach them, the applicator's name and license number if a license is required, the pesticide used, the amount and area treated, any post-application precautions on the label, the date and approximate times, that a copy of the label is available on request, and a specific description of where it was applied. For an application inside a unit, the applicator must leave the information with an adult resident 'or shall prominently post the information at the entrance to that dwelling unit' (Wis. Admin. Code ATCP § 29.55(3)(b)); for common areas or a perimeter barrier, it must be posted 'in common entryways or other conspicuous locations so that all residents are likely to see the notices' (Wis. Admin. Code ATCP § 29.55(3)(c)). If the label prescribes a restricted entry interval, a warning sign must be posted at each entrance to the treated area before the application and left until the interval ends (Wis. Admin. Code ATCP § 29.55(4)); the person who operates or controls the premises and the applicator are 'individually and jointly responsible for posting warning signs' (Wis. Admin. Code ATCP § 29.52(3)(b)). The rule's own note says 'a landlord making a residential application to the landlord’s own rental units must provide information to tenants residing in those units' (Wis. Admin. Code ATCP § 29.55(3)). A tenant who applies a pesticide only inside the tenant's own unit is not covered (Wis. Admin. Code ATCP § 29.55(1)(d)). Give the required notice of entry before going in to treat ("Entering a Tenant's Unit").

title: No Mold Disclosure Rule
bodyText: Wisconsin has no statute or administrative rule requiring a mold disclosure, notice or pamphlet for rentals. Mold still matters in three ways. (1) Before entering into the lease or accepting any earnest money or security deposit, you must disclose conditions you know of or could find by reasonable inspection that 'constitute a substantial hazard to the health or safety of the tenant' (Wis. Admin. Code ATCP § 134.04(2)(b)4.; "Code Violations and Habitability Conditions" clause), which can include serious mold. (2) For local rental inspection programs, a unit that 'contains excessive mold' has a habitability violation, if the condition is an ordinance violation (Wis. Stat. § 66.0104(1)(ah)9.; "Local Rental Inspections"). (3) Your repair duty covers the causes, such as leaks, and cannot be waived in a residential lease (Wis. Stat. § 704.07(1), (2); "Repair Duties Cannot Be Waived"); if the tenant's acts or inaction caused the damage, the tenant pays the reasonable cost of repair (Wis. Stat. § 704.07(3)(a); "Damage Caused by Tenant" clause). See also "Pests, Bed Bugs and Mold". Milwaukee, Madison and other municipalities may have their own rules.

title: Contamination and Continuing Obligations
bodyText:
Wisconsin's cleanup rules can put an environmental condition into your lease. When an agency closes a contaminated site under Wis. Stat. ch. 292, it may impose a continuing obligation, such as keeping a cap or cover in place, operating a vapor mitigation system, keeping an inspection log or long-term monitoring.

Anyone who owns or occupies the property must 'Comply with the requirements imposed by the agency, without regard to when the person obtained or occupied the property' and allow the agency reasonable access to inspect (Wis. Admin. Code NR § 727.05(1)).

The owner must tell anyone buying the property about the obligation (Wis. Admin. Code NR § 727.05(2)), and 'For cases where occupants are responsible for maintenance of a continuing obligation under either s. NR 708.17 or 722.15 or ch. NR 726, the property owner shall include the continuing obligation in the lease agreement' (Wis. Admin. Code NR § 727.05(3)); use "Environmental Continuing Obligation" clause. The private agreement does not move your own responsibility to the agency.

Separately, before entering into the lease or accepting any earnest money or security deposit you must disclose structural or other conditions that 'constitute a substantial hazard to the health or safety of the tenant' that you know of or could find by reasonable inspection, and known uncorrected code violations that present a significant threat to health or safety (Wis. Admin. Code ATCP § 134.04(2)(a), (b)4.; "Code Violations and Habitability Conditions" clause), which can include contamination inside the unit. The federal lead disclosure is separate ("Lead-Based Paint Disclosure" clause).

title: No Defective Drywall Disclosure
bodyText: Wisconsin has no statute or administrative rule requiring you to disclose defective, corrosive or imported drywall to tenants. A search of the Wisconsin Statutes, Administrative Code, Constitution and 2025 session laws found none. The general disclosure still applies: before entering into the lease or accepting any earnest money or security deposit, you must disclose conditions you know of or could find by reasonable inspection that 'constitute a substantial hazard to the health or safety of the tenant' (Wis. Admin. Code ATCP § 134.04(2)(b)4.; "Code Violations and Habitability Conditions" clause), so drywall known to give off corrosive gases or damage wiring would need to be disclosed.

title: No Chemical Warning Rule
bodyText: Wisconsin has no law like California's Proposition 65 requiring warnings about chemicals known to cause cancer or reproductive harm on rental property, and no formaldehyde notice for rentals. A search of the Wisconsin Statutes, Administrative Code, Constitution and 2025 session laws found none. Chemical hazards are handled by the disclosure rules that do exist: substantial hazards to the tenant's health or safety that you know of or could find by reasonable inspection, disclosed before entering into the lease or accepting any earnest money or security deposit (Wis. Admin. Code ATCP § 134.04(2)(b)4.; "Code Violations and Habitability Conditions" clause), the federal lead disclosure for pre-1978 housing ("Lead-Based Paint Disclosure" clause), radon, methamphetamine contamination ("Drug Lab Contamination"), environmental continuing obligations and pesticide application notices ("Notice When Pesticides Are Applied").

title: Ordnance, Demolition and Shared Meters
bodyText: Wisconsin has no statute or administrative rule requiring you to tell prospective tenants about nearby former military ordnance locations or about a demolition permit you have applied for. A search of the Wisconsin Statutes, Administrative Code, Constitution and 2025 session laws found none. Related Wisconsin rules: you may not rent or advertise for rent premises on which 'a notice of intent to placard and condemn, or an order to raze, or to rehabilitate or raze, or any similar order has been received' until the required repairs are done (Wis. Admin. Code ATCP § 134.09(1); "Condemned Premises"); if units and common areas are not separately metered and the charges are not included in the rent, you must disclose the basis for splitting the charges before entering into the lease or accepting any earnest money or security deposit (Wis. Admin. Code ATCP § 134.04(3); "Utility Charge Allocation" clause); and military air zone disclosure is covered in "Military Installation and Airport Zones". If you plan to demolish or convert the building, the termination notice rules still govern ending the tenancy ("Ending a Month-to-Month Tenancy" clause), and a conversion to condominiums or time-shares adds a 120-day notice period during which the tenancy is protected (Wis. Stat. § 703.08(2); Wis. Stat. § 707.50(1m)(b); "Condominium Conversions", "What a Notice to Vacate Can Add").

title: Shoreline Access and Tenants
bodyText: Wisconsin has no statute or administrative rule requiring you to tell tenants about public rights of access to a shoreline, beach or navigable water on or next to the property. A search of the Wisconsin Statutes, Administrative Code, Constitution and 2025 session laws found none. One public-use rule can affect a waterfront rental on a stream: a 'riparian' is 'the owner, lessee or occupant of land that abuts a navigable body of water' (Wis. Stat. § 30.134(1)(d)), and 'Members of the public may use any exposed shore area of a stream without the permission of the riparian only if it is necessary to exit the body of water to bypass an obstruction' (Wis. Stat. § 30.134(2)). Neither you nor your tenant may prohibit that use or charge a fee for it (Wis. Stat. § 30.134(4)(a), (b)); it does not apply to impoundments, artificial ditches or dry streambeds (Wis. Stat. § 30.134(5)). If you rent waterfront property, you may tell the tenant about this rule and describe any piers, boat access or shore areas that come with the unit; zoning and shoreland rules for docks and structures are separate.

title: No Key-Control Mandate
bodyText: Wisconsin has no statute or administrative rule requiring a key-control policy, master-key log or background checks for employees who have access to tenants' units, for apartment complexes of any size. A search of the Wisconsin Statutes, Administrative Code, Constitution and 2025 session laws found none. What the law does control is use of the keys. You or your employees may enter a unit only to inspect, repair or show it, at reasonable times and on at least 12 hours' advance notice unless the tenant consents to a shorter time or an exception applies, and must announce yourselves before entering (Wis. Admin. Code ATCP § 134.09(2); "Entering a Tenant's Unit"). If a tenant gives you a certified copy of a qualifying injunction, release condition or criminal complaint, 'A landlord shall have the locks changed, or may give the tenant permission to change the locks, within 48 hours after receiving a request and certified copy' (Wis. Stat. § 704.16(4)(b)); a tenant you let change the locks must give you a key 'within a reasonable time' (Wis. Stat. § 704.16(4)(b); "Locks and Rekeying"). Keeping keys locked up, logging who holds master keys and screening staff who can enter units are sensible practices that help you show reasonable care.

title: Smart Locks and App-Based Entry
bodyText: Wisconsin has no statute or administrative rule regulating smart locks, keypads, key fobs, app-based or biometric entry systems in rentals, and none letting a domestic-violence survivor demand that whoever manages a connected device's accounts cut off another person's access. A search of the Wisconsin Statutes, Administrative Code, Constitution and 2025 session laws found none. The ordinary rules apply to these systems. Entry by you or your staff, including by remote unlock, is limited to inspecting, repairing or showing the unit, at reasonable times and on at least 12 hours' advance notice unless the tenant consents to a shorter time or an exception applies, and you must announce yourself before entering (Wis. Admin. Code ATCP § 134.09(2); "Entering a Tenant's Unit"). You may not lock a tenant out by disabling a credential, because no landlord may 'exclude, forcibly evict or constructively evict a tenant from a dwelling unit, other than by an eviction procedure specified under ch. 799' (Wis. Admin. Code ATCP § 134.09(7)). When a tenant gives you a qualifying injunction, release condition or criminal complaint, 'a landlord shall change the locks to the tenant’s premises' (Wis. Stat. § 704.16(4)(a)); the statute speaks of locks, and whether reprogramming codes or revoking another person's app credentials satisfies it is not settled, so the cautious course is to do both within the 48-hour period, including any physical key ("Locks and Rekeying"). Entry logs and other data the system collects are not regulated by a landlord-specific statute, but if a business entity holds a tenant's name with fingerprint or other unique biometric data and learns that someone unauthorized has acquired it, the general data-breach statute requires reasonable efforts to notify the tenant within a reasonable time, not over 45 days, unless the data was encrypted or unreadable or the acquisition creates no material risk of identity theft or fraud (Wis. Stat. § 134.98(1)(b)5., (2)(a), (2)(cm), (3)(a)). Tell tenants what the system records and use it only to run and secure the building.

title: No Tenant Cooling-Device Right
bodyText:
Wisconsin has no statute or administrative rule giving tenants a right to install a portable or window air conditioner, or limiting how a lease may restrict one.

Unless a signed lease says otherwise, 'The tenant can make no physical changes in the nature of the premises, including decorating, removing, altering or adding to the structures thereon, without prior consent of the landlord' (Wis. Stat. § 704.05(3)), so a window-mounted or through-the-wall unit needs your consent while a plug-in portable unit usually does not alter the premises.

If you supply air conditioning, you must keep it in a reasonable state of repair (Wis. Stat. § 704.07(2)(a)2.). A tenant with a disability may ask for a reasonable accommodation or modification, such as a cooling unit ("Disability Accommodations and Modifications").

The optional clause "Air Conditioners and Cooling Units" lists the cooling equipment you supply and sets conditions for tenant units.

Milwaukee, Madison and other municipalities may have their own rules.

title: Recycling Notices for 5+ Unit Buildings
bodyText: If your building has 5 or more residential units, Wisconsin's recycling law, carried out through your local recycling ordinance, requires you to provide recycling and tell tenants how to use it. A local recycling program counts as an effective program only if it includes 'A requirement that owners of buildings containing 5 or more dwelling units in the region' (Wis. Stat. § 287.11(2)(c)) provide adequate separate containers, 'Notify tenants at the time of renting or leasing the dwelling and semiannually thereafter of the programs', and provide for collection of the materials tenants separate and their delivery to a recycling facility (Wis. Stat. § 287.11(2)(c)). The Department of Natural Resources' rule for the required local ordinance spells this out for owners or designated agents of a 'Multiple-family dwelling', 'a structure containing 5 or more residential units' (Wis. Admin. Code NR § 544.03(13)): unless the building's waste goes to a processing facility that recovers the recyclables, you must 'Notify tenants in writing at the time of renting or leasing the dwelling and at least semi-annually thereafter of how to appropriately recycle', including what is collected on site, how to prepare it and where drop-off sites are, and provide recycling containers that equal or exceed the number of trash containers and meet one of the volume tests (Wis. Admin. Code NR § 544.06(2)(b)). The ordinance must also require all occupants, including tenants of 1- to 4-unit buildings, to separate the listed recyclables or send the waste to a licensed processing facility that recovers them (Wis. Admin. Code NR § 544.06(2)(a)). Give the move-in notice with the lease and repeat it at least every six months. Your municipality's ordinance sets the details; Milwaukee, Madison and other municipalities may have their own rules.

title: Candidates, Canvassers and Political Signs
bodyText: Wisconsin has no statute or administrative rule requiring you to let political candidates, campaign workers or petition circulators into a rental building to reach tenants, or barring you from limiting canvassing in common areas. Tenants do have a political sign right. During an election campaign period 'any individual may place a sign containing a political message upon residential property owned or occupied by that individual' (Wis. Stat. § 12.04(2)), and 'The renter of residential property may exercise the same right as the owner to place a sign upon the property under sub. (2) in any area of the property occupied exclusively by the renter. The terms of a lease or other agreement under which residential property is occupied shall control in determining whether property is occupied exclusively by a renter' (Wis. Stat. § 12.04(5)(a)). Your lease therefore decides which areas are the tenant's alone; the owner keeps the sign right in areas not occupied exclusively by a renter (Wis. Stat. § 12.04(5)(b)). See "Flags and Political Signs". Tenants may invite guests, including campaign workers, to their own units, and a building access rule should apply the same way whatever the visitor's politics. Milwaukee, Madison and other municipalities may have their own rules.

title: Religious and Cultural Displays
bodyText: Wisconsin has no statute or administrative rule giving tenants a right to display religious or cultural items, such as a mezuzah or holiday decorations, on their door or elsewhere, or limiting how a lease may restrict them. Wisconsin's flag-display protections bind homeowners' associations, cooperatives and condominium associations, not landlords ("Flags and Political Signs"). Your lease may set reasonable, neutral rules for doors, hallways and other common areas, and by default a tenant may not make physical changes to the premises without your consent (Wis. Stat. § 704.05(3)). Apply any display rule the same way to everyone: under the fair housing law, 'Discriminate' includes treating a person 'unequally in a manner described in sub. (2), (2m), or (2r)' because of religion and other protected characteristics (Wis. Stat. § 106.50(1m)(h)), and it is unlawful to discriminate 'By refusing to permit inspection or exacting different or more stringent price, terms or conditions for the sale, lease, financing or rental of housing' (Wis. Stat. § 106.50(2)(b); "Wisconsin Fair Housing"). Milwaukee, Madison and other municipalities may have their own rules.

title: Caring for a Tenant's Animal
bodyText: Wisconsin has no statute or administrative rule giving you a right to enter a rental to feed, check on or remove a tenant's animal, or setting a procedure for an animal a tenant leaves behind, and none that makes a person who feeds or shelters an animal for a set number of days its owner. Your entry rights are the general ones: to inspect, repair or show the unit on advance notice of at least 12 hours, and without that notice when the tenant consents knowing the time, when 'A health or safety emergency exists' (Wis. Admin. Code ATCP § 134.09(2)(b)2.) (an animal in real distress may be one), or when the tenant is absent and you reasonably believe entry is necessary to protect the premises from damage. Entry for any other purpose needs a signed NONSTANDARD RENTAL PROVISIONS document ("Nonstandard Rental Provisions: Entry" clause). A pet is the tenant's property, and you are 'prohibited from seizing or holding a tenant’s property' (Wis. Admin. Code ATCP § 134.09(4)(a)) except as the law allows or under a separate signed NONSTANDARD RENTAL PROVISION, and although Wis. Stat. § 704.05(5) lets you dispose of personal property a departed tenant leaves behind, its text does not say whether it reaches a live animal, so do not keep, rehome or dispose of an animal yourself: call a humane officer or law enforcement officer, who may take custody of 'An abandoned or stray animal' (Wis. Stat. § 173.13(1)(a)1.). Taking a dog in has a cost: for dog-injury liability, 'Owner' 'includes any person who owns, harbors or keeps a dog' (Wis. Stat. § 174.001(5)), and 'the owner of a dog is liable for the full amount of damages caused by the dog' (Wis. Stat. § 174.02(1)(a)). Merely letting a tenant keep a dog does not make you a harborer (Malone v. Fons, 217 Wis. 2d 746 (Ct. App. 1998), as summarized in the annotation to Wis. Stat. § 174.02). The library's pet clause ("Pets" clause) already lets you enter as Wisconsin law permits and notify the tenant's contact, animal control, a humane officer or law enforcement. Milwaukee, Madison and other municipalities may have their own rules.

title: Association Documents for Tenants
bodyText:
Condominium units: if you rent a residential condominium unit for more than one month (or month to month), the tenant is bound by statute to follow the condominium law, the association's rules and bylaws and the declaration, and 'Before a tenant occupies a unit, the unit owner shall provide a copy of the declaration and the association bylaws and rules to the tenant or place the information in the unit' (Wis. Stat. § 703.315(5)).

You must also give the association a copy of a written rental agreement within 5 business days after entering into or renewing it (Wis. Stat. § 703.315(3)).

The library's condominium clause ("Condominium Documents" clause) records the delivery, and "Homeowner / Condominium Association Compliance" clause binds the tenant to the association's rules.

Other associations: Wisconsin has no statute or administrative rule requiring a lease of a home in a homeowners' association or other planned community that is not a condominium to disclose the association's obligations or documents to the tenant, and none that treats a tenant under a long lease as a purchaser owed the condominium sale disclosures, which run to 'the purchaser' in a 'sale of a unit' (Wis. Stat. § 703.33(1)).

Giving the tenant a copy of any covenants or association rules that limit the use of the home is still good practice: you may not misrepresent the 'characteristics' of a unit to induce a rental (Wis. Admin. Code ATCP § 134.09(9)(a)1.), and any written rules you establish, including association rules you adopt as your own, must be furnished for inspection before the lease is entered into and before any earnest money or security deposit is accepted (Wis. Admin. Code ATCP § 134.03(1); "Rules and Regulations" clause).

title: No State Approval of Tribal Land Leases
bodyText: Wisconsin has no statute or administrative rule requiring a government officer to approve a lease of communal, tribal or trust land before it is valid. A search of the Wisconsin Statutes, Administrative Code, Constitution and 2025 session laws found none. Land held in trust for a tribe or its members within a reservation is governed by federal and tribal law; if the home is on such land, check with the tribe and the federal agency before signing.

title: Designated Repairers and Repair Contacts
bodyText: Wisconsin has no statute or administrative rule letting a tenant make repairs and deduct the cost from rent, and none requiring or regulating a lease term that names the repairer a tenant must use. You must, however, disclose to the tenant in writing, at or before the time the lease is entered into, the name and address of the person authorized to manage and maintain the premises who can readily be contacted by the tenant, and give written notice of any change within 10 business days (Wis. Admin. Code ATCP § 134.04(1)(a)1., (b)); this does not apply to an owner-occupied building of 4 or fewer units (Wis. Admin. Code ATCP § 134.04(1)(c)). A search of the Wisconsin Statutes, Administrative Code, Constitution and 2025 session laws found no other. A tenant's remedy when you fail to repair is to move out or have rent abate under Wis. Stat. § 704.07(4), which 'does not authorize rent to be withheld in full, if the tenant remains in possession' (Wis. Stat. § 704.07(4)); see "Tenant Remedies for Untenantable Conditions". One court remedy involves rent: if you fail to comply with a state lead hazard order, a circuit court 'may order the occupants of the affected dwelling or premises to withhold rent in escrow until the owner of the dwelling or premises complies with the order' (Wis. Stat. § 254.30(1)(b)). Where the tenant caused the damage, the choice of repairer is yours: 'the landlord may elect to allow the tenant to remediate or repair the damage' or do the work and be reimbursed its reasonable cost (Wis. Stat. § 704.07(3)(a)); see "Damage Caused by Tenant" clause. The tenant may make no physical changes to the premises without your prior consent (Wis. Stat. § 704.05(3)). You may add your own clause naming a repair contact or the contractors a tenant must use for work you allow, but it may not shift your repair duties to the tenant, since a lease that waives them is void ("Repair Duties Cannot Be Waived").

title: Drug-Free Housing Addenda
bodyText: Wisconsin has no statute or administrative rule requiring, or prescribing the form of, a drug-free or crime-free lease addendum. You do not need one to act on drug activity: you may end a tenancy without a chance to cure, on a written notice, given as Wis. Stat. § 704.21 requires, to vacate at least 5 days later that contains the statements Wis. Stat. § 704.17(3m)(b)1. lists (the basis, a description of the activity, its date and who engaged in it, where to get legal help, and the right to contest), if the tenant, a household member or a guest 'engages in any drug-related criminal activity on or near the premises' (Wis. Stat. § 704.17(3m)(b)1.), which means 'criminal activity that involves the manufacture or distribution of a controlled substance' (Wis. Stat. § 704.17(3m)(a)2.), but not against a tenant who is the victim of the crime, and lease terms for termination contrary to that subsection are invalid (Wis. Stat. § 704.17(5)(b)). The library’s criminal-activity clause uses that route. Be careful with any addendum of your own: a residential rental agreement is void and unenforceable in its entirety if it 'Allows the landlord to terminate the tenancy of a tenant for a crime committed in relation to the rental property and the rental agreement does not include the notice required under s. 704.14' (Wis. Stat. § 704.44(10)), so it must never be used without the domestic abuse protections notice ("Notice of Domestic Abuse Protections" clause). Federally assisted housing programs set their own lease terms on drug-related criminal activity. Milwaukee, Madison and other municipalities may have their own rules.

title: Emergency Contacts and Numbers
bodyText:
Wisconsin has no statute or administrative rule requiring a lease to give an emergency telephone number, a management website or a social-services hotline, and none requiring or limiting a tenant's emergency contact.

What you must disclose in writing at or before signing is the name and address of the person authorized to collect rent and manage and maintain the premises, 'and who can readily be contacted by the tenant' (Wis. Admin. Code ATCP § 134.04(1)(a)1.), and of the owner or agent for service of process, with written notice of any change within 10 business days ("Landlord and Agent Identification" clause); this does not apply to an owner-occupied building of 4 or fewer units.

Asking the tenant for an emergency contact is optional ("Tenant's Emergency Contact" clause), and is separate from the contact to notify if the tenant dies or becomes incapacitated ("Contact Person" clause).

title: Screening Your Employees
bodyText: Wisconsin has no statute or administrative rule requiring you to run background checks on apartment managers, maintenance workers or other employees who have access to tenants' homes, or setting how you must do it. If you do screen, general employment law applies. Wisconsin's fair employment law treats refusing to hire because of a conviction record as discrimination unless an exception applies, chiefly that the person 'has been convicted of any felony, misdemeanor, or other offense the circumstances of which substantially relate to the circumstances of the particular job' (Wis. Stat. § 111.335(3)(a)1.); judge each record against the duties of the job (for example, entering occupied units) rather than using a blanket ban. Do not ask about arrests other than pending charges: requesting an applicant or employee 'to supply information regarding any arrest record of the individual except a record of a pending charge' is employment discrimination unless a bonding requirement applies (Wis. Stat. § 111.335(2)(a)), and you may refuse to hire because of a pending charge only if its circumstances substantially relate to the job (Wis. Stat. § 111.335(2)(b)). If you use a consumer reporting agency, federal law requires a written disclosure 'in a document that consists solely of the disclosure' and the applicant's written authorization before you obtain the report (FEDERAL: 15 U.S.C. § 1681b(b)(2)(A)). Residential care apartment complexes and other licensed care settings have their own caregiver background-check rules.

title: Hunting Rights on Rented Land
bodyText:
Wisconsin has no statute or administrative rule deciding whether you or your tenant holds the hunting, fishing or trapping rights on rented land.

The trespass law lets either the owner or the occupant give permission: a person who enters land 'without the express or implied consent of the owner or occupant' (Wis. Stat. § 943.13(1m)(a)) commits trespass, and a lawful occupant who is not the title holder may post the land in the occupant's own name (Wis. Stat. § 943.13(2)(am)1.). The owner or occupant and family members may also hunt or trap certain small animals on the land without a license (Wis. Stat. § 29.337(1)).

So unless the lease reserves them, a tenant in possession can let others hunt. If you want to keep those rights, use the optional reservation clause ("Hunting, Fishing and Trapping Reserved" clause).

If you receive wildlife damage payments, the land must be kept open to hunting the damaging species: anyone who 'owns, leases or controls the land where the wildlife damage occurred shall permit hunting of the type of wild animals causing the wildlife damage on that land' (Wis. Stat. § 29.889(7m)(a)), so make sure the lease does not conflict.

title: Tenant Guest Rights
bodyText:
Wisconsin has no general statute or administrative rule giving tenants a right to have guests, visitors or suppliers, or barring a lease from limiting guests or charging for them.

The one exception is employer-provided housing: 'Any authorized occupant of employer-provided housing shall have the right to decide who may enter, confer and visit with the occupant in the housing area the occupant occupies' (Wis. Stat. § 943.13(5)).

For other rentals, reasonable guest limits are a matter for the lease ("Guest Policy" clause, "Guest Policy (14-Day Limit)" clause). Any guest fee is a non-rent charge, and you may not 'Fail to disclose, in connection with any representation of rent amount, the existence of any non-rent charges' (Wis. Admin. Code ATCP § 134.09(9)(a)3.).

A tenant may be made liable for damage by 'the tenant or the tenant’s guests or invitees' but not by others (Wis. Stat. § 704.44(7)(b)), and if the tenant, a household member or a guest engages in criminal activity listed in Wis. Stat. § 704.17(3m), you may end the tenancy on a 5-day notice with the contents that subsection requires, but not against a tenant who is the victim of the crime (Wis. Stat. § 704.17(3m)(b)1., (c); "Criminal Activity" clause).

A guest who overstays a lease limit is not a trespasser while the tenancy continues; you must first end the tenancy by proper notice (Johnson v. Blackburn, 220 Wis. 2d 260 (Ct. App. 1998), as summarized in the annotation to Wis. Stat. § 704.17).

title: Home Businesses
bodyText:
Wisconsin has no statute or administrative rule making a home business a permitted use of a rented dwelling or limiting a lease that restricts one.

The state provisions on home businesses govern building codes and land use, not leases: a 'home-based business, as defined by the department by rule' is not a 'place of employment' or a 'public building' for building-code purposes (Wis. Stat. § 101.01(11)(c), (12)(c)); the Lower St. Croix shoreland rules allow a conditional use permit for a home occupation conducted by the owner or a full-time renter (Wis. Admin. Code NR § 118.07(11)); and a municipality may not keep a licensed family child care home out of a zone where single-family homes are permitted (Wis. Stat. § 66.1017(2)).

Whether a tenant may run a business from the home is therefore up to the lease: the library's residential-use clause ("Residential Use Only" clause) bars commercial use, and you may add your own clause permitting a named business on conditions.

Any such clause should limit the tenant's repair liability to damage caused by the tenant or the tenant's guests or invitees, because a lease that makes a tenant liable for 'Property damage caused by natural disasters or by persons other than the tenant or the tenant’s guests or invitees' is void (Wis. Stat. § 704.44(7)(b)).

The tenant may never use the premises 'for any unlawful purpose' (Wis. Stat. § 704.05(3)). Local zoning, a condominium declaration or association rules may also limit home businesses.

title: No Landlord Insurance Mandate
bodyText: Wisconsin has no statute or administrative rule requiring a residential landlord to carry liability insurance, alone or as a condition of registering a rental. The Wisconsin Statutes, Administrative Code, Constitution and 2025 session laws contain none. State law also narrows what a municipality may demand: except as that subdivision allows, no city, village, town or county may require that 'a residential rental property owner register or obtain a certification or license related to owning or managing the residential rental property' (Wis. Stat. § 66.0104(2)(e)4.), and a registration may require only one name of an owner or contact person and contact details, with a one-time fee of no more than $10 per building outside a 1st class city; nor may a municipality require a landlord to communicate information to it unless state or federal law requires it or it is required of all residential property owners (Wis. Stat. § 66.0104(2)(d)2.). On that reading, a local rule making insurance a condition of renting would conflict with state law. Carrying liability insurance is still prudent, because you must exercise ordinary care toward tenants and others on the premises (Pagelsdorf v. Safeco Insurance Co. of America, 91 Wis. 2d 734 (1979)), and a lease cannot excuse your own negligence ("Lease Terms That Void the Whole Lease"). See also "Local Rental Registration".

title: No Lease-Type Parity Rule
bodyText: Wisconsin has no statute or administrative rule barring terms that are more burdensome for a month-to-month tenant than for a fixed-term tenant (or the reverse), or capping how much more rent you may charge for a month-to-month tenancy. You may price the two differently, but the rent and every non-rent charge for the option offered must be stated accurately ("Disclosing Non-Rent Charges"), and the void-lease list applies to both kinds of tenancy alike ("Lease Terms That Void the Whole Lease"). The termination rules differ by tenancy type: unless the parties have expressly agreed on another method of termination, a month-to-month tenancy ends only on at least 28 days' written notice effective at the end of a rental period (Wis. Stat. § 704.19(2), (3); "Ending a Month-to-Month Tenancy" clause), while the notice periods for a tenant's breach depend on the lease type, and a lease for more than one year may set its own breach-termination terms except for the criminal-activity rule (Wis. Stat. § 704.17(5); "Ending a Periodic Tenancy"). Milwaukee, Madison and other municipalities may have their own rules.

title: No Lease Type-Size Rule
bodyText: Wisconsin has no statute or administrative rule setting a minimum type size for a residential lease, or excluding a small-print lease from evidence. What Wisconsin does prescribe is form for particular items: the Notice of Domestic Abuse Protections must appear in the lease or an addendum in the statute's words, and deposit-withholding, entry and lien terms beyond the statutory list must be in a separate document entitled "NONSTANDARD RENTAL PROVISIONS" ("Nonstandard Rental Provisions: Deposit Withholding" clause, "Nonstandard Rental Provisions: Entry" clause). Use a readable type size anyway: written rental agreements and rules must be furnished for the tenant's inspection before the lease is entered into and before any earnest money or security deposit is accepted (Wis. Admin. Code ATCP § 134.03(1); "Showing the Lease and Rules Before Signing"). Self-storage rental agreements and manufactured home community site leases have their own form rules.

title: Drug, Gang and Disorderly House Nuisances
bodyText:
A building used to deliver, distribute or manufacture controlled substances, or used as a meeting place of a criminal gang or to facilitate its activities, is a public nuisance (Wis. Stat. § 823.113(1), (1m)(b)).

The municipality may sue to abate it and to enjoin 'every person guilty of creating or maintaining the nuisance, the owner, lessee or tenant of the building or structure where the nuisance exists and the owner of the land' (Wis. Stat. § 823.113(2)), and on a verified complaint or affidavit the court must issue a temporary injunction that can include closing the property. Before ordering closure, the court must weigh the effect on residents not named in the action, including alternative housing and any pending eviction (Wis. Stat. § 823.113(4)(d)).

If the nuisance is established, the judgment orders the property closed and sold, or razed (Wis. Stat. § 823.114(1)).

A place of prostitution or lewdness is also a nuisance that the district attorney or 'any citizen of the county' may sue to abate (Wis. Stat. § 823.10), and if the lessee is convicted of keeping the place for prostitution or the place is adjudged a nuisance, 'the lease by which such place is held is void' (Wis. Stat. § 823.16); see "Leases Voided by Illegal Use".

To protect yourself, act on a written notice from police or the district attorney that a drug or gang nuisance exists in a unit: you may then end that tenancy on a 5-day notice (Wis. Stat. § 704.17; "Drug-Free Housing Addenda", "Criminal Activity" clause). Wisconsin does not require a lease to summarize the nuisance or criminal laws.

title: Nuisance Receivership and Tenant Actions
bodyText: Two Wisconsin statutes let a court put a receiver in charge of a nuisance rental. First, if a residential property is alleged to be a nuisance, the city, village or town may apply for a receiver after at least 60 days' written notice to owners and lienholders (Wis. Stat. § 823.23(2)). The receiver may take possession, enter into and terminate tenancies, and 'charge and collect rents derived from the residential property, applying the sum of those rents to the costs incurred due to the abatement and receivership' (Wis. Stat. § 823.23(3)(a)1.). Unpaid abatement costs become a lien that, apart from tax and assessment liens and some purchase money mortgages, is 'prior and superior to all other liens, mortgages, and encumbrances' (Wis. Stat. § 823.23(6)(c)). While such an action is pending or expected, you may not raise rent, cut services, evict or refuse to renew a tenant because of it, if the tenant shows it would not have happened but for the action and also that no nuisance was found for the unit, that the tenant was found not to cause it, or that your action is not necessary to abate it; any notice you give must state its basis and the tenant's right to contest (Wis. Stat. § 823.23(4)(b), (e)). Second, if a property violates the health or safety provisions of a municipal building code or a local board of health order, tenants may petition the municipality to sue and, if it does not act within 20 days, sue directly; if the court adjudges the property a nuisance and the violation is not eliminated within 60 days after judgment, a receiver collects the rents and makes the repairs (Wis. Stat. § 254.595(1), (2), (3)), and 'The commencement of an action by a tenant under this section is not just cause for eviction' (Wis. Stat. § 254.595(8)). This does not apply to owner-occupied one- or two-family dwellings.

title: Lease With an Option to Purchase
bodyText: Wisconsin has no separate statute governing lease-option or rent-to-own contracts for a home (no non-waivable early-exercise right, special cure period or bar on forfeiting the option payment). A search of the Wisconsin Statutes, Administrative Code, Constitution and 2025 session laws found none. The library offers no purchase-option clause; if you add your own, the seller-disclosure law applies to it. An owner transferring real property by sale, exchange or land contract (unless the transfer is exempt from the real estate transfer fee) must furnish the real estate condition report 'not later than 10 days after acceptance of a contract of sale or option contract' (Wis. Stat. § 709.02(1)). If the report does not arrive in time, the prospective buyer may rescind within 2 business days after the 10-day period and get back 'any deposits or option fees paid in the transaction' (Wis. Stat. § 709.02(1)); a report received after the option contract is submitted that discloses a defect the buyer did not already know of also lets the buyer rescind in writing within 2 business days, with the option fees returned; a buyer who receives a complete report before submitting the contract may not rescind on that ground (Wis. Stat. § 709.05(1), (2), (3)). Unlike some states, Wisconsin lets the buyer waive the report: 'A buyer may waive in writing the right to receive the report required under s. 709.02' (Wis. Stat. § 709.08). Until the option is exercised the tenancy is an ordinary residential tenancy, so the lease's other terms remain subject to the void-lease list ("Lease Terms That Void the Whole Lease"); once the occupant holds under a contract of sale, the rental practices rules no longer apply (Wis. Admin. Code ATCP § 134.01(3)). Get legal advice before combining a lease and a purchase option.

title: Parking Rules and Towing Notice
bodyText:
Wisconsin has no statute or administrative rule written specifically for residential parking rules: none requires a separate parking document or heading, limits the vehicle information you may ask for, ties a parking permit to the lease term, requires the lease to state whether parking is provided, or bars changing a parking fee during the lease.

The general rental rules cover the ground: written rules, including parking rules, 'shall be furnished to prospective tenants for their inspection before a rental agreement is entered into, and before any earnest money or security deposit is accepted' (Wis. Admin. Code ATCP § 134.03(1)), and a parking fee is a non-rent charge that must be disclosed whenever you quote the rent (Wis. Admin. Code ATCP § 134.09(9)(a)3.).

The library's rules clause ("Rules and Regulations" clause) binds the tenant to a new or changed rule during the term only if the tenant agrees in writing.

There is no waiting period before towing a resident's vehicle, but the lot must be posted: on private property with clearly visible notice that it is private and that unauthorized vehicles may be immediately removed, a vehicle 'not authorized to be parked there' may be removed immediately by a towing service at your request (Wis. Stat. § 349.13(3m)(a)2., (c), (d)1.); on an unposted lot, only after a citation for illegal parking or a repossession judgment (Wis. Stat. § 349.13(3m)(b)).

Whether a resident's vehicle with expired registration is unauthorized depends on your lease, so state in the lease which vehicles are authorized ("Parking & Vehicle Requirements" clause) and follow the towing rules ("Towing From Rental Property").

title: No Pet Eviction Fact Sheet
bodyText: Wisconsin has no statute or administrative rule requiring you to give a tenant a state fact sheet or notice about pets and eviction, and none setting out what happens to a tenant's pet when a writ of restitution is executed. A search of the Wisconsin Statutes, Administrative Code, Constitution and 2025 session laws found none. If a pet is left behind after a move-out or eviction, the cautious course is to contact the tenant and a humane officer or law enforcement rather than treating the animal as abandoned property ("Caring for a Tenant's Animal", "Property After an Eviction").

title: No Plain-Language Lease Law
bodyText: Wisconsin has no plain-language or readability statute or administrative rule reaching residential leases, and none requiring a lease to be divided into captioned sections. A search of the Wisconsin Statutes, Administrative Code, Constitution and 2025 session laws found none. The consumer-protection rules that do reach every residential rental are DATCP's rental practices rules, issued under the trade-practices law with no dollar ceiling; a tenant who suffers a money loss from a violation may recover twice the loss plus costs and reasonable attorney fees ("DATCP Enforcement and Double Damages"). The Wisconsin Consumer Act's debt-collection rules do not govern a residential lease with rent payable monthly. Clear wording still matters: you may not misrepresent rent, non-rent charges or the unit to induce a rental (Wis. Admin. Code ATCP § 134.09(9)(a)), and written agreements and rules must be furnished to the prospective tenant for inspection before the lease is entered into and before any earnest money or security deposit is accepted (Wis. Admin. Code ATCP § 134.03(1); "Showing the Lease and Rules Before Signing").

title: No Consumer Restrictions Statement
bodyText: Wisconsin has no statute or administrative rule requiring a residential lease to carry a statement of consumer restrictions listing the rights the tenant gives up, offering attorney general preapproval of lease forms, or excluding high-rent leases above a dollar amount. A search of the Wisconsin Statutes, Administrative Code, Constitution and 2025 session laws found none. Wisconsin instead makes certain terms void outright, and a lease containing one is void and unenforceable in its entirety ("Lease Terms That Void the Whole Lease"). Terms that Wisconsin lets you add only with the tenant's specific agreement (deposit deductions, extra entry rights and liens) must be in a separate document entitled "NONSTANDARD RENTAL PROVISIONS" that you identify and discuss with the tenant before signing ("Nonstandard Rental Provisions: Deposit Withholding" clause, "Nonstandard Rental Provisions: Entry" clause, "No Landlord Lien on Tenant Property"). The Real Estate Examining Board approves the contract forms real estate licensees use (Wis. Admin. Code REEB § 16.03); that is a licensing rule, not a lease-content requirement for landlords.

title: What Tenants May Not Do
bodyText:
Wisconsin has no single list of prohibited tenant acts; the tenant's duties come from a few statutes, which apply unless a signed writing provides otherwise where the statute allows it.

The tenant 'can make no physical changes in the nature of the premises, including decorating, removing, altering or adding to the structures thereon, without prior consent of the landlord', and 'cannot use the premises for any unlawful purpose nor in such manner as to interfere unreasonably with use by another occupant of the same building or group of buildings' (Wis. Stat. § 704.05(3)).

A tenant who damages the premises must repair them or reimburse your reasonable cost (Wis. Stat. § 704.07(3)(a)), and must comply with any local housing code (Wis. Stat. § 704.07(3)(c)); see "Tenant Duties Under Wisconsin Law".

You may enter on advance notice at reasonable times to inspect, repair or show the unit ("Entering a Tenant's Unit").

A tenant who 'intentionally absconds without paying all current and past rent due' commits a misdemeanor (Wis. Stat. § 943.215(1)), but has a defense if the security deposit covers what is owed or if, within 5 days after vacating, the tenant pays or gives you a complete and accurate forwarding address in writing (Wis. Stat. § 943.215(2), (3)).

Lease terms describing prohibited conduct may make the tenant answer only for the tenant and the tenant's guests or invitees ("Lease Terms That Void the Whole Lease"); the library uses "No Disturbance or Nuisance" clause, "No Alterations" clause and "Damage Caused by Tenant" clause for these points.

title: Leases Voided by Illegal Use
bodyText:
Two Wisconsin nuisance statutes void a lease outright when the premises are used for a prohibited purpose.

If the lessee has been convicted of keeping the place as a place of prostitution, or the place has been adjudged a nuisance, 'the lease by which such place is held is void and the lessor shall have the same remedies for regaining possession of the premises as the lessor would have against a tenant holding over the tenant’s term' (Wis. Stat. § 823.16).

The same rule applies when the lessee is convicted of commercial gambling for operating the place as a gambling place or the place is adjudged a gambling nuisance (Wis. Stat. § 823.20(3)).

You would still recover possession through a court eviction, never by self-help ("No Self-Help Evictions").

For other illegal use, the lease is not void by statute: the tenant 'cannot use the premises for any unlawful purpose' (Wis. Stat. § 704.05(3)), and you end the tenancy by the notice routes in Wis. Stat. § 704.17, including the 5-day no-cure notice for drug-related or other listed criminal activity.

Any lease term allowing termination for a crime must be accompanied by the domestic abuse protections notice ("Notice of Domestic Abuse Protections" clause). Drug and gang house nuisances are covered in "Drug, Gang and Disorderly House Nuisances".

title: No Rent Escrow Exemption Notice
bodyText: Wisconsin has no general rent-escrow repair remedy for tenants, so there is no small-landlord exemption from one and no exemption notice to put in the lease. A search of the Wisconsin Statutes, Administrative Code, Constitution and 2025 session laws found none. The only rent escrow in Wisconsin law is court-ordered: if an owner of a rented dwelling fails to comply with a state lead hazard order, the circuit court 'may order the occupants of the affected dwelling or premises to withhold rent in escrow until the owner of the dwelling or premises complies with the order' (Wis. Stat. § 254.30(1)(b)). A tenant's general remedy for repair failures is to move out or have rent abate ("Tenant Remedies for Untenantable Conditions"), and tenants may also bring a code-violation nuisance action that leads to a receiver collecting rents ("Nuisance Receivership and Tenant Actions").

title: No Senior Housing Work Cards
bodyText: Wisconsin has no statute or administrative rule requiring work cards, permits or background screening for staff of apartments or other housing for persons 55 or older. Licensed care settings, such as residential care apartment complexes and community-based residential facilities, have their own caregiver background-check rules. If you choose to screen staff, the general employment rules apply ("Screening Your Employees").

title: Subsidized Housing Inspections
bodyText: Wisconsin has no statute or administrative rule giving subsidized housing its own eviction procedure when a tenant refuses an inspection. A search of the Wisconsin Statutes, Administrative Code, Constitution and 2025 session laws found none. The general rules apply: you may enter on advance notice of at least 12 hours and at reasonable times to inspect (Wis. Stat. § 704.05(2); Wis. Admin. Code ATCP § 134.09(2)), and that includes accompanying a program inspector. A tenant who unreasonably refuses lawful entry breaches the lease; under a lease of one year or less you may give a notice requiring the tenant to 'remedy the default or vacate the premises on or before a date at least 5 days after the giving of the notice' (Wis. Stat. § 704.17(2)(b)), with similar notices for month-to-month tenancies ("Ending a Periodic Tenancy"). In the federal Housing Choice Voucher program, the housing agency 'must inspect the unit at least biennially during assisted occupancy' (FEDERAL: 24 C.F.R. § 982.405(b)), and a voucher owner may end the tenancy during the term only on federal grounds such as 'Serious violation ... or repeated violation of the terms and conditions of the lease' (FEDERAL: 24 C.F.R. § 982.310(a)(1)). The federal family-obligations rule requires a family to allow inspections; ask the housing agency to schedule a refused inspection again before treating the refusal as a lease violation.

title: Rent Abatement in Subsidized Units
bodyText: Wisconsin has no statute or administrative rule dividing a habitability rent abatement between the tenant's share of the rent and a subsidy. A search of the Wisconsin Statutes, Administrative Code, Constitution and 2025 session laws found none. The general rule is that when a condition materially affects health or safety or substantially affects use of the unit, 'rent abates to the extent the tenant is deprived of the full normal use of the premises' (Wis. Stat. § 704.07(4)), with no special rule for assisted tenancies. In the federal Housing Choice Voucher program the subsidy side is handled separately: the agency may withhold and then must abate its housing assistance payment if you do not correct a deficiency in time, 'The PHA does not make any payments to the owner for the period of time that the payments were abated' (FEDERAL: 24 C.F.R. § 982.404(d)(4)), and you may not end the tenancy because of that withholding or abatement. The family 'is not responsible for payment of the portion of the rent to owner covered by the housing assistance payment' (FEDERAL: 24 C.F.R. § 982.310(b)(1)), so never try to recover an abated subsidy from the tenant. How a court would measure a tenant's own abatement in a voucher unit is not settled by statute; the cautious course is to apply any abatement to the tenant's share in proportion to the lost use.

title: Disclosing Tenant Information
bodyText: Wisconsin has no landlord-specific statute or administrative rule barring disclosure of information about a tenant or applicant, or setting the consent needed to share it. A search of the Wisconsin Statutes, Administrative Code, Constitution and 2025 session laws found none. The general right-of-privacy statute does apply to you: a person whose privacy is unreasonably invaded, including by 'Publicity given to a matter concerning the private life of another, of a kind highly offensive to a reasonable person' where you acted unreasonably or recklessly as to whether there was a legitimate public interest, may obtain an injunction, damages and attorney fees, though passing on information that is a matter of public record is not an invasion of privacy (Wis. Stat. § 995.50(1), (2)(am)3.). Specific rules also apply. If a tenant gives you a notification form under the state address confidentiality program, you may not refuse to use the assigned address, require the tenant to disclose the actual address, or 'intentionally disclose to another person the actual address of a program participant' (Wis. Stat. § 165.68(5)(c)). A consumer report you obtain for screening may be used only for a permissible purpose: 'A person shall not use or obtain a consumer report for any purpose unless' it is obtained for an authorized purpose (FEDERAL: 15 U.S.C. § 1681b(f)); see "Federal Notice When a Screening Report Leads to a Denial". When a prospective landlord or the applicant asks you for a reference about a former tenant, you are 'presumed to be acting in good faith' and immune from civil liability unless it is shown by clear and convincing evidence that you knowingly gave false information or acted maliciously (Wis. Stat. § 895.489(2)). If you keep applicants' Social Security, driver's license or financial account numbers, the security-breach notice law may apply ("Tenant Records and Data Security"). Share tenant information only as the law requires or with the tenant's written consent, and keep it no longer than you need it.

title: Fire Losses and Insurance Claims
bodyText: Wisconsin has no statute protecting a tenant from suit by you or your insurer for a fire the tenant accidentally causes, and none governing insurance claims, subrogation or mutual waivers between landlord and tenant. A search of the Wisconsin Statutes, Administrative Code, Constitution and 2025 session laws found none. The ordinary rule applies: if the premises are damaged 'due to the acts or inaction of the tenant', the tenant must repair or reimburse your reasonable cost (Wis. Stat. § 704.07(3)(a)), and that duty applies whether or not your insurer pays first (Bennett v. West Bend Mutual Insurance Co., 200 Wis. 2d 313 (Ct. App. 1996), as summarized in the annotation to Wis. Stat. § 704.07; opinion not read). A lease may not make the tenant liable for 'Property damage caused by natural disasters or by persons other than the tenant or the tenant’s guests or invitees' (Wis. Stat. § 704.44(7)(b)). The library offers no mutual waiver of insured losses: you may give up your own claims against the tenant, but a waiver by the tenant of claims against you would make the lease state that you are not liable for your own negligence, which voids the whole agreement (Wis. Stat. § 704.44(6); "Lease Terms That Void the Whole Lease"). If you want your own clause limited to your side (for example, a waiver of your insurer's subrogation against the tenant), check it against your policy first. You may require renter's insurance ("Requiring Renter's Insurance", "Tenant's Property & Renter's Insurance" clause).

title: Tenant Portals
bodyText: Wisconsin has no statute or administrative rule written for tenant portals, requiring or forbidding online rent payment, or capping portal fees. A search of the Wisconsin Statutes, Administrative Code, Constitution and 2025 session laws found none. Three rules shape a portal term. First, a lease may let you deliver four things electronically: a copy of the lease and related documents, the security deposit and its accounting, pre-lease promises to clean or repair, and advance notice of entry (Wis. Stat. § 704.10); see "Electronic Delivery of Documents" clause. Second, Wisconsin's electronic transactions law applies only between parties who have agreed to transact electronically, and 'A party that agrees to conduct a transaction by electronic means may refuse to conduct other transactions by electronic means. The right granted by this subsection may not be waived by agreement' (Wis. Stat. § 137.13(3)), so a lease cannot make portal-only signatures or records permanent. Third, that law does not cover notices of default, eviction or the right to cure under a rental agreement for a primary residence (Wis. Stat. § 137.12(2r)(b)), so notices to pay or vacate and other termination notices must be given by a method in Wis. Stat. § 704.21 ("How to Serve a Notice"). For payment, list the methods you accept ("Acceptable Forms of Payment" clause), keep a non-electronic method available, and disclose any portal or convenience fee as a non-rent charge (Wis. Admin. Code ATCP § 134.09(9)(a)3.).

title: Tenant Records and Data Security
bodyText: Wisconsin has no statute or administrative rule requiring a landlord to keep a rent ledger or give a tenant a payment history on request, and none requiring a written information security program. A search of the Wisconsin Statutes, Administrative Code, Constitution and 2025 session laws found none. The record duties that do exist are specific: a written receipt for any earnest money or security deposit, and for rent paid in cash (Wis. Admin. Code ATCP § 134.03(2)); a copy of any consumer credit report or background check you charge an applicant for (Wis. Stat. § 704.085); and the security deposit accounting when the tenant leaves ("Return of Security Deposit" clause). A real estate firm managing rentals must keep trust account ledgers for each landlord-tenant transaction (Wis. Admin. Code REEB § 18.13). If your business is not an individual (for example, an LLC or corporation) and it keeps applicants' or tenants' names together with unencrypted Social Security numbers, driver's license or state identification numbers, financial account numbers, DNA profiles or biometric data such as fingerprints, the breach-notice law applies: if it learns that someone unauthorized has acquired that information, it must make reasonable efforts to notify each person within a reasonable time, not more than 45 days, unless there is no material risk of identity theft or fraud or the data was acquired in good faith by your own employee or agent for a lawful business purpose (Wis. Stat. § 134.98(1)(b), (2)(cm), (3)(a)). Anyone who keeps consumer report information for a business purpose must dispose of it by 'taking reasonable measures to protect against unauthorized access to or use of the information in connection with its disposal' (FEDERAL: 16 C.F.R. § 682.3(a)), for example by shredding.

title: Tenant Organizing
bodyText: Wisconsin protects tenant organizing through its retaliation rule. You may not end a tenancy, refuse to renew a lease or constructively evict a tenant (for example by cutting heat, water or electricity) in retaliation because the tenant has 'Joined or attempted to organize a tenant’s union or association' (Wis. Admin. Code ATCP § 134.09(5)(b)), or because the tenant asserted any right given to tenants by state or local law (Wis. Admin. Code ATCP § 134.09(5)(c)). The retaliation statute also bars raising rent, decreasing services, suing for possession or refusing to renew because a tenant exercised 'a legal right relating to residential tenancies' (Wis. Stat. § 704.45(1)(c)); see "Retaliation". Wisconsin has no statute or administrative rule giving tenants a right to meet in common areas, post or hand out literature, or have organizers enter the building. A search of the Wisconsin Statutes, Administrative Code, Constitution and 2025 session laws found none. Do not put a lease term in your rules that bars or penalizes tenant association activity, and apply common-area rules evenly. In employer-provided housing, a union representative may confer with an employee in the employee's living quarters with the employee occupants' consent (Wis. Stat. § 943.13(4)).

title: No Rent-Cap Exemption Notice
bodyText: Wisconsin has no statewide rent cap or just-cause eviction statute, so there is no exemption from one and no exemption notice to put in a lease. A search of the Wisconsin Statutes, Administrative Code, Constitution and 2025 session laws found none. Local governments may not fill the gap: 'No city, village, town or county may regulate the amount of rent or fees charged for the use of a residential rental dwelling unit' (Wis. Stat. § 66.1015(1)); see "No Local Rent Control in Wisconsin". Rent limits can still come from your own agreements, such as a subsidy or housing-authority contract (Wis. Stat. § 66.1015(2)). Manufactured home community site rentals are the one place Wisconsin requires grounds to end or refuse to renew a tenancy ("No Just-Cause Requirement").

title: No Tenant Protection Act Notice
bodyText: Wisconsin has no statewide rent-cap or just-cause statute and therefore no required lease notice telling the tenant the property is covered by one ("No Rent-Cap Exemption Notice", "No Local Rent Control in Wisconsin"). A search of the Wisconsin Statutes, Administrative Code, Constitution and 2025 session laws found none. Wisconsin also gives tenants no general right of first refusal or opportunity to purchase when you sell a rental building. The one exception is a conversion to condominium: you must give each tenant prior written notice, and 'During the 60-day period immediately following the date of delivery of the notice a tenant has the first right to purchase the unit, if the unit is offered for sale at any time during that period' (Wis. Stat. § 703.08(1)); for 120 days the tenant may not be required to vacate unless the tenant breaches the lease or fails to pay rent, and the tenant may waive these rights in writing (Wis. Stat. § 703.08(2), (3)). See "Condominium Conversions".

title: No Tenant-Protection Sunset
bodyText: Wisconsin's core residential tenancy law (chapter 704 of the statutes and DATCP's rental practices rules) is not on a dated repeal clock, and Wisconsin has no statewide rent-cap or just-cause statute that could expire. A search of the Wisconsin Statutes, Administrative Code, Constitution and 2025 session laws found no sunset provision in these tenant-protection laws. What does change on fixed dates are particular amendments that take effect later, such as the small-claims dollar limits that change on January 1, 2027 under 2025 Wis. Act 105 (eviction actions themselves use small claims regardless of the rent claimed); the library notes those dates in the rows they affect.

title: No Lease Translation Duty
bodyText: Wisconsin has no statute or administrative rule requiring a residential lease, or any notice in it, to be translated or given in a language other than English, even when you advertise or negotiate in another language. A search of the Wisconsin Statutes, Administrative Code, Constitution and 2025 session laws found none. Wisconsin's language rules reach other transactions: a merchant who regularly uses another language must give the Consumer Act's cancellation notice in that language as well (Wis. Stat. § 423.203(2)), and a home improvement contract negotiated primarily in another language must be written in both languages (Wis. Admin. Code ATCP § 110.05), but neither governs a residential lease. If you negotiate in another language, giving the tenant a translation (while signing the English lease) helps show the tenant understood the terms, including any NONSTANDARD RENTAL PROVISIONS you must identify and discuss before signing ("Nonstandard Rental Provisions: Deposit Withholding" clause).

title: No Truth-in-Renting Statement
bodyText: Wisconsin has no truth-in-renting statute and no requirement that you give tenants a state statement or guide to their rights with the lease. A search of the Wisconsin Statutes, Administrative Code, Constitution and 2025 session laws found none. Wisconsin protects tenants against unfair lease terms in a different way: listed terms make the whole lease void and unenforceable ("Lease Terms That Void the Whole Lease"), and the specific notices Wisconsin does require are the Notice of Domestic Abuse Protections in every lease, the check-in sheet at move-in ("Check-in and Preexisting Damage" clause), and the pre-signing disclosures of the landlord's identity, code violations, habitability conditions and utility charges ("Wisconsin Disclosure Checklist").

title: No Unbundled Parking Rule
bodyText: Wisconsin has no statute or administrative rule requiring you to rent parking separately from the dwelling, or regulating parking offered as a separate charge. A search of the Wisconsin Statutes, Administrative Code, Constitution and 2025 session laws found none. If you charge for parking separately, it is a non-rent charge, and you may not 'Fail to disclose, in connection with any representation of rent amount, the existence of any non-rent charges which will increase the total amount payable by the tenant during tenancy' (Wis. Admin. Code ATCP § 134.09(9)(a)3.). State the parking charge, the space and the terms in the lease or a signed parking addendum; the library's parking clauses ("Parking" clause, "Assigned Parking Space(s)" clause) cover a space provided with the unit. Whether an unpaid separate parking fee can support a 5-day notice to pay rent or vacate is not settled by the statutes; the cautious course is to treat it as a breach of the lease rather than as unpaid rent ("Late Fees in a Nonpayment Notice").

title: Leasing as a Life Tenant
bodyText: If you hold the property only for your life or someone else’s (a life estate) and lease it, the lease cannot give the tenant more than you hold: a conveyance by 'a tenant for life or years purporting to grant a greater estate than the tenant possessed or could lawfully convey' passes 'all the estate which such tenant could lawfully convey' (Wis. Stat. § 710.07). When the measuring life ends, the tenant who stays is liable to the owner of the remainder for the reasonable rental value (Wis. Stat. § 704.40(1)). The remainder owner can remove the tenant only lawfully, including by eviction: a tenant with no lease for a term after a periodic termination notice under Wis. Stat. § 704.19, and a tenant with a lease for a term 'upon termination of the lease or one year after written notice to the occupant given in the manner provided by s. 704.21 whichever occurs first, except that a farm tenancy can be terminated only at the end of a rental year' (Wis. Stat. § 704.40(2)(b)). The tenant must promptly answer a written demand describing the nature of the tenant’s possession, or may be treated as a month-to-month tenant (Wis. Stat. § 704.40(3)). The library offers no life-estate clause; if you lease as a life tenant, tell the prospective tenant before signing, since you may not misrepresent the characteristics of a unit to induce a rental (Wis. Admin. Code ATCP § 134.09(9)(a)1.), or have the remainder owners join in the lease, and get legal advice.

title: EV Chargers at Move-Out
bodyText: Wisconsin has no statute or administrative rule on what happens to a tenant's electric vehicle charger when the tenancy ends, and no right for a tenant to install one ("Electric Vehicle Charging"). A search of the Wisconsin Statutes, Administrative Code, Constitution and 2025 session laws found none. The general rules apply. A tenant may make no physical changes to the premises without your prior consent (Wis. Stat. § 704.05(3)). Unless a signed writing says otherwise, 'the tenant may remove any fixtures installed by the tenant if the tenant either restores the premises to their condition prior to the installation or pays to the landlord the cost of such restoration' (Wis. Stat. § 704.05(4)). Anything the tenant leaves behind falls under the abandoned-property rules ("Handling of Property Left Behind" clause). If you allow a charger, agree in writing before installation whether it stays or goes, who restores the wiring, and who pays; a tenant can be charged only for damage caused by the tenant or the tenant's guests or invitees ("Lease Terms That Void the Whole Lease").

title: Rules for EV Chargers You Provide
bodyText: If you provide an electric vehicle charger at a rental property, several Wisconsin rules may apply, though none requires you to provide one and no state building or energy code provision found requires EV-ready parking ("Electric Vehicle Charging"). Utility status: a person who supplies electricity through its own charging station is not a public utility if the fee is 'based on the amount of kilowatt-hours of electricity that the user consumes' (Wis. Stat. § 196.01(5)(b)8.b.), the person is a retail customer of the utility or cooperative serving it, all the electricity comes from that provider, and the person does not otherwise provide electricity to the public (Wis. Stat. § 196.01(5)(b)8.). Tax and registration: Wisconsin taxes electricity delivered by Level 3 chargers, and by Level 1 and Level 2 chargers installed on or after March 22, 2024, at 3 cents per kilowatt-hour, collected by a registered operator (Wis. Stat. § 77.9972(1)); but 'No tax under this section applies to electricity delivered or placed by any charger of an electric vehicle charging station located at a residence' (Wis. Stat. § 77.9972(1)(b)), and no registration is required for a station located at a residence (Wis. Stat. § 77.9971(2)). Weights and measures: from July 1, 2026, commercial electric vehicle supply equipment must meet NIST Handbook 44 accuracy tolerances (with a transition for DC systems installed before July 1, 2026) and be labeled under the federal alternative-fuel labeling rule (Wis. Admin. Code ATCP § 92.70, Wis. Admin. Code ATCP § 92.75). Whether a charger serving an apartment building is located at a residence for the tax (Wis. Stat. § 77.9972(1)(b)), and whether a charger used only by tenants is a commercial device (Wis. Admin. Code ATCP § 92.01(5m)), are not settled by the text; ask the Department of Revenue and DATCP before charging tenants. Any charging fee is a non-rent charge that must be disclosed (Wis. Admin. Code ATCP § 134.09(9)(a)3.).

title: Shared EV Chargers
bodyText: Wisconsin has no statute or administrative rule on electric vehicle chargers in shared parking areas of rental property: none requires you to provide them, gives a tenant a right to install one in a common area, or regulates reserving a charging space or allocating its costs. A search of the Wisconsin Statutes, Administrative Code, Constitution and 2025 session laws found none. If you offer shared chargers, set the rules in writing before the lease is signed ("Rules and Regulations" clause), disclose any charging or space fee as a non-rent charge (Wis. Admin.
