Code ATCP § 134.09(9)(a)3.), and follow the utility, tax and weights-and-measures rules for chargers you provide ("Rules for EV Chargers You Provide"): in particular, charge by the kilowatt-hour if you want to stay outside the definition of a public utility (Wis. Stat. § 196.01(5)(b)8.). Tenants may be held responsible only for damage they or their guests or invitees cause ("Lease Terms That Void the Whole Lease").

title: Excluding Appliances
bodyText:
Some states let a lease exclude appliances left in a unit from what the landlord supplies and maintains. The library does not offer that clause for Wisconsin.

Wisconsin has no statute or administrative rule allowing such an exclusion or presuming that appliances present are landlord-supplied.

Instead, the 'premises' you lease include 'any personal property furnished with the realty' (Wis. Stat. § 704.01(3)), and unless a local housing code applies you must 'repair or replace any plumbing, electrical wiring, machinery, or equipment furnished with the premises and no longer in reasonable working condition' (Wis. Stat. § 704.07(2)(a)4.).

That duty cannot be waived ('An agreement to waive the requirements of this section in a residential tenancy, including an agreement in a rental agreement, is void' (Wis. Stat. § 704.07(1))), and a lease that waives your duty to maintain the premises is void in its entirety (Wis. Stat. § 704.44(8)).

A clause declaring an appliance you leave in the unit "not included" therefore risks the whole lease. List what you furnish ("Appliances & Equipment Included" clause); if you do not want to supply an appliance, remove it before the tenancy begins. Appliances the tenant brings are the tenant's property and need no clause.

You may add your own clause on this subject, but have it reviewed against Wis. Stat. § 704.07 and Wis. Stat. § 704.44 first.

title: Habitability Rules Wisconsin Does Not Have
bodyText: Several habitability rules found in other states have no Wisconsin counterpart. (1) No statutory list of imminently dangerous conditions that triggers special tenant remedies. The nearest lists are the conditions you know of or could find by reasonable inspection and must disclose before entering into the lease or accepting any earnest money or security deposit, such as no hot or cold running water or heating that cannot keep all living areas at 67 degrees Fahrenheit (Wis. Admin. Code ATCP § 134.04(2)(b); "Code Violations and Habitability Conditions" clause), and the same conditions plus missing detectors, rodent or insect infestation and excessive mold, which, where they violate a local ordinance, count as a 'Habitability violation' for local rental inspection programs (Wis. Stat. § 66.0104(1)(ah)); such a program may give less than 30 days to correct one only 'if the violation exposes a tenant to imminent danger' (Wis. Stat. § 66.0104(2)(e)1m.). The tenant’s remedies turn instead on whether a condition makes the unit untenantable or materially affects health or safety ("When a Repair Problem Is Serious Enough"). (2) No duty to provide air conditioning or cooling. If you supply it, you must keep the equipment in a reasonable state of repair (Wis. Stat. § 704.07(2)(a)2.; "No Tenant Cooling-Device Right"). (3) No minimum indoor temperature you must keep a unit at. You must disclose, before entering into the lease or accepting any earnest money or security deposit, any heating that is unsafe or cannot maintain 67 degrees Fahrenheit in all living areas (Wis. Admin. Code ATCP § 134.04(2)(b)2.), and you must keep heating equipment in repair if you agreed to supply heat. (4) No presumption that a code violation or a repair delay proves a breach ("No Habitability Presumptions"). The nearest rule is for lead: failing to comply with a lead hazard reduction order on time 'shall be prima facie evidence of negligence' in a later injury suit (Wis. Stat. § 254.166(2m)). (5) No right for a tenant to withhold rent or pay it into escrow on the tenant’s own. A tenant who stays in an untenantable unit pays reduced rent but may not withhold all of it (Wis. Stat. § 704.07(4); "Tenant Remedies for Untenantable Conditions"). The only escrow is court-ordered: if an owner fails to comply with a state lead hazard order, the court 'may order the occupants of the affected dwelling or premises to withhold rent in escrow until the owner of the dwelling or premises complies with the order' (Wis. Stat. § 254.30(1)(b); "Tenant Remedies When You Breach"). (6) No general repair deadline: you must repair promptly, or the tenant of an untenantable unit may move out (Wis. Stat. § 704.07(4)). Fixed periods apply only to particular items: 5 days after written notice to fix a smoke or carbon monoxide detector ("Smoke and Carbon Monoxide Detectors"); 5 days to reduce an imminent lead hazard and 30 days for other lead hazards under a health department order (Wis. Stat. § 254.166(2m)); and a correction period of at least 30 days, or less for imminent danger, in a local rental inspection program (Wis. Stat. § 66.0104(2)(e)1m.). (7) No duty to provide or pay for alternative housing during repairs ("Alternate Housing During Repairs"). (8) Unlike some states, Wisconsin does bar renting condemned units: you may not rent or advertise premises that have been placarded and condemned, or on which a notice of intent to condemn or a raze order has been received, until the required repairs are complete (Wis. Admin. Code ATCP § 134.09(1); "Condemned Premises", "Demanding Rent for a Unit With Code Problems"). (9) Wisconsin also has code-enforcement receivership: a municipality, or a tenant if the municipality does not sue within 20 days after the tenant’s petition, may have a building that violates health or safety codes declared a nuisance, and if the owner does not fix it within 60 days a court-appointed receiver collects the rents and makes the repairs (Wis. Stat. § 254.595; Wis. Stat. § 823.23; "Code Orders and Nuisance Receivership"). (10) No small-landlord exemption from tenant remedies based on how many units you own. The exemptions turn on the building: the tenant nuisance action does not apply to owner-occupied one- or two-family dwellings (Wis. Stat. § 254.595(7); "Small-Landlord Exemptions and Unit Thresholds"). Your repair duties themselves cannot be waived ("Repair Duties Cannot Be Waived"). Milwaukee, Madison and other municipalities may have their own rules; a local rent-abatement ordinance may allow abatement only for conditions that materially affect health or safety or substantially affect use and occupancy (Wis. Stat. § 704.07(5)).

title: Other Rules Wisconsin Does Not Have
bodyText: Several rules found in other states do not exist in Wisconsin. (1) No statute bans renting the same unit to two tenants for the same period or gives a special remedy for it; instead, 'No landlord shall fail to deliver possession of the dwelling unit to the tenant at the time agreed upon in the rental agreement, except where the landlord is unable to deliver possession because of circumstances beyond the landlord’s control' (Wis. Admin. Code ATCP § 134.09(6)), and a tenant who loses money because of a violation can sue for twice the loss ("Renting the Same Unit Twice", "Possession Delay" clause, "DATCP Enforcement and Double Damages"). (2) No statute makes your compliance with the smoke or carbon monoxide detector rules inadmissible in an injury case or limits what an insurer may do because of it. The only liability rule is narrow and covers carbon monoxide detectors: 'The owner of a dwelling is not liable for damages resulting from any of the following' (Wis. Stat. § 101.647(5)), namely a false alarm from a detector you reasonably maintained, or a failure caused by someone else’s tampering, removal or destruction or by a faulty detector you reasonably maintained; the same rule covers buildings of 3 or more units (Wis. Stat. § 101.149(3)(c)). Smoke detectors have no such rule, and an annotation reports that violating the smoke detector statute for one- and two-family dwellings is negligence per se (Johnson v. Blackburn, 220 Wis. 2d 260 (Ct. App. 1998), as summarized in the annotation to Wis. Stat. § 101.645). Keep the detectors installed and fix one within 5 days of written notice ("Smoke and Carbon Monoxide Detectors", "Smoke and Carbon Monoxide Detectors" clause). (3) No statute gives you a special right to end an ordinary residential lease because the rental application was false. Make accuracy a lease term ("Accuracy of Rental Application" clause), so a material falsehood is a breach you handle with the ordinary breach notices (Wis. Stat. § 704.17; "Notices for Other Lease Violations"). The one statutory ground is for manufactured home community sites, where a tenancy may be ended for 'Material misrepresentation in the application for tenancy or failure to meet any nondiscriminatory application criteria' (Wis. Stat. § 710.15(5m)(j), as amended by 2025 Wis. Act 67 (AB 424), in effect since December 11, 2025); those site rentals are outside this library ("Which Rentals Wisconsin's Rules Cover"). (4) No statute bans or caps a convenience or processing fee for a particular way of paying rent. If you charge one, disclose it: you may not, to induce a rental, 'Fail to disclose, in connection with any representation of rent amount, the existence of any non-rent charges which will increase the total amount payable by the tenant during tenancy' (Wis. Admin. Code ATCP § 134.09(9)(a)3.; "Disclosing Non-Rent Charges"). List the payment methods you accept ("Acceptable Forms of Payment" clause, "Tenant Portals"), and give a written receipt for rent paid in cash (Wis. Admin. Code ATCP § 134.03(2)(b); "Receipts for Deposits and Cash Rent"). Milwaukee, Madison and other municipalities may have their own rules.

title: Squatters, Receipts and Registration
bodyText: Four things landlords ask about. (1) There is no squatter-specific removal procedure. You remove anyone not entitled to be there through an eviction action, which may be brought 'to remove therefrom any person who is not entitled to either the possession or occupancy of such real property' (Wis. Stat. § 799.40(1)). Criminal trespass to a dwelling covers a person who enters or remains without consent 'under circumstances tending to create or provoke a breach of the peace' (Wis. Stat. § 943.14(2)), and every law enforcement agency’s written policy must require an officer who has probable cause to arrest a person for that crime 'to remove the person from a dwelling' (Wis. Stat. § 175.403(2)); whether that applies is for the police. Hold a trespasser’s leftover belongings for 7 days before disposing of them (Wis. Stat. § 704.055(2)(a)), and never use self-help ("Squatters and Unauthorized Occupants", "No Self-Help Evictions"). (2) Wisconsin does require a receipt for cash rent: 'If a tenant pays rent in cash, the landlord upon receiving the cash payment shall provide the tenant with a written receipt stating the nature and amount of the payment' (Wis. Admin. Code ATCP § 134.03(2)(b)); earnest money and security deposits need a receipt too, unless paid by a check marked with its purpose (Wis. Admin. Code ATCP § 134.03(2)(a); "Receipts for Deposits and Cash Rent"). (3) No state statute makes landlord registration or a rental license a condition of filing or winning an eviction. State law also limits local programs: a municipality may require only a simple registration listing one owner or contact person and how to reach them, and may not otherwise require that a rental unit or owner be certified, registered or licensed (Wis. Stat. § 66.0104(2)(e)4.; "Local Rental Registration"). (4) General business law can still stop an eviction if you own through an out-of-state entity. An out-of-state limited liability company 'doing business in this state may not maintain an action or proceeding in this state unless it has registered to do business in this state' (Wis. Stat. § 183.0902(2)), and an out-of-state corporation that needs a certificate of authority 'may not maintain a proceeding in any court in this state until it obtains a certificate of authority' (Wis. Stat. § 180.1502(1)). Its leases and title stay valid and it may defend a suit, but it owes the missed fees plus the lesser of half that amount or $5,000 for each year (Wis. Stat. § 183.0902(3), (6); Wis. Stat. § 180.1502(4), (5)). 'Owning, without more, property' is not doing business (Wis. Stat. § 183.0905(1)(j); Wis. Stat. § 180.1501(2)(i)); whether renting it out is depends on the facts and on case law, so register before you file ("Who May Appear in Court for an LLC or Corporation Landlord", "Nonresident Landlords Must Name a Wisconsin Agent"). Wisconsin has no general assumed-name filing that bars suing. Milwaukee, Madison and other municipalities may have their own rules.

title: Checks Marked 'Paid in Full'
bodyText: Wisconsin follows the Uniform Commercial Code rule on checks marked 'paid in full' (Wis. Stat. § 403.311). If a tenant, or anyone else you have a claim against, gives you a check or other payment instrument for less than you claim, with a conspicuous statement, on the check or in a writing with it, that it is offered in full satisfaction of the claim, then cashing it settles your whole claim, the unpaid balance included. This applies only when the payment was offered in good faith and the amount was not yet fixed or was subject to a genuine (bona fide) dispute, so writing 'paid in full' on a short check for rent nobody disputes does not by itself settle the rent owed. Writing 'under protest' or 'without prejudice' when you endorse the check does not save the balance: the rule on reserving your rights does not apply to an accord and satisfaction (Wis. Stat. § 401.308(2)). There are two ways out. If you are an organization (for example an LLC) and, within a reasonable time before the check, sent the tenant a conspicuous statement that communications about disputed debts, including checks offered in full satisfaction, must go to a named person, office or place, the claim is not settled if the check or the writing with it was not received there. And whether or not you are an organization, the claim is not settled if you offer to repay the amount of the check within 90 days after it is paid; an organization that sent the statement just described cannot use this second way out. Neither way out works if you, or your agent responsible for the disputed debt, knew within a reasonable time before the check was collected that it was offered in full satisfaction. The cautious course: don't cash a check for less than you claim that is marked as payment in full of a disputed amount; return it, and if one is cashed by mistake, offer the money back within 90 days.

title: Duty of Good Faith
bodyText: Wisconsin's landlord-tenant statutes impose no general duty of good faith of the kind in the Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act (Wis. Stat. ch. 704 searched); good faith appears only in specific rules. Courts in many states read a covenant of good faith and fair dealing into every contract, a lease included; whether and how Wisconsin's courts do is case law, so act as if the duty applies. In practice: give notices, enter, handle the deposit, enforce lease terms and end a tenancy honestly and for the purpose the law or the lease gives you the right, not as a pretext.
